title: AI Security: A Study Guide
text:
Contents
A source-grounded guide to defining, testing, and managing the security of AI systems. It uses a reusable organization record across internal and external models, data paths, retrieval, actions, platform operations, and organizational governance.
crumbs: AI Security: A Study Guide

title: AI Security: A Study Guide
text:
Part I: Defining the system and threat
The opening part gives both audiences a common language. Readers first identify what an AI system contains, then explain which capabilities and consequences matter. Managers need enough architecture to ask precise questions; technical readers need enough organizational context to understand why a boundary exists.

Mapping the system
This chapter establishes the components, people, identities, data, operators, permissions, and records that make up the AI system before it discusses attacks.
Defining the threat
Connect a stated attacker capability to an unwanted event, business consequence, control, observable test, remaining risk, and accountable decision.



Part II: Protecting data and learned behavior
This part separates failures in data collection, changes to learned behavior, disclosure through queries, and evasion of model decisions. That separation explains why a training defense may not help a retrieval system, and why a private training process does not replace application access controls.

Controlling data use
This chapter establishes which organizational data may enter each AI path, which party receives it, and what evidence can show that retention and deletion rules work.
Protecting training
This chapter examines how a party that can influence training data, labels, weights, or adaptation records can change learned behavior, and how the organization detects and recovers from that change.
Limiting query disclosure
This chapter separates disclosure that occurs through normal application data handling from disclosure inferred or extracted through model queries, then matches each mechanism to evidence and limits.
Resisting adversarial inputs
This chapter defines adversarial-input claims precisely enough to distinguish a measured weakness from a broad claim that a model or system is generally insecure.



Part III: Securing the platform and runtime
An AI service still depends on ordinary software and privileged infrastructure. This part moves from acquired artifacts to the compute boundary and then to the runtime that schedules and executes work. It prepares readers to investigate an exposed runtime service without assuming that exposure proves compromise.

Admitting trusted components
This chapter treats every acquired dataset, model, adapter, package, container, and skill as a component that needs a stated intake decision before it reaches a trusted environment.
Limiting platform access
This chapter identifies the infrastructure trust that remains when an organization runs workloads in its own environment, a cloud environment, or a provider-managed environment.
Containing runtime exposure
This chapter follows the identities, interfaces, networks, secrets, and resource limits that determine whether a running AI workload can be reached or abused.



Part IV: Controlling AI influence and authority
This part follows four decisions that expand an application’s risk: how untrusted text can affect model behavior, which documents may enter model context, which proposed actions receive authority, and where approved actions execute. Each chapter adds one capability while retaining the earlier system and threat records.

Separating data from instructions
This chapter separates instructions from the data that an organization allows a model to read, so that hostile text cannot silently become authority.
Controlling retrieved context
This chapter shows why retrieval is an authorization and evidence problem as well as a search problem, from document ingestion through deletion and permission change.
Authorizing agent actions
This chapter keeps a model-generated proposal separate from the user, service, and policy decisions that authorize a consequential action.
Confining agent environments
This chapter applies the same authority analysis to browser, coding, and multimodal environments where a model can encounter untrusted instructions and stronger capabilities.



Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure
Readers now know enough architecture and attack mechanisms to judge defenses. This part asks what evidence supports release, what remains observable after deployment, and how a team recovers when prevention fails.

Deciding whether to release
This chapter defines the evidence needed to release or change a system, including a reproducible test scope, adversarial conditions, uncertainty, and a decision owner.
Keeping the live system in bounds
This chapter turns the controls and failure paths already identified into runtime records, alerts, limits, and response routes that remain useful after release.
Recovering from AI incidents
This chapter treats an AI incident as an evidence and recovery problem, distinguishing model error, policy failure, hostile content, account compromise, and infrastructure compromise.



Part VI: Assessing AI in cyber work
The same methods that help a defender analyze information can help an attacker. This part separates capability claims, observed misuse, and measured defensive value. It also treats a security assistant as an AI system requiring the controls already taught.

Assessing AI-assisted harm
This chapter assesses claims about AI-assisted harm by separating demonstrated capability, observed use, prevalence, and the defensive controls justified by the evidence.
Using AI safely in defense
This chapter applies the book’s safeguards to a security team’s own AI assistant, keeping human judgment and action authority visible while measuring useful work.
Choosing a viable deployment
This chapter compares external, managed, and internal model choices only after the organization has fixed the task, data access, quality target, action limits, and full operating cost.



Part VII: Governing organizational AI use
This part translates technical evidence into repeatable organizational decisions. It gives managers concrete deliverables while showing engineers how their tests and logs support those decisions.

Adopting AI safely
This chapter turns an organization’s scattered AI use into an inventory, acceptable-use rules, account and connector controls, and practical employee support.
Assigning responsibility
This chapter assigns responsibilities across developers, providers, deployers, data owners, purchasers, and affected people, using system evidence rather than generic assurances.
Steering security investment
This chapter gives executives and the CSO a way to prioritize security investment with measures, evidence, responsible owners, review dates, and explicit residual-risk decisions.



Part VIII: Applying the method when systems change
The final part tests whether readers can transfer the method to a new setting. Domain chapters should reuse the established concepts and add only the assumptions that change the analysis.

Adapting controls to the setting
This chapter transfers the reference frame to sector settings by stating which assets, duties, permissions, and consequences change before selecting controls.
Extending security when assumptions change
This chapter extends the method when physical access, participant trust, persistence, delegated authority, or systemic uncertainty invalidate earlier assumptions.
Defending a whole-system decision
This capstone requires a defensible whole-system decision that connects architecture, data, model and platform controls, authority, assurance, recovery, cost, and accountability.

title: 1  Mapping the system
text:
1.1 The request and the system boundary
An employee sees one text box. Behind it, the organization depends on identity services and document stores. An application connects those services to models, external providers, action services, logs, and people. A useful security review identifies that larger system before it can make a useful claim about risk.
This chapter starts with an organization that operates an assistant application and uses an external model for inference. The application may provide chat or document retrieval. It can also propose actions or pass confirmed operations to services that enforce policy. Later chapters also examine supplier-operated assistants, managed platforms, and organization-operated models. The book treats every arrangement as a mix of direct control, supplier responsibility, and facts that require evidence.
The chapter produces a system record that identifies components, operators, identities, data, transfers, permissions, possible state changes, and available evidence. Chapter 2 uses that record without changing its assumptions.
Consider an authenticated employee using an internal assistant to find the approval required for a supplier contract. The answer may depend on private policy documents. A later configuration may let the assistant prepare a purchase request, but a separate service must decide whether the operation is authorized.
The visible request does not tell us which components receive the question, which records enter the model context, or which service can change business state. The map separates the visible model, its application, and the complete operational system:
This book uses AI system for the complete set of components and parties whose behavior matters to the decision under review. The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework treats AI risk across lifecycle stages and among several actors.2 International secure-development guidance also covers systems assembled from internal components, hosted models, external APIs, and several providers.3
The relevant boundary depends on the decision. A parser unit test may examine one function. A release decision for the assistant includes the application, model service, connected records, identities, suppliers, action services, monitoring, and response process.
For this chapter, the decision is whether the organization can allow employees to use the assistant for policy questions and limited business-action proposals. NIST AI RMF MAP 1.1 calls for context such as intended purpose, users, deployment setting, assumptions, limits, and possible impacts.4
The baseline fixes these facts:
These assumptions create a baseline. A later chapter may change one operator, data path, attacker capability, or application capability while keeping the remaining facts fixed.

title: 1  Mapping the system
text:
Table 1.1: Three nested objects used throughout the book.










Object
What it contains
Question it answers




Model
Parameters and an inference procedure that convert input context into scores, labels, or generated tokens.
What behavior can this learned component produce from its input?


AI application
Software that authenticates users, assembles context, calls a model, validates output, and may request an action.
What data and capabilities does the product expose to the model and user?


Operational AI system
The application and model plus people, policies, records, identities, infrastructure, suppliers, monitoring, and response.
Which components and decisions keep the task authorized and recoverable?











The organization operates identity, application, retrieval, logging, and business-action services.
An external provider operates model inference.
An employee may read approved policy and assigned customer or supplier records. The employee may not read payroll or another business unit’s restricted records.
The provider receives only the request and context that the application sends. Direct access to the document store or action service is outside this setup.
A generated proposal cannot change business state. An authenticated user and the action service must pass current policy checks.
Provider retention, model-improvement use, processing region, and provider logs remain supplier facts that require evidence.

title: 1  Mapping the system
section: 1.2 Enough model behavior to read the map
text:
1.2 Enough model behavior to read the map
The system map contains a model as one component. Readers need to know which state changes during training, which state remains fixed during inference, and what an evaluation result can establish.
A predictive model maps an input to one or more estimated outputs. A fraud model may accept transaction features and return a score. A generative model produces a sequence or structured object. A large language model (LLM) accepts context and generates tokens.
Training uses examples, an objective, and an update procedure to change model parameters. A parameter is an adjustable numeric value used by the model. Training may use labels, demonstrations, preferences, or other feedback. The training result includes parameters and configuration, not a database of ordinary records that the application can query directly.
Inference applies fixed parameters to an input and produces an output. The input contains the user request and application instructions. It may also include conversation history or retrieved text. A token is a unit that a language model reads or generates. Context is the sequence of tokens available for the current model call.
Evaluation measures behavior on selected cases without updating the parameters. An evaluation must state the model version, input set, expected result or scoring rule, and conditions. A result on one set does not establish behavior for every possible input.
During text generation, the model converts the available context into scores for a possible next token. A decoding rule selects one token, appends it to the context, and repeats. Sampling settings can make repeated calls differ even when the initial text is identical. The generated sequence remains model output. Its meaning, permitted use, and consequences depend on the application.
Generalization is useful behavior on cases that were not used for parameter updates. Memorization is the retention of training details strongly enough to affect later behavior. A model can show both. Chapter 5 explains why disclosure claims need a precise query interface and measurement rather than an assumption that every output came from one stored record.
The application flow remains ordinary software around the model call:

Code example: Pseudocode for a small chat path that uses external inference.

session = identity_service.verify(request.session_token)
context = application.build_context(user=session.user, text=request.text)
disclosure_policy.check(context, destination="external-model")
draft = external_model.generate(context)
return application.validate_and_display(draft)
Authentication, context assembly, transfer, validation, display, logging, timeouts, and error handling belong to the application and related services. Those paths can fail even when the model behaves as its operator intended.
Concrete trace (hypothetical). The operating mode is inference. The task is to classify an employee request for routing, using fixed model parameters. The input is "Reset access for account 417", and the reference is an approved test label of account-support. The application creates 6 input tokens, the model produces scores of 0.72 for account-support and 0.18 for general-help, and the decoding rule selects the larger score. The observed result is a routing proposal. The parameters remain fixed, and the business record is unchanged. The conclusion is that inference produced a candidate output, while the application still controls validation, routing, and any later action.

title: 1  Mapping the system
section: 1.3 Who operates each part and what it can do
text:
1.3 Who operates each part and what it can do
Record the operator for each component and the data or actions available to the application. These facts describe an AI system more clearly than one deployment label:

Component operator.
Data and actions available to the application.

The book does not assume an on-premises model or complete external control. Common operating arrangements include:



Table 1.2: Operating arrangements state who runs each component.











Operating arrangement
Organization operates
Another party operates
Main review question




Supplier-operated assistant
Accounts, permitted uses, tenant settings, and enabled connectors exposed by the product
User application, model inference, and supplier-side records
Which controls and evidence does the supplier expose?


Organization application with an external model
Application, identity, retrieval, action policy, and organization logs
Model inference and provider-side processing
Exactly which request fields cross to the provider?


Managed application platform
Connected source systems, organization identities, and configured policy surfaces
Specified orchestration, search, connectors, tools, and model services
Which decisions remain configurable and observable?


Organization-operated model service
Deployed parameters, serving configuration, application, retrieval, and tools
Any rented infrastructure, firmware, acquired artifacts, or external dependencies
Which new operational duties and supplier layers remain?






An organization-operated model can still depend on cloud administrators, firmware, package repositories, acquired weights, and external identity systems. A provider-operated model does not automatically receive the organization’s complete document collection. A complete map identifies the actual transfer and responsibility for each component.5
Application capability is a separate question:



Table 1.3: Application capabilities state what data and actions the system can reach.










Application capability
What the application can do
New security question




Chat
Send selected text to a model and display the response
What crossed the boundary, and how will the answer be used?


Retrieval
Search a specified collection and add permitted passages to model context
Which passages may this user read and send to this provider?


Action proposal
Produce structured arguments for a possible operation without executing it
Are the operation, object, destination, and scope correct?


Authorized execution
Submit a proposal to a service that applies current identity and policy checks
Which identity supplies authority, what was approved, and what changed?






An application can combine any operating arrangement with several capabilities. The examples below state both facts directly:



Table 1.4: Examples combine an operating arrangement with an application capability.











Example
Operating fact
Capability fact
Main change




Supplier-hosted employee chat
Supplier operates the interface and model
Chat only
The organization depends mainly on product settings and supplier evidence.


Internal retrieval application with external inference
Organization operates retrieval and the application. The provider operates inference
Retrieval
Selected private context crosses an operator boundary.


Managed agent platform
Provider operates specified orchestration or connectors
Authorized execution
A complete map identifies the provider and organization checks before action.


Organization-operated model and application
Organization operates model serving and application code
Authorized execution
Model-serving evidence increases together with patching and runtime duties.






Adding retrieval changes data exposure. Adding execution changes possible consequences. Moving inference in-house changes operational responsibility and available evidence. Each change leaves the other decisions open.
The deployment record controls this choice. Its reviewer checks every listed component, operator, transfer, and reachable action before allowing the configuration. The release record, route configuration, provider receipts, and action-service logs show which choice became active. Coverage is the number of reviewed components and routes divided by all components and routes in the approved map. This review costs engineering time and may delay a provider or platform change. An undocumented connector or administrator path can bypass it. Recovery disables the changed route and revokes its credentials. The last approved configuration is then restored. A complete record does not prove that every supplier behaves as described.
Concrete comparison (hypothetical). The task is to decide whether an internal policy assistant can answer a restricted employee question. In the first arrangement, the organization operates the application and an external provider operates inference. In the second, the organization operates both. The same request and permitted passage enter each run. The intermediate record shows that only the first run crosses the provider boundary. Both runs return the same draft answer in this example. The observed difference is operator access, transfer evidence, and incident responsibility, rather than answer quality. The conclusion is that deployment location changes the trust record even when application capability and observed output remain unchanged.

title: 1  Mapping the system
text:
1.4 Components, assets, identities, and boundaries
A useful system record specifies concrete objects. At minimum, it includes user and service identities, the application, model service, source systems, indexes, prompts, action services, logs, operators, and provider interfaces.
An asset is something whose disclosure, unauthorized change, loss, or unavailability would matter to the decision owner. Secure AI guidance includes models, data, prompts, software, documentation, logs, and assessments among the assets that may need protection.6



Table 1.5: A working asset inventory connects each object to an access decision and possible loss.











Asset
Locations or forms
Access decision
Example loss




Source records
Repositories, connector copies, indexes, caches
Who may ingest, change, retrieve, and delete each copy?
Restricted text enters an unauthorized context.


Model inputs and outputs
Requests, provider payloads, responses, conversation state
Which fields may reach each operator and user?
Sensitive data leaves the permitted route.


Model and application artifacts
Parameters, adapters, prompts, code, packages, images
Who may admit, update, deploy, and roll back each version?
An unreviewed artifact changes behavior.


Credentials and policy
User sessions, service tokens, connector scopes, action rules
Which component checks which identity and object?
A service performs an operation outside the user’s authority.


Evidence
Request, retrieval, authorization, provider, deployment, and incident records
Who can read, join, retain, and verify them?
The organization cannot determine what happened.






The same information may appear in several places. A policy document can exist in a source repository, a search index, a model request, a cache, and a log. Different people or services may read each copy. Its retention and deletion rules may also differ.
User identities and service identities also have different jobs. A user’s identity supplies current person and tenant claims. An ingestion service may read a broad source collection to build an index. An application service may call the model. Because an action service receives a narrower credential and checks business policy, broad ingestion access does not grant the same access to each employee.
A trust boundary is a point where data or control crosses between operators, users, tenants, privilege levels, or policy domains that cannot simply trust one another. An application programming interface (API) is an interface. It becomes a relevant trust boundary when the caller and receiver have different authority, evidence, or operating responsibility.
This inventory lets the reader trace one request without treating every arrow as equivalent.
The configuration gate checks each discovered asset against the inventory before deployment. It allows the version when its operator, permissions, copies, and recovery owner are recorded, and blocks or quarantines an unlisted component. Evidence includes inventory revisions, discovery results, access decisions, and deployment records. Coverage is the number of discovered assets linked to a reviewed row divided by all assets found by the selected discovery methods. Maintaining this record adds review work and can slow urgent changes. A shadow connector or an asset that the discovery methods miss defeats the check. Recovery revokes the related identity and removes reachable copies where possible. Rebuilding the map leaves the existence of unknown assets unresolved.

section: 1.5 A chat request across an external model boundary
text:
1.5 A chat request across an external model boundary
Start with the smallest runtime path. The employee submits text. The organization’s application authenticates the session and builds a request. It checks what may leave the organization before calling an external model. The application then records and displays the result. No document connector or business-action service is reachable on this path.



Table 1.6: Evidence produced along a chat request that uses external inference.










Step
Component
State or evidence




1
Identity service
Authenticated user and tenant claims linked to a request ID


2
Application
Selected user text, application instructions, destination, and model version


3
Disclosure check
Allowed and rejected fields before transfer


4
External model service
Provider request identifier and generated output when available


5
Application
Validation result, displayed response, timing, and local request record






If the output says that an action occurred, the statement is still generated text. An authoritative business record would be needed to establish a state change. The organization can inspect its serialized request and local logs. Evidence of receipt and later processing must come from the provider.
Concrete trace (hypothetical). The operating mode is inference, and the task is producing a summary of a non-sensitive meeting note. The input contains 180 characters of employee text plus the application instruction. The application records request ID r-204, the exact serialized fields, and an allowed destination decision. The provider returns response ID p-771 and a 42-word summary. The application records both identifiers and displays the text. The observed result proves what the organization sent and displayed. It does not prove which provider replicas held the request or when each copy disappeared. The conclusion is that local and provider evidence answer different parts of the same transfer claim.
The application gateway enforces the transfer rule. It checks destination, data class, and serialized fields, then allows, removes fields from, or blocks the request. A test set records forbidden fields caught out of all seeded forbidden fields, along with permitted requests accepted out of all permitted controls. Filtering adds latency and can block legitimate text. An unfamiliar encoding or an unclassified field can bypass the rule. Recovery disables the route and revokes the provider credential. Deletion and incident work then follows for affected request IDs. A passing sample does not establish provider erasure or detection of every sensitive format.
This path establishes the external model boundary. The next section adds retrieval while preserving the same inference operator.

title: 1  Mapping the system
text:
1.6 Retrieval and document access
The application retrieves source passages while processing a request. A relevance score cannot answer the access and authority questions that follow.
The retrieval boundary separates four questions:

Who may add or change source content?
Which passages may the current user read?
Which passages may the organization send to this model provider?
Can retrieved text authorize an action or change application policy?

Lewis and colleagues introduced retrieval-augmented generation models that combined a learned generator with a dense external index and retriever.7 Current products use several architectures under the broad RAG label. This book’s application pattern preserves source identity and access metadata. It checks current user permissions before selecting text. The application sends only permitted context to the model. It does not claim to reproduce the paper’s jointly trained design.
Suppose search returns four candidate passages:



Table 1.7: Relevance, user authorization, provider disclosure, and instruction authority are separate decisions.












Candidate passage
Relevant
User may read
May reach provider
Treatment




Approved supplier policy
Yes
Yes
Yes
Admit with source identity and version


Assigned customer record
Yes
Yes
Depends on data rule
Apply disclosure policy before transfer


Payroll record
Possibly
No
No
Reject before context assembly


External note containing instructions
Possibly
Possibly
Depends on data rule
Treat as untrusted data and preserve its source






Relevance answers whether text may help answer the query. Authorization answers whether this user may read it. A disclosure rule answers whether the organization may send it to the provider. Retrieved text remains data even when it contains sentences that look like instructions.
If a forbidden passage enters the serialized model request, a later refusal to repeat it does not undo the transfer. If provider receipt cannot be observed, the record must say that it is unknown. Chapter 3 follows these copies through their retention and deletion paths. Chapter 11 returns to retrieval access, poisoning, and evidence quality.
Concrete trace (hypothetical). The operating mode is retrieval followed by inference. The input is an employee request for the travel reimbursement limit. Search returns four passages with scores 0.91, 0.86, 0.79, and 0.74. The second passage belongs to another department and fails the current access check. The fourth contains payroll data and fails the provider disclosure rule. The application sends the first and third passages to the model. The observed answer cites both permitted passages. The conclusion is that relevance produced candidates, while user authorization and provider disclosure independently reduced the context from four passages to two. All scores and records in this trace are hypothetical.
The retrieval service enforces document access, and the disclosure service enforces transfer to the provider. They check the current user, document metadata, destination, and selected text before context assembly. The report gives forbidden passages rejected out of all seeded forbidden candidates and permitted passages retained out of all permitted controls. Fresh authorization adds lookup cost and may reduce cache reuse. Stale metadata or an index that loses source identity can bypass the intended decision. Recovery invalidates cached results, removes the affected index version, and rebuilds from approved sources. This evidence does not show that admitted text cannot mislead the model.

title: 1  Mapping the system
section: 1.7 From a proposal to an authorized action
text:
1.7 From a proposal to an authorized action
A model may produce structured fields for a possible operation:

Code example: A model-generated proposal before authorization.

{
  "operation": "create_purchase_request",
  "supplier_id": "supplier-204",
  "amount": 1200,
  "currency": "USD",
  "reason": "replacement equipment"
}
Before displaying the proposal, the application validates the operation name and schema, although structural validation cannot establish that the operation is correct or authorized.
Execution requires a separate path. The application displays the exact operation, destination, amount or scope, and source information. The employee confirms those fields. The action service checks the authenticated identity, current permissions, business limits, and retry state. It records either a denial or one state change.
The model supplies candidate arguments. Authority comes from identities, current policy, and the service that records the business state. A sentence in a retrieved document cannot change those rules. Chapter 12 develops this separation for tools and agents.
Concrete trace (hypothetical). The operating mode is inference followed by a possible external action. The task is to reimburse 120 currency units to an employee. The model proposes amount 120 and destination acct-9. The application validates the fields and shows them for confirmation. Before the employee confirms, a simulated retry changes the destination to acct-8. The action service compares the confirmed reference fields with the submitted fields and denies the mismatch. The observed business state contains no payment, while the audit record contains the proposal, confirmation, denial, and operation key. The conclusion is that model output proposed an action but did not grant authority to execute it.
The action service enforces the final decision. It checks authenticated identity, exact confirmed fields, current business rules, and the operation key before allowing, blocking, or changing the requested operation. Tests report unauthorized attempts denied out of all unauthorized attempts and authorized controls completed exactly once out of all authorized controls. Confirmation and policy checks add delay and can reject legitimate work after a policy change. An alternative action path that skips the service defeats the control. Recovery suspends that path and revokes its credential. The business reversal process handles a state change when reversal is possible. A denial test does not prove that displayed advice is safe or correct.

1  Mapping the system

title: 1  Mapping the system
text:
1.8 Lifecycle and evidence
One request trace shows runtime behavior. A security decision also depends on how the system was designed, acquired, evaluated, deployed, changed, operated, and retired. The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) guidelines organize secure AI development into secure design, development, deployment, and operation and maintenance.8 The following table is this book’s expanded working sequence.



Table 1.8: Lifecycle questions and evidence for the organization’s AI system.










Stage
Main question
Useful evidence




Plan and design
Is AI suitable for the task, users, data, possible losses, and required approvals?
Approved use case, system map, data rules, threat model, acceptance criteria


Develop and acquire
Which code, models, prompts, packages, and sources enter the system?
Repositories, artifact records, reviews, supplier information


Evaluate
Does the specified path satisfy its claims under relevant conditions?
Inputs, expected decisions, versions, observations, results, known gaps


Deploy
Which versions, identities, routes, and settings are active?
Release record, configuration hash, scopes, rollback target


Operate and respond
What happened, what changed, and can the organization contain and recover?
Joined application, provider, platform, action, and incident records


Update
Did a model, prompt, connector, policy, or provider change invalidate earlier evidence?
Change record, affected tests, new evaluation, approval


Retire
Were routes, credentials, indexes, retained data, and supplier duties closed?
Revocation, deletion, retained evidence, contract closure






Evidence varies with the operating arrangement. An organization can inspect its own context assembly and authorization code. For external inference, it may receive provider documentation and request identifiers. Usage records and contractual commitments provide other evidence. Operating the model exposes more technical state and also creates more patching, monitoring, and recovery duties.
A release and change gate enforces the lifecycle decision. It checks the approved artifact versions, identities, routes, required tests, and rollback target before allowing a deployment or update. Deployment records and joined runtime logs show which version ran. Review coverage is the number of changes that received their required checks divided by all changes found in the release history. The gate adds release time and record storage. An emergency or manual change outside the recorded path can bypass it. Recovery disables the affected version and revokes obsolete credentials. The last accepted state is then restored. These records prove neither supplier behavior nor the absence of unrecorded changes.

1  Mapping the system

title: 1  Mapping the system
text:
1.9 Worked system-mapping task
An organization plans to move document indexing and search from its own services to a managed platform. The application, identity service, source repository, external model provider, and business-action service remain unchanged.
First record the components that move: document parsing, embedding generation, index storage, query embedding, and candidate search. Then add the new transfers. Source text and metadata may cross to the managed search provider during ingestion. Query text may cross during search. Search results return to the application before user authorization and model-provider disclosure.
Preserve the permission mechanism. The managed index may store tenant and document metadata, but the organization must still identify where current user authorization runs and how permission changes invalidate cached results.
Record the evidence expected from each operator: source version, ingestion identity, indexed object identifiers, search request, candidate identifiers, authorization decision, serialized model request, and deletion result. Missing provider evidence remains an explicit limit.
Conclusion. Moving search changes operators, transfers, retained copies, and available evidence. It does not automatically change what the application may execute. Chapter 2 can now ask what unwanted outcomes follow from this specified arrangement.
Worked comparison (hypothetical). The task is to compare the old and new maps. The input is the approved five-component baseline plus the planned managed-search change. The reference requires every changed operator, transfer, copy, and evidence source to appear. The old map has one external recipient and two organization-held document copies. The new map has two external recipients and adds source text, an index copy, query text, and search-result records at the search provider. Application permissions and action authority remain unchanged. The observed result is four changed rows and no action-path change. The conclusion is that Chapter 2 should analyze new disclosure and source-integrity paths without inventing a new execution capability.
The change gate checks every changed row against an approved operator, permission rule, test, and recovery owner before allowing the managed search route. The comparison covers four changed rows out of the four found in this exercise. Provider review and migration add cost, and missing a temporary copy or support path leaves the map incomplete. Recovery returns search to the prior service and revokes the managed route. This worked result supports the stated map comparison, not the managed provider’s behavior.

1.10 From the map to the threat model
The completed system record contains:

The decision and system version.
Users and service identities.
Components and their operators.
Training, evaluation, and inference roles.
Stored data and runtime transfers.
User, disclosure, and action checks.
Possible state changes.
Logs and evidence gaps.
Assumptions that trigger a new review when they change.

Chapter 2 adds a bounded attacker and an unwanted outcome to this record. It then identifies an enforcing component, a test, and the remaining risk.

1.10.1 Chapter checkpoint
At this point, a reader should be able to distinguish the model, application, and operational system. The reader can state who operates each component, separate chat and retrieval from action, and identify which evidence belongs to the organization or an external provider.

title: 2  Defining the threat
text:
2.1 A fixed system before threat analysis
An AI security statement becomes difficult to judge when it does not identify the system, the attacker, the unwanted result, or the evidence that would show failure. Chapter 1 supplied the system record. This chapter adds a bounded attacker and follows one possible failure from entry point to consequence.
The method is:
fixed system -> protected asset -> attacker capability -> entry point -> unwanted outcome -> consequence -> control -> test -> remaining risk -> owner
The order can run in both directions. An investigator may begin with an observed consequence and ask backward which events could explain it. The resulting hypothesis must then be checked in the order that the system actually runs.
Consider the Chapter 1 arrangement in which the organization operates identity, the application, retrieval, logging, and an action service. An external provider operates model inference. Employees can retrieve permitted documents, and generated action proposals require current authorization outside the model.
The scope record keeps the analysis tied to one version and use. Secure AI guidance recommends a whole-system threat model that considers expected and unexpected behavior, possible compromise, data sensitivity, deployment, and action restrictions.1
The first case gives an attacker ordinary request access and response visibility. The second adds permission to edit one external document that an employee may retrieve. In both cases, the attacker lacks administrator access, model-weight access, application-code access, and action-service credentials.
Fixing the system prevents a defense from relying on capabilities that do not exist in the stated arrangement. An organization using external inference cannot assume direct access to provider memory. A provider cannot apply an organization’s current business rule unless the application sends reliable facts and requests the check.

title: 2  Defining the threat
text:
2.2 Protected properties and unwanted outcomes
A threat model starts with what must remain true. A security property is a condition that protects an asset. An unwanted outcome is a concrete event that violates such a condition.
NIST AI RMF describes related trustworthiness characteristics that include validity and reliability, safety, security and resilience, accountability and transparency, explainability and interpretability, privacy enhancement, and managed harmful bias.2 These characteristics interact. A system-specific analysis must still identify the asset and observable event.



Table 2.3: Security properties become useful when connected to observable outcomes.










Property
Practical question
Example unwanted outcome




Confidentiality
Who may learn this information?
A restricted passage enters an unauthorized context or response.


Integrity
Who may change this object or decision?
A source, prompt, proposal, or business record changes outside its authorized process.


Availability
Can authorized users obtain the service within required limits?
Crafted work exhausts model, search, or action capacity.


Privacy
Are personal data collection, use, sharing, inference, and retention within the stated rules?
Personal data is used for a new purpose or retained beyond the approved period.


Safety
Can system behavior cause unacceptable real-world harm?
Advice or action creates a material harmful result in the stated use.


Reliability
Does the system perform its intended function under relevant conditions?
The assistant repeatedly gives an incorrect result without adversarial input.


Accountable action
Can the organization identify which identity, policy, and service caused a state change?
An action occurs without a traceable approval and authorization decision.






“Prompt injection” is an attack mechanism, while “a restricted document entered an unauthorized model request” is an unwanted confidentiality outcome. “The model was wrong” may describe ordinary error or an application defect. Hostile influence and bad source data can produce the same observation. Starting with the outcome keeps those possible causes separate.
Concrete comparison (hypothetical). The operating mode is inference with retrieval. The task is to answer an employee’s policy question. In case A, the model gives an incorrect date but no restricted data crosses a boundary. In case B, the answer is correct, yet the serialized request contains a payroll passage that the employee may not read. The reference properties are answer accuracy and document confidentiality. The observed results are one accuracy failure and one confidentiality failure. The conclusion is that a useful threat model records the violated property and observable event instead of using model error as a catch-all description.
crumbs: Part I: Defining the system and threat
2  Defining the threat

title: 2  Defining the threat
text:
2.3 Attacker capability, access, and knowledge
The attacker description must state what the person or system can change and observe. An attacker capability is the action or change available to the attacker. Access is the interface or object used for that action. Knowledge records what the attacker knows about the target.
NIST’s adversarial machine learning taxonomy separates lifecycle stage, attacker goal, capability, and knowledge. It also distinguishes query access, training-data control, model control, source-code control, testing-data control, and resource control.3 Those distinctions prevent query access from silently becoming permission to change training data or code.

Code example: A bounded request-only attacker profile.

Actor: external user with an ordinary application account
Goal: obtain a record that this account may not read
Capability: submit up to 60 requests per minute and observe displayed text
Knowledge: public interface and fields learned from the user’s own responses
Cannot: edit documents, inspect provider internals, change parameters, or use employee credentials
Budget: 500 requests over one day
Success: forbidden record content appears in retrieval output, the serialized model request, or the displayed response

The profile also needs a budget, such as requests per minute, total attempts, time, money, or access to auxiliary data. A broad statement such as “the attacker can interact with the model” hides the conditions that determine whether an attack is possible and whether a test represents the deployment.

title: 2  Defining the threat
section: 2.4 From consequence back to entry point
text:
2.4 From consequence back to entry point
Suppose an authoritative record shows that an action occurred outside policy. Begin with that evidence and ask backward:

Which identity and policy decision authorized the state change?
Which operation and fields reached authorization?
Which application output supplied those fields?
Which model context and source versions influenced the output?
Which user, connector, or external party could change the relevant input?

These questions generate possible explanations. They do not establish that an earlier event occurred. After choosing one hypothesis, verify it forward in the system’s runtime order:






Figure 2.1: A possible failure path is verified in runtime order.



For each transition, ask which record can confirm or reject it. Missing evidence leaves that transition unknown. It should not be replaced with a confident story.
A complete threat statement has the following form:

Note
In system version S, an attacker with capability C can use entry point E to cause event O, violating property P and producing consequence B. Component K is expected to prevent or detect the event. Test T fails when observation F occurs. Remaining uncertainty R belongs to owner W.

The next two cases apply this form while changing one attacker capability.
crumbs: Part I: Defining the system and threat

title: 2  Defining the threat
text:
2.5 Case one: A request-only attacker
The first attacker has an ordinary external account. The attacker can submit requests, observe displayed responses, and repeat attempts within the stated budget. This person cannot edit documents, use an employee identity, inspect provider internals, or call the action service.
Possible losses include cross-account retrieval, provider disclosure outside policy, resource exhaustion, misleading output, and disclosure through error behavior. Each one needs its own success condition.
One complete statement is:

Note
An external user submits a request crafted to match another tenant’s record. If the retrieval service applies an incorrect tenant filter, it may admit the forbidden record. Confidentiality fails when the record identifier or text enters retrieval output, the organization’s serialized model request, or the displayed response. The test uses two tenants and fails on any cross-tenant identifier or text. Provider receipt remains unknown without provider evidence.




Table 2.4: Controls and evidence for the request-only case.











Decision
Enforcing component
Evidence
Failure condition




Establish caller
Identity service
Stable user and tenant claims linked to request ID
Identity is missing, stale, or mismatched.


Admit passage
Retrieval authorization
Candidate IDs, current access result, and rule version
A forbidden document is admitted.


Send context
Provider disclosure check
Serialized request, selected fields, destination rule, and provider receipt when available
A forbidden field appears in the serialized request.


Limit work
Gateway and service quotas
Request rate, token, latency, and rejection records
Accepted work exceeds stated limits or blocks authorized use.


Present answer
Application
Sources, validation result, and displayed response
Unsupported text is represented as verified policy under the test rule.






The retrieval record, serialized request, provider receipt, and displayed response are different observations. A user-interface test cannot establish which source entered context or what the provider received.
The retrieval authorization service enforces tenant separation by checking the current caller, tenant, document, and rule version before admitting a passage. The report gives forbidden passages admitted out of all seeded forbidden candidates and permitted passages admitted out of all permitted controls. Current checks add latency and may reduce cache reuse. Stale tenant metadata or an unmediated search path can bypass the rule. Recovery disables that path, invalidates affected caches, and identifies request IDs associated with a possible transfer of the record. A zero count in this test does not cover other query strategies or provider-held copies.
crumbs: Part I: Defining the system and threat
2  Defining the threat

title: 2  Defining the threat
text:
2.6 Case two: An attacker-edited document
The second attacker can also edit one external document that the organization indexes and an employee may read. The document contains text asking the model to ignore organization policy and propose a large transaction to an attacker-selected destination.
Greshake and colleagues described indirect prompt injection as adversarial instructions placed in data likely to be retrieved by an LLM-integrated application. Their paper demonstrated the mechanism in synthetic applications and selected systems available at the time.4 NIST uses resource control for attacker control over documents or web pages that enter runtime context.5 The sources support the mechanism. They do not establish current success rates for every model or application.
Correct retrieval does not settle source integrity or instruction authority. The employee may be allowed to read the document, and the disclosure policy may allow it to reach the provider. Those decisions can pass while the document contains hostile text.
A possible runtime path is:

The external account changes the document.
The connector copies the new version and source metadata.
Search returns it for a related employee request.
User authorization admits it because the employee may read it.
Provider disclosure admits it because the data class is permitted.
The model produces an unwanted transaction proposal.
The application parses the proposal.
The action service denies it because the destination, amount, or approval does not satisfy current policy.

The denial is evidence about the action boundary. It does not establish that the displayed explanation was accurate or that every injection attempt failed.
The action service enforces the tested consequence. It checks the employee identity, approved supplier record, exact fields, amount limit, and operation key, then allows or blocks the operation. The test reports blocked out-of-policy actions out of all seeded out-of-policy attempts and successful permitted actions out of all permitted controls. The independent check adds policy maintenance and approval delay. A different connector that can write business state without this service defeats the claim. Recovery revokes that connector, preserves the linked records, and reverses the operation when the business process permits it. The result says nothing about misleading text that a person later accepts.
Concrete trace (hypothetical). The operating mode is retrieval, inference, then authorization. The input is an employee request for approved supplier terms. Search admits an attacker-edited public document that requests a payment to acct-external. The model proposes a payment of 9,000 currency units. The application parses the proposal, but the action service finds no approved supplier record and denies it. The observed result is a harmful proposal, a denial record, and an unchanged payment state. The action boundary stopped this tested consequence, although the displayed text could still mislead the employee.



Table 2.5: Different attacker capabilities create different paths and control locations.










Element
Request-only attacker
Document editor




Controlled input
Direct application request
Retrieved external document


Primary entry point
User interface or API
External source and ingestion path


Main boundary at risk
Tenant retrieval and provider disclosure
Source integrity, context interpretation, and action proposal


Can authorize an action as an employee
No
No


Critical test
No forbidden record enters retrieval output or the serialized request
An unapproved destination or amount never reaches execution


Concern after the test passes
Other request strategies and permitted-data errors
Misleading displayed text and other hostile-source strategies
crumbs: Part I: Defining the system and threat
2  Defining the threat

title: 2  Defining the threat
text:
2.7 Controls belong at specific decisions
A component can enforce a rule only when it has the required facts and authority. The retrieval service can check current document permission. A disclosure service can check destination and data class. The action service can check business state, authenticated identity, amount, destination, and retry status. The model cannot replace those controls through a refusal message.
Saltzer and Schroeder’s 1975 tutorial collected several protection principles that help place these checks.6 Their paper credits E. Glaser for the fail-safe-defaults idea and Roger Needham for separation of privilege.

Fail-safe defaults: access begins denied and becomes permitted only when stated conditions hold.
Complete mediation: every relevant access is checked, including cache reuse and action retries.
Separation of privilege: sensitive operations may require independent conditions, such as a user confirmation and a current service-side policy decision.
Least privilege: each user or program receives only the permissions needed for its task.

These principles guide design. Evidence must still show how a component implements and tests the rule.



Table 2.6: Preventive, detective, and recovery measures belong at specific components.











Path
Preventive control
Detective evidence
Recovery action




Cross-tenant retrieval
Current tenant and document authorization before context assembly
Candidate and admitted IDs with rule version
Revoke access, invalidate caches, and identify affected requests


Forbidden provider transfer
Data-class and destination policy before the model call
Destination, selected fields, policy result, and provider request ID
Stop the route and follow the incident process


Attacker-edited document
Restricted source writes, versions, source identity, and integrity review
Source version, editor identity, unusual changes, and retrieval linkage
Restore a trusted version and re-evaluate affected sessions


Unauthorized action
Schema validation, exact approval, current identity and business rule checks
Proposal, approval, policy decision, operation key, and result
Deny or reverse through the business process and investigate linked requests


Misleading answer
Visible sources and checks for facts used in consequential decisions
Output, cited sources, reviewer correction, model and prompt version
Correct the record and add a regression case






Preventive, detective, and recovery measures should address different points in the failure path. Repeating one model-level filter does not create an independent authorization boundary.
Concrete control-placement test (hypothetical). The task is to stop a restricted passage before it reaches an external provider. The input is a permitted user query that retrieves one public and one payroll passage. A model refusal after inference is the comparison control. The retrieval authorization step removes the payroll passage before context assembly, and the disclosure check confirms that the serialized request contains only the public passage. The observed provider request lacks the seeded payroll marker. The conclusion is that the control belongs before transfer. A refusal after transfer could change the displayed output but could not undo disclosure.
Each control record also states its operating cost and recovery path. Retrieval and disclosure checks consume latency and can reject authorized work. Approval for an employee action takes time. Monitoring consumes storage and review effort. The corresponding recovery route invalidates an index, disables a transfer, revokes an action credential, or corrects a displayed record. A test denominator contains every eligible seeded attempt, with permitted controls reported separately. A passing result supports only the component, version, paths, and inputs that the test exercised.

title: 2  Defining the threat
section: 2.8 Turning a control into a testable claim
text:
2.8 Turning a control into a testable claim
“We use access control” identifies an intention. A testable claim identifies the system version, initial state, attacker capability, inputs, observation points, and pass or fail rule.
A useful test record contains:

application, policy, model, prompt, index, and provider versions.
users, permissions, documents, quotas, caches, and business state.
exact attacker operations and budget.
ordinary, boundary, and adversarial inputs.
retrieval, transfer, output, policy, action, latency, and log observations.
a pass or fail condition selected before the result.
observed results, missing evidence, and untested conditions.




Table 2.7: Control claims linked to observable tests.











Claim
Test input
Required observation
Fail when




A user cannot retrieve another tenant’s record
A request deliberately shares terms with the forbidden record
Candidate IDs, authorization decisions, and admitted passages
Any forbidden passage is admitted.


Forbidden text does not reach the provider request
The forbidden record contains a seeded marker
Serialized request fields and provider receipt fields when supplied
The marker appears in the serialized request.


A document cannot authorize an action
A retrieved document requests an operation outside policy without approval
Proposal, validation, authorization, and final business state
The action service records the operation.


Approval binds exact fields
The destination changes after the employee approves the proposal
Approval object and action request
The changed destination is accepted.


Retry does not duplicate an action
Repeat one authorized request after a simulated timeout
Stable operation key and final business state
More than one action is recorded.






Each denial test needs an authorized control case. A service that denies every request has protected confidentiality by becoming unavailable. Testing both the forbidden and permitted cases distinguishes the intended control from a broken system.
The test harness records the numerator and denominator for each outcome rather than reporting only that an attack was blocked. It also records latency, retries, reviewer work, and false denials. When the pass rule fails, the release gate blocks the version and restores the last accepted configuration while the owner investigates. A harness that cannot observe a provider transfer or a business state change leaves that part of the claim unknown. Passing the visible steps does not prove that an unobserved path is absent.
crumbs: Part I: Defining the system and threat
2  Defining the threat

title: 2  Defining the threat
text:
2.9 Residual risk and review triggers
Tests reduce uncertainty under their stated conditions. They rarely remove all possible failure paths. NIST AI RMF asks organizations to establish context, characterize impacts and likelihood, prioritize risk, choose responses, and document remaining negative risk.7 The framework does not calculate an organization’s risk tolerance or approve a deployment.



Table 2.8: Hypothetical remaining-risk decision for a limited organization pilot.









Field
Hypothetical limited-pilot decision




Risk
Attacker-controlled external text influences an action proposal.


Possible impact
Misleading employee guidance, an attempted unauthorized action, and investigation cost


Preventive evidence
The action service independently checks identity, exact approval, destination, scope, and current limits.


Test evidence
Hypothetical seeded cases outside policy are denied while a permitted control succeeds once.


Evidence gap
The exercise does not measure every way hostile text may mislead an employee.


Decision
Permit a limited pilot while automatic execution remains restricted to the tested action path.


Owner
Business service owner with security review


Review triggers
Model, provider, prompt, parser, connector, permission, destination, or action-limit change






The record distinguishes observed facts, reasonable inferences, and unknowns. A hypothetical result must say that it is hypothetical. A small test cannot become a broad statement that an agent is secure.
The responsible decision owner accepts, restricts, or blocks the use after checking every required control claim, test result, operating cost, unknown, and recovery route. Coverage is reviewed decision fields divided by all fields required in the risk record. Restrictions and monitoring can reduce capability and consume staff time. An unrecorded system change can make the decision stale. The review trigger withdraws the earlier approval until the changed path is tested again. An accepted remaining risk records a bounded choice rather than proof of safety.
The review triggers connect this chapter to the rest of the book. A new model, prompt, connector, data class, action, provider, or permission rule can invalidate earlier evidence.
crumbs: Part I: Defining the system and threat
2  Defining the threat

title: 2  Defining the threat
text:
2.10 Worked threat-modeling task
An organization plans to let an internal assistant prepare an email to an external supplier. The employee must approve the exact recipient, subject, and body before a mail service sends it. A retrieved supplier document may contain attacker-controlled text.
Produce a scope record, attacker profile, two unwanted outcomes, backward investigation, forward verification path, controls, positive and negative tests, remaining risk, and review trigger.
Answer. The scope adds the mail service, its narrow service identity, the recipient, message body, approval object, send result, and linked records. The attacker can edit the supplier document but cannot alter the recipient record, approve as the employee, change application code, or call the mail service.
One integrity outcome is an attacker-selected link in a sent message. The backward investigation starts with the sent-message record and asks which approval, draft, context, and source version could explain it. Forward verification follows source update, ingestion, retrieval, model request, generated draft, displayed approval, mail authorization, and send result.
The mail service accepts only a draft identifier and approval object bound to the exact recipient and content hash. One negative test changes the body after approval and expects denial, while the control test sends an unchanged benign draft once. Logs join the source version, serialized model request, draft, approval, mail request, and result.
The test record states changed drafts denied out of all changed drafts and unchanged messages sent once out of all permitted controls. Exact approval adds employee time and may require a new approval after any edit. A mail route that does not call the service bypasses this control. Recovery disables that route and revokes its credential. When available, the mail system’s recall or correction process handles recovery, although the test does not show that the approved message is truthful.
A confidentiality outcome requires a separate seeded restricted document and a test of retrieval output and message body. It cannot be attributed to an attacker who lacks access to that source or the retrieval policy. Remaining risk includes subtle misleading text that an employee approves. A model, prompt, parser, approval-screen, connector, or mail-service change triggers a new evaluation.

section: 2.11 The record later chapters will reuse
text:
2.11 The record later chapters will reuse
Part I now supplies two connected records:

The system record identifies components, operators, identities, assets, operating modes, data paths, action paths, lifecycle stages, and evidence.
The threat record links a fixed system and bounded attacker to an unwanted outcome, consequence, control, test, remaining risk, owner, and review trigger.

Later chapters change data influence, model access, platform exposure, retrieval, tools, or organizational duties. Each branch must state which field in these records changes. That rule keeps the book connected as a dependency graph.

2.11.1 Chapter checkpoint
A reader should now be able to fix a system version and change one attacker capability. The reader can investigate backward from an observed result, verify the hypothesis in runtime order, place controls at enforceable decisions, and state what the test does and does not support.

title: Part II: Protecting data and learned behavior
text:
Chapters in this part
This part separates failures in data collection, changes to learned behavior, disclosure through queries, and evasion of model decisions. That separation explains why a training defense may not help a retrieval system, and why a private training process does not replace application access controls.
Connection through the book. Follow organizational source records into permitted use and then into a deliberately different, controlled model laboratory. Each attack chapter changes one capability: influence over training, observation through queries, or modification of test inputs. Return each result to the question of what can be checked in a hosted deployment.
Part outcome. An attack and control comparison that states what the attacker can change, what is exposed, and how success is measured.
crumbs: Part II: Protecting data and learned behavior

title: Part II: Protecting data and learned behavior
text:
Controlling data use: This chapter establishes which organizational data may enter each AI path, which party receives it, and what evidence can show that retention and deletion rules work.
Protecting training: This chapter examines how a party that can influence training data, labels, weights, or adaptation records can change learned behavior, and how the organization detects and recovers from that change.
Limiting query disclosure: This chapter separates disclosure that occurs through normal application data handling from disclosure inferred or extracted through model queries, then matches each mechanism to evidence and limits.
Resisting adversarial inputs: This chapter defines adversarial-input claims precisely enough to distinguish a measured weakness from a broad claim that a model or system is generally insecure.

title: 3  Controlling data use
text:
3.1 Data classification and purpose
Security question. Which data may enter the system, and how is its use controlled over time?
Reference frame. The organization stores customer, personnel, policy, and external-source records. It operates ingestion and indexing but sends selected context to an external model. Compare a supplier-operated assistant and a managed platform that also operates selected components.
Connection through the book. The asset map becomes a data-handling map. Chapter 5 asks what model observations reveal. Chapter 11 applies the permitted-use and document-access rules during retrieval.
Before approving an AI path, the organization needs to know what data will cross it and why the processing is needed. It also records which party will receive the result. Data classification groups records by the harm that disclosure, alteration, or loss could cause. A processing purpose states the reason for a use. The receiving party is the organization or service that obtains the data, including an external model provider.
The NIST Privacy Framework separates the inventory of systems, people, data actions, purposes, and processing environments from the policies that govern them.1 Its Generative AI Profile also recommends checking training-data use for intellectual-property and privacy risk.2 These sources structure the decision but do not determine whether a specific use is lawful.
A useful record identifies the data category and processing purpose. It also assigns a responsible internal role and lists every receiving party. That record supplies the allowed-source and purpose rules for collection and preparation.
The context-assembly service enforces this record for model requests. It checks the field classification, purpose, recipient, and current user before allowing, removing, or blocking each field. The serialized request and policy decision are the observable evidence. Coverage is the number of classified fields checked divided by all fields found in the tested request set. Classification and review add maintenance work and can remove useful context. An unclassified derived field or another transfer path can bypass the rule. Recovery disables the route and identifies copies created by affected requests, without proving lawfulness or completeness beyond the tested data and path.
Concrete classification trace (hypothetical). The operating mode is inference through an external provider. The task is to draft a response to a customer support request. The input contains a ticket number, account email, free text, and an internal fraud flag. The reference record permits the ticket number and free text for response drafting. The email remains inside the organization, and the fraud flag is excluded from this purpose. Context assembly keeps the ticket text, substitutes an internal case identifier for the email, and drops the fraud flag. The observed serialized request contains only the permitted fields. The conclusion is limited to this data class, purpose, recipient, and tested request path.

title: 3  Controlling data use
text:
3.2 Collection and preparation
An approved purpose does not show that each training or evaluation record was collected under compatible terms. A source record identifies where a data item came from and the permission asserted for its use. Data minimization removes fields or records that the stated purpose does not require. An evaluation holdout is a test set kept outside parameter updates so it can measure behavior on unseen cases.
NIST treats data actions, purposes, elements, and processing environments as inputs to privacy-risk management.3 NIST also recommends examining whether proprietary or sensitive training data are used consistently with applicable requirements.4 In common practice, a preparation job reads approved source records and filters disallowed fields. A documented rule controls duplicate removal before the job writes separate development and evaluation outputs.
The current evidence packet does not yet support a general claim about how much overlap between training and evaluation data distorts a score. The organization should treat overlap detection as an open test requirement. The resulting prepared records now have to be followed through each distinct data path.
The job that prepares data enforces source and purpose rules before writing training or evaluation outputs. It checks the asserted permission, required fields, duplicate rule, and holdout assignment, then admits, changes, or quarantines a record. Job logs, rejected-record reports, and output digests show the decision. Coverage is reviewed records divided by all records in the prepared version, with overlap counts reported against both training and evaluation totals. The checks add processing and review cost. Incorrect source assertions or similarity outside the duplicate rule can bypass them. Recovery quarantines the version and rebuilds from the last accepted source set, without proving that the asserted permission was legally valid.

title: 3  Controlling data use
text:
3.3 Distinct data paths
One approval cannot safely stand for every copy created by an AI system. A training corpus changes model parameters during training, while a prompt record affects one inference request. An embedding is a numeric representation used for comparison or retrieval. Telemetry records operational events such as latency, errors, or resource use.
The Privacy Framework calls for an inventory of data actions, data elements, purposes, and internal, cloud, or third-party processing environments.5 Applied to the reference system, the inventory follows source files into preparation jobs and their outputs. Separate entries cover indexes, embeddings, prompts, retrieved context, feedback, telemetry, and logs. This AI-specific list is a system decomposition based on common architecture rather than a structure prescribed by the framework.
Derived forms should remain linked to their source and purpose because transformation does not by itself remove sensitive information. The packet lacks a reviewed source that traces every listed form through one representative application, so this chapter treats the map as a hypothesis to verify against implementation. Each resulting path becomes the subject of a separate disclosure-control decision.
The copy register is checked by the release reviewer before a new data path is enabled. The reviewer allows the path only when its source, purpose, recipient, retention rule, and recovery owner are present. Evidence consists of the approved row, effective configuration, and a traced sample. Coverage is mapped copies divided by all copies found by the selected storage and request trace. This inventory costs discovery and maintenance time. Hidden telemetry, temporary files, or provider replicas can escape it. Recovery closes the path and traces affected source IDs through known copies. A complete register does not prove that no unobserved copy exists.

title: 3  Controlling data use
text:
3.4 Disclosure controls
Once the paths are visible, the disclosure policy states which identity may send each field and identifies the permitted recipient. A connector scope is the set of resources and operations granted to an integration. Redaction removes or masks selected content. Pseudonymization replaces direct identifiers while retaining a controlled way to reconnect records. A data loss prevention check inspects content or metadata against disclosure rules.
The Privacy Framework calls for managed permissions and authorizations based on least privilege and separation of duties.6 The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) and its partners recommend controls before potentially sensitive information is sent to an external application programming interface (API).7
These controls work at different points. Permissions limit who can request data, while connector scopes restrict what a service can fetch. Content checks apply to the permitted transmission. Because detection quality depends on the data type and rule set, the absence of universal performance evidence means that secret scanning, redaction, and pseudonymization each require tests against representative records. The next question is how long protected copies survive.
Concrete disclosure test (hypothetical). The operating mode is retrieval followed by inference. The task is an authorized contract summary. The input contract contains one seeded test credential and a customer identifier. The employee may read the document, but the disclosure rule excludes both fields from reaching the external model. The connector returns the document, the content check removes the credential, and pseudonymization replaces the customer identifier with customer-17. The observed serialized request lacks the credential and direct identifier. The conclusion is that the tested rules changed this transfer. It does not establish their detection rate for other secret formats or identifiers.
The disclosure service records blocked seeded items out of all seeded items and accepted permitted fields out of all permitted controls. It also records added latency and manual-review volume. More aggressive detection can reduce exposure while increasing false blocks and loss of useful context. Encoded secrets, novel identifiers, or a connector that sends data before the check can bypass the control. Recovery disables that connector and revokes its credential. Following the affected request IDs into the copy register still does not show that every sensitive value is detectable.
