title: 3  Controlling data use
text:
3.5 Retention and deletion
A retention rule is incomplete if it mentions only the original file. A retention period specifies how long a copy may remain. Logical deletion removes ordinary access to a record, while media sanitization makes access to target data on storage media infeasible for a specified level of effort. A derived artifact is a later object, such as an index or embedding, created from source data.
NIST defines media sanitization by the effort needed to recover target data and treats sanitization as a managed program.8 That definition is useful for storage media but does not establish deletion from a provider replica, conversation history, index, cache, backup, or learned parameter.
The mechanism is a copy register in which each source record points to active stores, derived artifacts, provider-held copies, backups, expiry rules, and the evidence available after deletion. This register exposes an evidence gap because the packet does not yet supply a general method for verifying erasure across all those locations. A deletion request or interface response remains weaker than recovery testing, storage records, and provider evidence taken together. Those distinctions become inputs to the chapter’s review.
Concrete deletion trace (hypothetical). The task is to remove customer record C-104 after its approved retention period. The input is a copy register with the source file, search index entry, cached passage, conversation record, daily backup, and provider request ID. The reference rule requires immediate logical deletion, cache invalidation within one hour, backup expiry after 30 days, and provider deletion evidence under the contract. The source, index, cache, and conversation checks return no accessible record. The backup remains until day 30, and the provider returns only a deletion receipt. The observed result supports removal from tested organization stores while leaving backup expiry and provider erasure as bounded claims.
A deletion coordinator enforces expiry across the copies that the register can address. It checks the source identifier, copy type, retention rule, legal hold, and provider obligation, then deletes, expires, or preserves each copy. Evidence includes deletion results, failed operations, backup expiry records, and provider receipts. Coverage is completed deletion actions divided by all copies listed for the request. Longer backup windows reduce recovery risk but extend retention. An unregistered replica or learned parameter lies outside this mechanism. Recovery retries failed actions and disables access to unresolved copies. Missing provider evidence is escalated. Completion does not prove physical erasure from an external system.

title: 3  Controlling data use
text:
3.6 Data-use review
Policies describe intended handling, but the review tests whether the running system follows them. Configuration evidence records effective settings and permissions. Contract evidence records supplier commitments. A handling test submits controlled data and observes where it appears, who can retrieve it, and whether expiry changes that result.
NIST Privacy Framework Profiles compare current outcomes with target outcomes so an organization can identify gaps and plan improvements.9 NCSC guidance asks providers to explain where and how user data may be used, accessed, or stored.10 A statement about design or settings does not prove that the effective configuration or supplier behavior matches it.
A review compares policy and contract with effective configuration, access logs, and controlled tests. In a hypothetical employee disclosure test, a unique marker first enters a restricted document. The reviewer queries only approved paths before searching authorized logs and stores for that marker. The result is evidence about the tested path and time, not every future request. Chapter 4 uses this controlled, traceable data as the input to training-integrity analysis.
The review owner can keep, change, or suspend a data path after comparing those records. The handling test reports locations containing the marker out of every location in the copy register, along with permitted control requests that still work. Repeated tests consume model calls, log searches, and reviewer time. A path omitted from the register or a provider store hidden from the organization limits the result. Recovery suspends the route, corrects configuration, and starts deletion and incident work for the affected copy IDs. A passing review does not establish future supplier behavior.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. A support assistant uses an external model. Its source ticket contains an email address, free text, an internal fraud flag, and a seeded test credential. Specify the allowed processing purpose, the fields sent to the provider and every copy to track. Include one handling test.
Answer. Permit response drafting from the free text and a case identifier. Keep the email and fraud flag inside the organization, and reject or remove the credential before transfer. Track the source ticket, prepared record, retrieval index, cache, serialized request, conversation history, logs, backups, and any provider copy. Submit a controlled ticket containing the marker, then inspect authorization decisions, the exact provider request, accessible stores, expiry results, and provider evidence. A passing run supports only the tested fields, path, configuration, and time. It does not prove that every identifier is detected or every external copy is erased.

title: 4  Protecting training
text:
4.1 Training influence
Security question. How can an attacker change what a model learns?
Reference frame. Switch explicitly to the isolated model laboratory: the laboratory operator controls training examples and the deployed artifact, and the attacker can alter a stated subset. This does not give the organization access to an external provider’s base-model training.
Connection through the book. Data handling from Chapter 3 becomes a question about training integrity. Chapter 7 later asks how to review an acquired artifact when the training process cannot be inspected.
A training failure can begin at several write points, so the first decision is which point the attacker can influence. Data poisoning changes the examples used during parameter updates. Model poisoning directly changes a trained artifact or a contributed update. Ordinary data errors may cause similar symptoms, but the security analysis adds an attacker capability and objective.
NIST classifies poisoning as a training-stage attack and distinguishes data poisoning from direct model poisoning.1 The taxonomy organizes access and attack classes but does not estimate how likely any class is in this laboratory.
The mechanism starts with a path from attacker-controlled input to a training-stage write: source record, label, preprocessing result, contributed update, checkpoint, or final weights. Recording that path separates a corrupt source record from a directly altered model. The next section attaches a measurable objective and budget to the identified influence point.
Concrete influence trace (hypothetical). The operating mode is training a small message classifier. The task is to distinguish ordinary support messages from account-abuse reports. The input contains 1,000 reviewed examples, and the accepted dataset digest is the reference. An external contributor can change 20 source records but cannot write labels, code, checkpoints, or final weights. The preparation job imports 18 altered messages and rejects 2 malformed ones. The observed run record links those 18 record identifiers to the new dataset digest and model output. The conclusion is that the attacker influenced source content within an 18-record effective budget. It is not evidence of direct model poisoning or of a successful attack objective.
The training-data admission service enforces the first boundary. It checks source identity, writable fields, review status, and dataset version before allowing or quarantining records. Evidence includes source IDs, rejected records, the prepared-data digest, and the training job that consumed it. Coverage is admitted and rejected records divided by all records presented to the preparation job. Review and isolation add delay and storage. A write path outside the importer or a false source assertion can bypass the check. Recovery quarantines the affected version and returns to the last reviewed data set. The record proves neither that admitted content is harmless nor that poisoning achieved its objective.

title: 4  Protecting training
text:
4.2 Poisoning objectives
Knowing that an attacker can write data is not enough to design a test. Availability poisoning seeks broad loss of useful performance. Targeted poisoning seeks an error for selected inputs or classes. A clean-label attack keeps the visible label unchanged, and an attack budget states how many records or updates the attacker may alter.
NIST separates availability and targeted poisoning and discusses changed-label and clean-label attacks under different constraints.2 Steinhardt, Koh, and Liang developed certified defenses that bound worst-case loss under explicit assumptions about clean-data concentration and outliers.3
A valid experiment fixes the attacker’s writable fields, budget, target, and success measure before modifying data. Fractions or thresholds reported for one data set are not universal. A targeted objective leads to the special case in which harmful behavior appears only when a trigger is present.
The release evaluator checks both ordinary and targeted test sets before allowing the trained artifact. It reports clean errors out of all clean holdout cases and attack successes out of all eligible target cases, with the modified training records and attack budget attached. Larger test sets and repeated training consume compute and review time. An attacker outside the stated writable fields or budget can bypass the tested model. If the threshold fails, the release gate blocks the artifact and rebuilds from the last accepted data version. Passing does not cover another objective, population, or attack budget.

title: 4  Protecting training
text:
4.3 Backdoors and triggers
A model can perform normally on the clean evaluation set yet fail on a narrow condition. A backdoor is conditional attacker-selected behavior learned during training. The trigger is the feature or pattern that activates it, and the target output is the result the attacker seeks.
NIST describes backdoor poisoning as associating a trigger with an attacker-selected target while clean inputs may retain expected behavior.4 This mechanism explains why aggregate clean accuracy can miss the change: the test distribution may contain no trigger-bearing inputs.
A hypothetical image classifier might retain its ordinary accuracy but map images containing a small, attacker-chosen patch to one class. The example demonstrates the test shape, not a general success rate. Trigger persistence depends on the model, training process, later adaptation, and tested trigger variants. The same conditional behavior may arrive through acquired weights or adapters, which shifts attention from examples to artifacts.
The targeted evaluator checks trigger-bearing and clean cases separately. It records target outputs produced out of all eligible trigger cases, clean-task errors out of all clean controls, trigger variants, and model version. Dedicated tests add design and execution cost, while broad trigger searches can become expensive. A trigger outside the selected variants or a condition absent from the test set can bypass detection. Recovery blocks the artifact and restores a known-good checkpoint. It also removes suspect source records before rerunning both test sets. A zero observed success rate does not prove that no backdoor exists.

title: 4  Protecting training
text:
4.4 Acquired and adapted models
An organization may receive a base model together with an adapter and preference data without observing how each was produced. An adapter is a smaller parameter set applied to change a base model. Behavioral regression is a measured change from an accepted baseline on selected tests.
NIST treats direct modification of a trained model as model poisoning and notes that compromised federated clients can submit malicious updates.5 Its generative-model taxonomy also includes data and model poisoning in the supply chain.6 These categories do not show that every unexpected behavior in an adapter or preference-tuned model is malicious.
The intake mechanism first compares the acquired artifact with an approved base identifier. Clean-task and targeted tests then produce a record of changed outputs before deployment. The current packet lacks a strong source on adapter poisoning and regression testing after preference tuning. Claims about those methods remain open research tasks. The next section focuses on the versions and access controls needed to reconstruct the pipeline.
Concrete adapter comparison (hypothetical). The operating mode is evaluation with fixed parameters. The task is to compare an approved base model with a supplier adapter. Both receive 200 clean cases and 20 targeted trigger cases. The base model returns 174 expected clean answers and rejects all 20 targeted requests. The adapted model returns 176 expected clean answers but follows 7 targeted requests. The intermediate record fixes the prompt set, decoder settings, base digest, adapter digest, and test harness. The observed result is a targeted behavioral regression despite similar clean performance. The conclusion is to withhold this adapter pending investigation. The numbers cannot establish why the behavior changed or whether the supplier acted maliciously.
The artifact intake gate enforces that decision by checking the base digest, adapter digest, loader, clean results, targeted results, and approved environment. It allows isolated evaluation, blocks production use, or admits the exact combination. The report keeps both denominators: 200 clean cases and 20 targeted cases. Testing consumes compute and delays an update. A behavior outside the selected prompts or a different base model can bypass the evidence. Recovery removes the adapter and restores the accepted combination while preserving the failed test record, which does not identify the cause of the regression.

4  Protecting training

title: 4  Protecting training
text:
4.5 Training pipeline controls
Recovery is difficult when a training run cannot be reconstructed. A dataset version identifies the exact records and transformations used by a run. An artifact digest is a cryptographic hash used to compare bytes. A checkpoint records model state during training, and a known-good baseline is a previously accepted artifact with recorded evidence.
NCSC and partner guidance recommends access controls for models, data, training and processing pipelines, plus cryptographic hashes or signatures for model files, data sets, and checkpoints.7
In common practice, a run record links code revision, dataset version, configuration, software dependencies, identities that approved the job, output digest, and evaluation results. A digest detects a byte change but does not show that behavior is safe. These records make rollback and comparison possible. They also supply the baselines needed for poisoning evaluation and response.
The training orchestrator checks this run record before starting a job and the release gate checks it again before admitting the output. Missing or mismatched inputs cause quarantine rather than training or release. Evidence includes resolved versions, access decisions, job logs, checkpoints, and output digests. Coverage is resolved required inputs divided by all inputs in the approved run specification. Reproducible records require storage and controlled build time. An undeclared dependency or compromised approved input can still bypass the check. Recovery stops the job and isolates its outputs. Work resumes from a trusted checkpoint only when that checkpoint and its inputs remain accepted.

4  Protecting training

title: 4  Protecting training
text:
4.6 Poisoning evaluation and response
The response decision is whether the organization can return to a trusted checkpoint or must rebuild from reviewed inputs. A clean holdout is the Chapter 3 evaluation holdout used for ordinary task behavior, with its data excluded from training. A targeted test measures the specified attacker objective. Evaluation contamination occurs when the data used to judge the model have also been changed or exposed to training.
NIST reports limits in poisoning and backdoor mitigations and notes that many certified results depend on narrow assumptions about models and data, including assumptions about triggers.8 NCSC guidance treats changes to data, models, or prompts as behavior-changing updates that need testing and version handling.9
The evaluation compares a clean holdout, targeted cases, and version records against the known-good baseline. Rollback is useful only if the checkpoint and its inputs remain trusted. Retraining is needed when the trusted point cannot be identified or when contaminated inputs persist. The packet still lacks direct empirical evidence comparing recovery choices after confirmed poisoning, so no universal rule is claimed. The reviewed artifact and its residual risk now become the target of Chapter 5’s query-disclosure analysis.
The response owner blocks release or removes the deployed version when either the clean or targeted threshold fails. The record reports clean errors against all clean holdout cases, attack successes against all eligible targeted cases, and affected training records against the complete prepared-data version. Rollback is faster but retains risk when the checkpoint or its inputs are uncertain. Rebuilding costs more compute and review time. Contaminated holdouts, unknown write paths, or triggers outside the test set can hide failure. Recovery preserves evidence and revokes training writes. It rebuilds the inputs before retesting and redeployment, without proving the absence of another poisoning objective.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. An isolated classifier retrains from 1,000 reviewed records after an external contributor can alter at most 20 source messages. Clean accuracy falls from 90 percent to 89 percent, while success on a fixed 20-case trigger set rises from 0 to 7. What must the training record and response decision contain?
Answer. Record the attacker’s writable fields and effective record budget, source and prepared-data versions, code and configuration, job identity, checkpoint and final digests, clean holdout results, and the separate targeted results. The clean score alone would hide the conditional failure. Restore a known-good checkpoint only if its data and build path remain trusted. Otherwise rebuild from reviewed inputs. The hypothetical results show a regression under one trigger test. They do not identify the cause or establish behavior under untested triggers.

title: 5  Limiting query disclosure
text:
5.1 Specifying query observations
Security question. What can an adversary learn by querying a deployed model?
Reference frame. Use a query interface to the laboratory model, then compare query-only access to a hosted service. State whether the attacker sees labels, scores, or generated text and which data they are trying to infer.
Connection through the book. Reuse the data and attacker definitions, then distinguish ordinary unauthorized access from inference through outputs. The resulting measurements feed Chapter 14 and supplier questions in Chapter 21.
A disclosure result has little meaning until the interface and attacker are fixed. Black-box access permits queries and observations without exposing model internals. The interface may return a label or generated text. Some systems also expose confidence scores and logits. The attacker may also possess auxiliary data and a fixed query budget.
NIST distinguishes black-box attackers by returned outputs, query access, and prior knowledge.1 These fields define a threat model but do not predict attack success.
The organization records the output fields, rate limits, account rules, adaptive-query allowance, prior knowledge, and target secret. Changing one can change the conclusion. This fixed observation model supports the first disclosure question: membership inference.
The query gateway enforces the exposed interface. It checks account identity, allowed output fields, rate state, and query budget before returning, changing, or blocking a response. Evidence includes accepted and rejected queries, returned fields, account state, and model version. Tests report exposed fields out of all requested fields and accepted queries out of all attempts, with authorized controls kept separate. Restriction can reduce utility and add latency. Distributed accounts or an unmetered route can bypass the budget. Recovery closes that route and revokes affected credentials while preserving query records. Allowed outputs can still disclose information.
Concrete interface comparison (hypothetical). The operating mode is inference through a hosted classifier. The task is to assess what a query-only attacker can observe about one target record. Interface A returns only a class label. Interface B returns the label and three class probabilities. Both allow 100 adaptive queries from one account. The same 10 inputs produce identical labels, while interface B also exposes how sharply the model separates the classes. The observed result is a larger attack input at the same query count. The conclusion is that a disclosure result from interface B cannot be assigned to interface A without a new test. These outputs and limits are hypothetical.
crumbs: Part II: Protecting data and learned behavior
5  Limiting query disclosure

title: 5  Limiting query disclosure
text:
5.2 Membership inference
The decision here concerns one record, not recovery of its content. Membership inference estimates whether a record was used in training. A shadow model is trained by the attacker to imitate the target setting and produce examples for an attack classifier. Results should report both true-positive and false-positive rates.
Shokri and colleagues introduced a membership-inference attack that uses target outputs and shadow-model data.2 NIST also summarizes loss-based and shadow-model attacks through a challenge game.3
An evaluation samples members and non-members under a stated distribution. The allowed outputs become inputs to the attack score. Its operating point matters because a high false-positive rate can make an apparent advantage unusable. The published experiments apply to their models and interfaces. The next section changes the secret from membership to record content, attributes, or population properties.
Worked membership test (hypothetical). The operating mode is evaluation. The input is a balanced set of 100 known training members and 100 non-members from the same reference population. An attack score and threshold classify 34 members as members and incorrectly classify 18 non-members as members. The observed true-positive rate is (34/100=0.34), and the false-positive rate is (18/100=0.18). Among the 52 positive decisions, only 34 are correct. The conclusion is that the attack separates these test groups at this threshold, but the result does not establish usefulness when real members are rare or the target population differs.
The release evaluator enforces the organization threshold by checking the member and non-member sampling rule, attack score, threshold, and model version. It allows release only at the accepted threshold. Otherwise, the interface changes or the version remains blocked. The report keeps 34 true positives over 100 members and 18 false positives over 100 non-members rather than one combined percentage. More attack runs improve coverage but consume queries and analyst time. A different population, prior, or adaptive strategy can bypass the tested conditions. Recovery restricts the interface or returns to the accepted model. It cannot undo information already released.

5  Limiting query disclosure

title: 5  Limiting query disclosure
text:
5.3 Reconstruction and property inference
Several privacy attacks are often grouped together even though they answer different questions. Data reconstruction seeks a record or a close representation. Attribute inference estimates a missing field about an individual. Property inference estimates a feature of the training population.
NIST separates reconstruction, attribute inference, and property inference and assigns different access and knowledge assumptions to them.4 A semantically similar reconstruction need not be the original record, and a population property is not an individual attribute.
The evaluation states the target secret and auxiliary knowledge. It also records the correctness criterion and comparison baseline. This separation prepares the stricter case where generated content can be checked against known training data.
The evaluation harness checks one stated secret at a time and records correct inferences out of all eligible targets, along with the baseline and false positives. The release owner changes or blocks the interface when the accepted threshold fails. Building representative targets and auxiliary data costs review time and may expose sensitive test material. Another secret, stronger auxiliary knowledge, or a shifted population can escape the test. Recovery limits outputs and access, then repeats the evaluation after a model or data change. A passing result does not cover secrets absent from the target set.

5  Limiting query disclosure

title: 5  Limiting query disclosure
text:
5.4 Training-data extraction
A plausible output is not yet evidence that the model revealed a training record. Training-data extraction produces content that can be verified against training data or another reliable record. A canary is a controlled sequence inserted into training data to measure memorization, and exposure measures how unusually easy it is to recover within the defined canary distribution.
Carlini and colleagues extracted verifiable examples from GPT-2 through a staged method. Candidate generation came first. A ranking step selected likely memorized text for checking against the training data.5 Earlier work by Carlini and colleagues defined exposure for inserted canaries as an empirical measure of unintended memorization.6
These results establish methods and examples, not a universal extraction rate. A canary test covers its chosen distribution and cannot prove the absence of other memorized content. The next target is model functionality rather than training data.
The extraction evaluator checks each generated candidate against an authorized reference and records verified recoveries out of all generated candidates. A canary test separately reports recovered canaries out of all inserted canaries and the query budget used. Candidate generation and verification can be costly, and the reference comparison may require restricted-data handling. A prompt strategy or memorized sequence outside the chosen distribution can bypass the test. Recovery restricts the interface and removes the model from release while the data and training path are reviewed. It cannot retract a verified sequence already disclosed.
crumbs: Part II: Protecting data and learned behavior
5  Limiting query disclosure

title: 5  Limiting query disclosure
text:
5.5 Model extraction
An organization may protect a model’s behavior even when no record is disclosed. Model extraction uses observations from a target model to build an extracted model. Functional agreement measures how often the two produce the same result over a stated input distribution.
Tramèr and colleagues defined black-box model extraction through prediction application programming interfaces and evaluated copies by agreement with the target over an input space.7 The studies cover specified model classes and services. Agreement does not show that original parameter values were copied.
A useful test separates queries used to build the copy from unseen inputs used to measure agreement. It also records query cost and the baseline agreement of a model trained without target outputs. This empirical risk leads to a mechanism-level privacy guarantee: differential privacy.
The query gateway can reduce returned detail and enforce account budgets. It blocks abusive access under the stated rule. The evaluator reports agreement on unseen inputs as matching outputs divided by all unseen test inputs, with extraction queries and cost reported separately. Output restriction may reduce legitimate use, and strict budgets may affect shared accounts. Distributed identities or another interface can bypass the control. Recovery rotates credentials or changes the exposed interface, then retests agreement. It cannot erase an extracted copy already built, and low agreement does not prove that the original weights stayed private.
crumbs: Part II: Protecting data and learned behavior

title: 5  Limiting query disclosure
text:
5.6 Differential privacy
Attack testing samples known methods, while differential privacy bounds how much a randomized mechanism’s output distribution may change when one protected unit changes. The neighboring-data relation states what one change means. The parameters epsilon and delta quantify the allowed distributional difference under the formal definition.
Dwork and Roth define differential privacy over neighboring data sets and a specified randomized mechanism.8 Their composition results show that privacy loss accumulates across repeated mechanisms.9 The applicable accounting method must match the mechanisms and sampling assumptions.
The guarantee does not cover data that bypass the mechanism, and its meaning depends on the protected unit and neighboring relation. A small parameter is not a complete privacy program. The final section compares this formal statement with empirical tests and operational controls.
The private training or release mechanism enforces this guarantee. Its accountant checks the protected unit, neighboring relation, mechanism parameters, sampling assumptions, and prior releases before allowing another release. Evidence is the mechanism configuration, accounting entries, and the resulting cumulative epsilon and delta. Epsilon and delta are guarantee parameters, not empirical success fractions. Utility is measured separately over a stated test denominator. Randomization can reduce utility and private training can add compute cost. Data sent outside the mechanism or omitted releases invalidate the account. Recovery stops further release and fixes the path, although spent privacy loss cannot be revoked and the guarantee does not prove that one output hides a person.
The formal relation makes those dependencies explicit. Let \(D\) and \(D'\) be neighboring data sets that differ in one protected person’s record. For a randomized mechanism \(M\) and any possible set of outputs \(S\),
\[ \Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta. \]
Here, ε limits the multiplicative change in output probability, while δ allows a small additive exception. The mechanism, neighboring relation, protected unit, and repeated releases are part of the claim.10
Small randomized example (hypothetical). The task is to release one person’s yes-or-no response with less direct disclosure. The input is the true bit. The mechanism reports the truth with probability 0.75 and the opposite with probability 0.25. If neighboring inputs change from yes to no, the largest probability ratio for either reported value is (0.75/0.25=3). This toy mechanism satisfies the relation with \(\varepsilon=\ln(3)\approx1.10\) and \(\delta=0\). The observed result is a distributional bound, not a promise that one output is false. The bound permits some learning about an individual.
Limited composition illustration (hypothetical). If the organization runs this same mechanism twice for the same protected unit, basic composition gives an upper bound of \(2\ln(3)\approx2.20\) with \(\delta=0\). The intermediate privacy record adds the two ε values. The conclusion applies to this simple accounting illustration. Other mechanisms, dependence, and sampling can require a different accountant, so the example does not set a deployment budget.

5  Limiting query disclosure

title: 5  Limiting query disclosure
text:
5.7 Privacy defenses and evidence
The organization now has to match each defense to the path it changes. An output restriction removes or coarsens returned information. A rate limit reduces query volume. An empirical attack test measures selected attacks, while a formal guarantee follows from a defined mechanism and assumptions.
NIST lists access restriction, query monitoring, output restriction, regularization, and privacy-preserving training as distinct mitigation classes.11 NCSC guidance recommends controls on query interfaces to detect or prevent attempts to access confidential information.12
Mitigation names alone do not establish effectiveness. Evidence should pair task quality with attack success, false-positive rates, query cost, privacy parameters where used, and operating cost. That comparison closes the disclosure branch and moves to Chapter 6, where the attacker changes inputs to alter decisions.
The release owner compares these unlike records without collapsing them into one score. Empirical attack records include successes over eligible targets and false positives over non-target controls. Query-control records include blocked attempts over all attempts and legitimate requests denied over all legitimate controls. For differential privacy, it includes the accounted parameters and utility measured on the stated test set. Tight limits can reduce service quality and increase support work. New interfaces, identities, models, or data paths can bypass earlier evidence. Recovery restricts access, restores an accepted version, and repeats the affected tests. These results provide bounded evidence for the stated disclosure mechanisms.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. A hosted classifier returns labels and probabilities. A membership test reports 34 true positives and 18 false positives on 100 members and 100 non-members. A separate private release uses the toy mechanism from this chapter twice. What can the organization conclude?
Answer. The membership test has a 0.34 true-positive rate and a 0.18 false-positive rate at the tested threshold. Its meaning remains tied to the interface, query budget, and balanced evaluation population. Basic composition for the two private releases gives a bound of about 2.20 for ε with δ equal to zero under the stated neighboring relation. This formal bound does not cover data sent outside the mechanism. Each result measures one stated property and leaves other privacy risks and the acceptable operating point unresolved.

title: 6  Resisting adversarial inputs
text:
6.1 Evasion threat models
Security question. How can a changed input cause a deployed model to make the wrong decision?
Reference frame. Use a small controlled classifier with a fixed deployed model. The attacker changes allowed test inputs, not training data. A later comparison considers an API where gradients and weights are unavailable.
Connection through the book. The laboratory from Chapter 4 supplies a baseline, but the allowed intervention changes. Chapter 14 reuses these constraints when judging robustness evidence.
An error caused by an unusual input becomes a security test only after the attacker’s goal and allowed changes are stated. An evasion attack changes an inference input to alter model behavior without changing model parameters. An adversarial example is the resulting input. A perturbation constraint defines the changes the attacker may make.
NIST classifies evasion as a deployment-stage attack and separates white-box, black-box, digital, and physical settings.1 These classes define access and setting. They do not show that a mathematically small change is feasible or harmless in the real system.
The threat model records the starting input, target or untargeted objective, permitted region, model knowledge, query budget, and physical constraints where relevant. That objective and feasible set supply the inputs to gradient-based attacks.
The evaluation harness enforces this test boundary. It checks that each candidate starts from an eligible input and remains within the stated digital, physical, or business constraint before counting an attack result. Evidence includes rejected candidates, valid candidates, model decisions, and the exact constraint. Coverage is valid attacked inputs divided by all eligible reference inputs. Validity checks add test design and review cost. A poor representation of real constraints can admit impossible inputs or reject feasible ones. Recovery blocks the model version when its accepted threshold fails and returns to the previous accepted version. Passing does not cover another attacker goal or feasible set.
crumbs: Part II: Protecting data and learned behavior
6  Resisting adversarial inputs

title: 6  Resisting adversarial inputs
text:
6.2 Gradient-based attacks
A loss function returns one scalar that measures how poorly the model meets the stated objective for an input and reference. The input gradient gives the local rate and direction of loss change for each input feature. An L-infinity budget limits the absolute change of every feature. A budget of 0.10 permits at most 0.10 of change in each feature. Projection returns a proposed update to the allowed set when a step leaves it. The mathematical set still requires the business or physical validity check introduced in the preceding section.
With white-box access, the attacker can use derivatives of the loss with respect to the input. The fast gradient sign method, or FGSM, takes a step in the sign of that gradient under a stated norm budget. Projected gradient descent, or PGD, repeats an update and projects the candidate back into the allowed set.
Goodfellow, Shlens, and Szegedy derived FGSM from a linear explanation of adversarial vulnerability.2 Madry and colleagues used iterative first-order updates with projection in their study of optimization against adversarial inputs.3
The mechanism follows the local gradient to increase loss while projection enforces the mathematical budget. Its strength is relative to that norm, step schedule, restart count, and optimization result. The next section removes direct gradient access and examines query and transfer attacks.
For a fixed model with parameters \(\theta\), input vector \(x\), reference label \(y\), and loss \(L(\theta,x,y)\), the input gradient \(\nabla_x L\) states how a small change in each input feature changes the local loss. FGSM under an \(L_\infty\) budget \(\varepsilon\) uses
\[ x_{adv}=\operatorname{clip}\left(x+\varepsilon\operatorname{sign}(\nabla_x L)\right). \]
The clip operation enforces valid feature limits. PGD uses smaller repeated steps and projects each candidate into the allowed region around the original input. The model parameters remain unchanged during both attacks.
Two-feature numerical step (hypothetical). The operating mode is inference against a fixed binary classifier. The task is to raise loss for the reference class \(y=0\). The input is \(x=(0.40,0.70)\), each feature must remain between 0 and 1, and the \(L_\infty\) budget is 0.10. Suppose \(\nabla_x L=(2.0,-0.5)\). FGSM uses the sign vector \((1,-1)\), producing \(x_{adv}=(0.50,0.60)\). For PGD with step size 0.06, the first candidate is \((0.46,0.64)\). A second equal-direction step reaches \((0.52,0.58)\), then projection returns it to \((0.50,0.60)\). The observed candidate is within 0.10 of each original feature. The conclusion is only that the update obeys this mathematical constraint. A changed model decision would still need to be measured.
The projection step enforces the attack’s mathematical input limit, while the release evaluator enforces the security decision. It records successful objective changes out of all eligible attacked inputs, clean results over the same reference set, restart count, and compute time. More restarts can find stronger candidates but increase evaluation cost. Vanishing or hidden gradients can make this attack appear to fail. Recovery withholds the model or restores the accepted version, then repeats the test with an adaptive method. The result does not cover black-box access or a physical constraint that the norm omits.

title: 6  Resisting adversarial inputs
text:
6.3 Black-box attacks and transfer
A remote interface may hide weights and gradients but still expose useful feedback. A score-based attack uses returned scores to estimate a productive direction. A decision-based attack sees only the final label or decision. A substitute model approximates the target and can produce inputs tested for transfer.
NIST separates score-based and decision-based black-box attacks and describes transfer attacks that use a surrogate against another model.4 Because transfer depends on the models, data, constraints, and query process, the taxonomy does not give a universal success rate.
The evaluation keeps the same objective and feasible set used for white-box tests while changing the observations available to the attacker. It reports query count and attack success separately. These attack families define what a robustness measurement includes or leaves outside scope.
Concrete black-box trace (hypothetical). The operating mode is inference through a remote label-only API. The task is to change one accepted transaction classification while each normalized feature may move by at most 0.05. The attacker cannot inspect parameters or gradients. It queries 40 nearby inputs, uses the returned labels to choose a direction, and tests 12 more candidates. Candidate 52 changes the output while remaining inside the recorded feature box. The observed result is one decision change after 52 queries. The conclusion applies to this input, interface, budget, and validity check. It does not establish transfer to another model or feasibility in the original business process.
The query gateway enforces account and request budgets, and the evaluator checks candidate validity before counting success. Evidence includes queries accepted and rejected, outputs returned, valid candidates, and final decisions. The report states successful attacks over all eligible starting inputs and queries used per successful and failed attempt. Strict limits can reduce abuse while also blocking legitimate repeated use. Distributed accounts or another output interface can bypass them. Recovery closes the unmetered path and changes the interface if needed. The evaluation then runs again. A failed search within one budget does not prove that no black-box attack exists.
crumbs: Part II: Protecting data and learned behavior
6  Resisting adversarial inputs

title: 6  Resisting adversarial inputs
text:
6.4 Robustness measurement
A defense may look successful because the test attack failed to optimize. Robust accuracy is task accuracy under the stated adversarial evaluation. Attack success rate is the fraction of eligible cases where the attack reaches its objective. Adaptive evaluation changes the attack to account for the defense.
NIST warns that stronger evaluations have defeated many proposed evasion mitigations and treats adaptive testing separately from certified results.5 Athalye, Carlini, and Wagner identified symptoms of obfuscated gradients and bypassed most defenses in their nine-defense case study with adaptive attacks.6
The report pairs clean accuracy with accuracy under the stated attack. It also records attack success, budget, restarts, and any adaptation to the defense, without extending the case study to every defense. A stable baseline under the same threat model is needed before judging adversarial training.
The release gate checks clean and attacked results from the same eligible set against separate thresholds. The report gives correct clean decisions over all clean cases, correct attacked decisions over all valid attacked cases, and successful attacks over all cases eligible for the attack objective. It also records invalid candidates and attack failures caused by resource limits. Adaptive evaluation costs more compute and analyst effort. A weak optimizer, unexamined randomization, or a changed input pipeline can make the defense look stronger than it is. A failed threshold blocks release and triggers a return to the prior version. Passing does not establish a universal robustness property.
crumbs: Part II: Protecting data and learned behavior
6  Resisting adversarial inputs

title: 6  Resisting adversarial inputs
text:
6.5 Adversarial training
One defense changes training so the model learns from difficult inputs. Adversarial training minimizes loss on adversarial examples produced inside the training procedure. In this min-max form, an inner maximization searches for a high-loss allowed input and an outer minimization updates parameters against that result.
Madry and colleagues formulated this process as a min-max problem and trained against PGD adversaries.7 NIST reports that adversarial training can reduce ordinary accuracy and increase training cost.8
The defense should be tested with the same constraint used in training and with attacks that were not part of parameter updates. Its evidence supports empirical robustness under that model, not general security. Other defenses make different claims, including detection, abstention, and formal bounds.
Worked training comparison (hypothetical). The operating mode is training, followed by evaluation with no further parameter updates. A baseline classifier and an adversarially trained classifier use the same 800 training cases. The reference test contains 200 clean cases plus PGD cases under an \(L_\infty=0.10\) constraint. The baseline records 184 correct clean decisions and 62 correct PGD decisions. The defended model records 178 clean and 131 PGD decisions, while training time rises from 10 to 34 minutes. The conclusion is a clean-performance and cost trade-off with stronger empirical robustness in this test. It is not a guarantee against other constraints, attacks, or data.
The training loop enforces the inner attack constraint and updates parameters against the resulting examples. The release gate then compares 178 correct clean decisions over 200 cases and 131 correct attacked decisions over 200 eligible attacked cases with the accepted thresholds. The run record also captures the increase from 10 to 34 minutes. A different norm, radius, attack, or population can bypass the tested protection. Recovery restores the baseline or another accepted checkpoint and repeats clean and attacked evaluation. The observed gain does not establish certified robustness.
crumbs: Part II: Protecting data and learned behavior
6  Resisting adversarial inputs

title: 6  Resisting adversarial inputs
text:
6.6 Other defense claims
Defense reports can refer to different outcomes. A detector flags suspected adversarial input. Abstention withholds a model decision under a stated rule. A certified bound proves a property for specified inputs and perturbations under its mathematical assumptions.
NIST separates empirical mitigations from certified defenses and notes that certificates are limited to their perturbation model and often to a subset of inputs.9 Athalye and colleagues showed that hidden or unusable gradients can make an unsuitable attack report false confidence.10
Each claim needs the defended property, threat model, coverage, failure rule, and cost. A certificate outside its assumptions says nothing about other attacks or the surrounding application. Chapter 7 applies the same evidence discipline when deciding which external components may enter the trusted environment.
Concrete defense comparison (hypothetical). The operating mode is evaluation on 100 eligible adversarial cases. The detector flags 70 cases and produces 15 false alarms on 100 clean cases. Under the abstention rule, 55 decisions are withheld and 10 attacks succeed among the remaining cases. A certificate covers 38 inputs under an \(L_2\) radius of 0.20. The intermediate record keeps these denominators and perturbation rules separate. The observed results cannot be ranked by one number because detection, abstention, and certification make different claims. The conclusion is to report each property, coverage set, error rate, and operating cost without extending an \(L_2\) certificate to the earlier \(L_\infty\) attack.
The application enforces detector and abstention decisions, while a certificate checker verifies the formal predicate for each covered input. Evidence records 70 detections over 100 adversarial cases, 15 false alarms over 100 clean cases, 55 abstentions over their 100 eligible cases, and 38 certificates over the specified input set. Detection review and abstention reduce throughput and may deny useful work. An adaptive attack can evade the detector, and the certificate says nothing beyond its radius and assumptions. Recovery disables the failed path, returns to an accepted model or policy, and retests. None of the three records proves that the whole application is secure.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. A fixed classifier receives \(x=(0.40,0.70)\). The input gradient is \((2.0,-0.5)\), and the allowed \(L_\infty\) change is 0.10. Give the FGSM candidate, then state what evidence is still needed before claiming robustness.
Answer. The gradient sign is \((1,-1)\), so FGSM gives \(x_{adv}=(0.50,0.60)\) after enforcing the feature limits. This proves only that the constructed candidate respects the stated numeric budget. A robustness report still needs the model decision or loss, clean and attacked results over eligible cases, attack success, restarts or query count, input validity, adaptation to defenses, and operating cost. The hypothetical step does not establish that the input is feasible in a physical or business setting.

title: Part III: Securing the platform and runtime
text:
Chapters in this part
An AI service still depends on ordinary software and privileged infrastructure. This part moves from acquired artifacts to the compute boundary and then to the runtime that schedules and executes work. It prepares readers to investigate an exposed runtime service without assuming that exposure proves compromise.
Connection through the book. Ask what must be acquired, trusted, and operated to run the laboratory or an organization-operated model. An external-model configuration still leaves the organization responsible for its own application dependencies and services; an internal model adds model-serving duties. The artifact, compute, and runtime chapters establish distinct layers beneath application behavior.
Part outcome. A deployment review covering the acquired artifact, the compute provider, and the running workload.
crumbs: Part III: Securing the platform and runtime

title: Part III: Securing the platform and runtime
text:
Admitting trusted components: This chapter treats every acquired dataset, model, adapter, package, container, and skill as a component that needs a stated intake decision before it reaches a trusted environment.
Limiting platform access: This chapter identifies the infrastructure trust that remains when an organization runs workloads in its own environment, a cloud environment, or a provider-managed environment.
Containing runtime exposure: This chapter follows the identities, interfaces, networks, secrets, and resource limits that determine whether a running AI workload can be reached or abused.
crumbs: Part III: Securing the platform and runtime

title: 7  Admitting trusted components
text:
7.1 The AI dependency inventory
Security question. What must be trusted before an acquired component is allowed to run?
Reference frame. The organization evaluates a model package, adapter, and dependencies for an internal-model configuration. For an external model, inspect the organization application’s dependencies and the available supplier evidence. Hidden provider weights remain outside the organization’s inspection scope.
Connection through the book. Chapter 4 explains harmful learned behavior. This chapter explains acquisition and loading, then hands an admitted component to the compute and deployment decisions in Chapters 8 and 9.
An intake review can miss the component that actually introduces risk. An AI dependency is a model, data set, library, service, prompt resource, or other component on which the AI path depends. A transitive dependency is used through another dependency rather than selected directly.
NCSC guidance includes models, data, libraries, modules, middleware, frameworks, external interfaces, prompts, logs, and assessments among AI supply chain components or assets to track.1 The NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) calls for an inventory of software components and their relationships.2
The inventory links each component to its version, supplier, acquisition channel, dependants, update path, and execution environment. SSDF covers software, so the organization must extend the record to data sets, weights, adapters, and remote model services. The next section separates inert data from formats and loaders that can execute code.
The admission gate checks the complete component record before allowing a build or deployment. It blocks a missing, unresolved, or unapproved dependency. Evidence includes the resolved dependency graph, supplier and version records, download locations, and the build that consumed them. Coverage is reviewed components divided by all direct and transitive components found by the selected resolver and runtime trace. Inventory work adds update delay and storage. A unrecorded runtime download or undeclared service can bypass the record. Recovery stops the build and revokes affected credentials. Using the last accepted graph for the next build still does not prove that every listed component is safe.
Concrete inventory trace (hypothetical). The task is to identify everything required to run an internal support model. The input is one deployment file that directly lists a model package, tokenizer, inference library, and container. Dependency inspection adds a numerical library and a model loader used through the inference library. The reference is the approved component record. The observed inventory has six components, two of them transitive, with versions, suppliers, download locations, and update paths. The conclusion is that reviewing only the four direct entries would leave two executable dependencies outside the intake decision.
crumbs: Part III: Securing the platform and runtime
7  Admitting trusted components

title: 7  Admitting trusted components
text:
7.2 Model loading and code execution
A file described as model weights may still cause code to run when loaded. Deserialization reconstructs software objects from stored bytes. A data-only artifact is intended to contain values under a restricted schema. An executable artifact can invoke code through its format, loader, package hooks, or custom model implementation.
PyTorch states that torch.load uses an unpickler and warns against loading data from an untrusted source.3 PyTorch also documents that weights_only=True restricts imports selected at load time and object construction but does not prevent denial of service and may not prevent every memory-safety problem.4
Intake starts in an isolated environment with no production credentials or unnecessary network access. The loader and file format determine what execution remains possible. Restricted loading reduces one class of risk but does not establish safe behavior. Distribution paths and supplier accounts are the next source of uncertainty.
Concrete loading test (hypothetical). The operating mode is isolated model loading, not inference. The input is a supplier package whose recorded digest matches the downloaded bytes. The reference environment has no production credentials, a read-only model directory, and blocked outbound network access. A general object loader attempts to create a custom class and open a network connection. The restricted data-only loader rejects the custom object before model construction. The observed result is a blocked load and one denied network attempt. The restricted loader reduced this execution path without establishing resistance to denial of service, memory-safety faults, or a different file format.
The isolated runner enforces filesystem, credential, process, memory, and network limits while the restricted loader checks the artifact schema. It allows data-only objects and blocks unsupported construction. The runner also records denied side effects. The test reports packages blocked out of all malicious fixtures and valid packages loaded out of all permitted controls. Isolation consumes extra compute and may differ from production. A kernel flaw, resource exhaustion, or another loader can bypass the tested boundary. Recovery destroys the environment, rotates any exposed test credential, and quarantines the artifact. A clean load does not establish safe inference behavior.

title: 7  Admitting trusted components
text:
7.3 Repository and registry attacks
The correct loader cannot protect an artifact replaced before download. Dependency substitution causes a build or user to obtain an attacker-controlled component in place of the intended one. A look-alike package uses a confusing identifier to attract mistaken installation.
Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) models threats where an attacker changes source, dependencies, build steps, or artifacts and connects them to verified build evidence.5 NCSC guidance recommends obtaining third-party AI components from verified developers and monitoring the supply chain through the system life cycle.6
The mechanism may start with a confusing package identifier or a compromised maintainer account. An altered release or transitive dependency can then enter the build. Without primary incident or measurement evidence for these paths in AI repositories, this section does not claim a frequency. It instead motivates byte identity, signatures, pinned versions, and build records.
Concrete substitution trace (hypothetical). The task is to rebuild the accepted model service from a locked component list. The input requests package vector-helper version 2.4 from the controlled registry. A test build with the registry setting removed resolves a confusingly spelled public package at version 9.1. The intermediate record shows a different supplier, download location, and digest. The observed build is rejected because those values do not match the approved reference. The conclusion is that identifier spelling alone cannot establish component identity. This trace demonstrates the check, not the frequency of substitution attacks.
The dependency resolver and registry policy enforce the source decision. They check the exact package identifier, version, registry, supplier identity, and digest before allowing resolution. Lock files, resolution logs, and downloaded digests show the outcome. Tests report substituted packages rejected out of all seeded substitutions and approved packages resolved out of all controls. A controlled registry adds maintenance and can delay updates. A compromised approved account or undeclared installer download can bypass the rule. Recovery revokes the supplier key or account, removes the affected release, and rebuilds from the accepted lock. Passing does not prove the supplier source was benign.
crumbs: Part III: Securing the platform and runtime

title: 7  Admitting trusted components
text:
7.4 Artifact integrity and builds
The organization needs evidence that downloaded bytes match an approved release. A digest is a cryptographic hash of an artifact. A signature binds a statement or artifact to a signing key under the verification scheme. A build origin record states how a build platform produced an artifact from a described definition.
NCSC guidance recommends hashes or signatures for model files, data sets, and checkpoints so consuming systems can validate them.7 SLSA defines a signed statement about how a build platform produced artifacts from a build definition.8
Verification recomputes the digest, checks the signature chain and expected identity, then compares the build record with the approved source and build policy. A match establishes identity or build evidence under those assumptions. It does not show that model behavior is acceptable, so behavioral intake tests remain necessary.
Concrete integrity check (hypothetical). The input is a model archive, signature, signer certificate, and build statement. The approved reference specifies supplier key K-7, source revision a41c, and build profile gpu-inference-3. The organization recomputes the archive digest and obtains d92e. The signature validates over d92e, and the build statement reports the expected revision and profile. The observed evidence supports byte identity and the asserted build path under the trusted key and builder. The conclusion does not cover training-data integrity, hidden behavior, or later runtime configuration.
The verifier enforces byte and build identity before admission. It checks the recomputed digest, signing identity, signature, source revision, and build policy, then accepts or quarantines the artifact. Evidence consists of each verification result and the exact trust anchors used. Coverage is verified artifacts divided by all artifacts in the release. Signing and controlled builds add key-management and build cost. A stolen trusted key or compromised approved builder can produce evidence that still passes. Recovery revokes trust, blocks affected digests, and restores an earlier accepted release. Verification does not establish harmless behavior.
crumbs: Part III: Securing the platform and runtime
7  Admitting trusted components

title: 7  Admitting trusted components
text:
7.5 Behavioral intake tests
An artifact can have an accepted digest and still behave harmfully. A behavioral intake test runs clean-task and targeted security cases against an acquired component. The isolated test also monitors side effects before admission.
NCSC guidance recommends security evaluation before release and continuing measurement of model and system behavior.9 NIST’s model-poisoning taxonomy shows that a model artifact can contain malicious functionality even when it loads correctly and its identity is known.10
The test compares behavior with an accepted baseline and monitors network, file, and process activity in isolation. The packet lacks a reproducible source for detecting all unexpected side effects during model and adapter intake. Passing selected tests is limited evidence, not proof of harmlessness. The final decision combines this result with supplier and rollback information.
The evaluator used at intake blocks admission when clean quality, targeted behavior, or side-effect thresholds fail. It reports clean results over all clean cases, targeted failures over all eligible targeted cases, and unexpected events over the complete monitored test run. Broader tests cost compute and analyst time, and isolation may change behavior. A dormant trigger, delayed action, or unmonitored interface can bypass the suite. Recovery quarantines the artifact, destroys the test environment, and restores the last approved version. Passing does not show that every input or side effect was examined.
crumbs: Part III: Securing the platform and runtime
7  Admitting trusted components

title: 7  Admitting trusted components
text:
7.6 Acquisition and change decisions
Admission is a recorded decision whose conditions come from the organization. An acceptance criterion states the evidence and threshold required for use. An approved artifact is the exact version admitted for a stated environment and purpose. A rollback point is a prior accepted state that can be restored.
SSDF supplies shared secure-development practices that producers and purchasers can use in supplier communication and acquisition.11 NCSC guidance recommends alternate solutions for mission-critical systems when suppliers do not meet security criteria and calls for versioned update processes.12
The intake record joins inventory, loader behavior, source identity, build evidence, behavioral tests, license conditions, supplier commitments, and rollback readiness. Approval applies only to the recorded version and environment. A rollback cannot remove every downstream effect of earlier execution. Chapter 8 takes accepted components and examines the platform trusted to execute them.
Concrete admission decision (hypothetical). The task is to decide whether model package 3.2 may enter a restricted test environment. The input record has matching bytes and signature, a data-only load, no unexpected side effects in selected tests, and one unresolved supplier commitment about update notice. The reference criteria require all technical checks plus a documented update condition. The organization approves only isolated evaluation for 14 days and blocks production credentials and network access. The observed result is a conditional admission tied to one version and environment. The conclusion is to reopen the decision if the package, loader, supplier key, or environment changes. Earlier side effects would still require investigation after rollback.
The release controller enforces the conditional admission. It checks the exact artifact, environment, time limit, network policy, credentials, supplier condition, and rollback point before allowing use. Evidence includes the policy decision, deployed digest, denied capabilities, and expiry event. The review reports satisfied criteria over all required criteria, while technical test denominators remain visible separately. Restricted admission consumes an isolated environment and reviewer time. Credential drift or a copy moved to a different environment can bypass it. Recovery stops the deployment and revokes its identity. The accepted artifact is restored, while effects produced before removal remain.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. A supplier model archive has a valid signature and matching digest. Its general loader creates a custom object, while a restricted loader rejects that object. Clean behavior tests pass. Can the organization approve production use?
Conclusion. The signature and digest support byte identity under the trusted signing key. They do not establish safe loading or acceptable model behavior. The rejected custom object shows that loader choice changes the execution path, and clean tests do not cover targeted behavior or every side effect. The defensible decision is limited admission to the tested isolated environment until loader, targeted-test, supplier, update, and rollback criteria are satisfied. Any later version requires a new decision.
