title: 12  Authorizing agent actions
text:
12.6 Human approval
Human approval can add an independent decision before a consequential action, but only if the person sees the operation that will execute. An approval object contains the operation, resolved destination, important arguments, expected effect, current state, expiry time, and a digest that binds approval to those details. The interface keeps retrieved text from untrusted sources visually separate from the trusted summary.
MCP recommends that a person retain the ability to deny tool invocations and that clients present confirmation for operations.[^c12-s06-mcp-tools] Its trust and safety principles also call for explicit consent and clear explanation before data exposure or tool use.[^c12-s06-mcp-trust] The specification states that the protocol cannot enforce every consent requirement, and it does not show that a confirmation interface produces informed decisions.
The application freezes the reviewed arguments, records the approval, then compares the digest and relevant external state immediately before execution. Any change in recipient, amount, object, or policy invalidates the approval. A short lifetime limits reuse. Research evidence comparing such interfaces and detecting review-to-execution changes is still needed. Once approval is bound to one request, the remaining problem is limiting execution and recovering from partial work.
Concrete approval trace (hypothetical). The operating mode is approval of a consequential payment after authorization has passed. The review screen shows invoice INV-311, supplier B-311, amount 900, current supplier status, and expiry time 14:10. It binds those fields to approval record approval-55 with digest 7f31.
At 14:08, the action service resolves the request again. The amount is now 9,000, so the current digest is c244 and does not match the approved object. The service records approval_mismatch and blocks execution. It then requests a new review. The payment-identifier field remains empty. The tested binding stopped a changed request. These values and shortened digests are illustrative, and the trace does not measure whether a person understood the original review screen.
Immediately before execution, the service checks the bound operation, resolved object, destination, arguments, state, digest, approver, and expiry. The test reports changed requests blocked over all mutation cases and valid approvals completed over all unchanged cases. Approval adds latency and can create reviewer fatigue. Misleading presentation, approver compromise, or an omitted field can bypass the intended decision. Recovery cancels the request and freezes affected actions. Any supported reversal precedes a fresh review. A valid binding does not prove informed human judgment.

title: 12  Authorizing agent actions
text:
12.7 Execution limits and recovery
An authorized action can still cause excessive harm through repetition or an expanded target set. Continued execution after partial failure creates another path. An action budget sets a maximum count, cost, time, data volume, or number of affected objects for one task. A transaction limit bounds each operation. A stopping condition ends the sequence when state, credentials, policy, or observed results differ from the approved assumptions.
The NIST Generative AI Profile recommends defining limits for third-party models and monitoring whether use remains within them.[^c12-s07-nist] OWASP’s 2026 list links prompt-injection impact to the functions, permissions, and autonomy available to an application.[^c12-s07-owasp] These sources support bounded authority as a risk response. They leave transaction semantics and retry safety to the system design, along with rollback behavior.
The executor decrements the budget before each operation. An idempotency key lets a supporting service recognize retries of the same intended operation. The executor checks the returned state and stops on an ambiguous result. It records partial completion and hands recovery to a person or a separate service with the needed authority. This design pattern requires system-specific failure tests. Chapter 13 carries these limits into browser, code, network, and multimodal environments.
The executor enforces the action budget and stopping rule from task identity, current count or cost, external result, credential state, and idempotency key. The suite reports over-budget steps blocked and duplicate effects over all retry cases, with ordinary completion measured separately. Tight budgets reduce possible harm but can stop legitimate long tasks. Unmetered side effects, reused identities, or a service that ignores the idempotency key can bypass the design. Recovery stops the loop and reconciles each external object. Reversible effects receive the supported compensation, while an authorized person handles ambiguous cases. Passing does not prove that every external action can be reversed.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. A hypothetical agent sees pay_invoice during tool discovery and proposes a payment after reading an invoice. List the records needed to decide whether the action may execute and to explain the final result.
Answer. Record the employee, agent process, credential audience and scope, MCP revision, server identity, negotiated capabilities, tool list, and exact schema. Parse the proposal into typed fields, resolve the invoice and supplier in trusted business records, and make an object-level authorization decision. For a consequential payment, bind approval to the resolved operation, amount, destination, expiry, and current state. Recheck both policy and approval immediately before execution, then retain the external payment identifier or the blocking reason. Tool visibility and schema validity alone do not grant authority.

The chapter retains explicit evidence limits for memory isolation, approval quality, and recovery from partial execution.

12  Authorizing agent actions

title: 13  Confining agent environments
text:
13.1 Handling workspaces with untrusted content
Security question. What changes when an agent can modify software or navigate accounts, and when it can interpret images and audio?
Reference frame. Change the support tool to a browser session or coding workspace. State the session identity, files, secrets, network access, and permitted operations. Keep the distinction between proposed and executed actions visible.
Connection through the book. Apply the instruction, retrieval, and authority analysis from Chapters 10-12 to richer environments. Chapter 9 supplied the general runtime containment matrix. This chapter adds model-selected steps, untrusted workspace state, state drift, and stopping behavior. The resulting traces become end-to-end test cases in Chapter 14.
An untrusted workspace contains files and messages needed for a task but not authorized to direct the agent. Source files, issue text, logs, test output, web pages, and downloads can all contain text that resembles a user instruction. The agent still needs to read that material without letting it replace the employee’s task or expand permitted actions.
Greshake and colleagues showed that external data retrieved during a task can deliver indirect prompt injection to an integrated language-model application.1 OWASP’s 2026 risk description includes retrieved content and tool output among possible injection inputs.[^c13-s01-owasp] These sources cover selected delivery paths and a community risk model. They do not measure every coding-agent workspace or build system.
The hypothetical coding assistant keeps the employee request in a trusted task record and labels repository, issue, and command output as data. Each proposed action still passes the tool contract and policy checks from Chapter 12. A test places conflicting text in an issue and verifies that the agent reports it without executing its request. This input boundary sets the review rules for generated software and dependencies.
The workspace reader preserves source labels, while the action gateway enforces the allowed task from the trusted request, current identity, proposed operation, and destination. The test reports unintended actions over all eligible hostile-workspace cases and clean completion over all ordinary cases. Restricting actions and reviewing conflicts can slow coding work. Encoded instructions, mislabeled trusted files, or an alternate tool route can bypass the tested path. Recovery stops the session and revokes its credentials. Unreviewed changes are discarded before attack and clean cases run again. A blocked request does not prove that the model ignored the instruction.

title: 13  Confining agent environments
text:
13.2 Generated software and dependencies
Generated code is a proposed software change whose effect depends on the repository, build configuration, dependencies, and deployment target. Review has to establish what changed, which package identities entered the build, what secrets or permissions are accessible to the code, and which tests cover the affected behavior. Fluency and successful compilation supply little evidence about security.
The NIST Secure Software Development Framework calls for verification of third-party components across their life cycle and for review and testing of executable code.[^c13-s02-ssdf] Pearce and colleagues found security weaknesses among GitHub Copilot suggestions in the scenarios and product version they studied.[^c13-s02-pearce] Their result does not describe later versions, all languages, or workflows with independent testing.
The organization records the generated diff, dependency lock changes, scanner results, tests, reviewer decision, and deployment scope. Package references resolve to approved repositories and fixed identities before installation. Synthetic credentials test for accidental secret disclosure. These checks treat model output like any untrusted change while adding evidence about its generation path. The reviewed artifact can then enter a browser or execution environment with limited authority.
The build service checks the exact diff, dependency identity, test results, secret scan, reviewer decision, and target environment before the release gate accepts a change. The denominator includes every changed file, dependency, required test, and synthetic secret case. Independent review and isolated builds consume compute and release time. Incomplete tests, build substitution, or a dependency that changes behind an accepted label can bypass the record. Recovery blocks deployment and reverts the change. The prior lock and artifact are restored before the full gate runs again. Passing does not prove security outside the covered behavior and environments.

title: 13  Confining agent environments
text:
13.3 Browser authority
A browser agent uses authority available through authenticated sessions, open tabs, browser storage, downloads, uploads, and clipboard access. A browser origin identifies a web protection domain based on scheme, host, and port. It helps isolate sites, but it does not express the employee’s business intent to submit a form or transfer data.
RFC 6454 defines origins as protection domains used by the same-origin policy.[^c13-s03-origin] The RFC also documents limits such as ambient authority and dependence on Domain Name System and transport security.[^c13-s03-limits] Those browser facts do not form a complete authorization model for an AI agent using an already authenticated session.
The hypothetical agent records the active tab, origin, session owner, target URL, form fields, upload or download path, and resulting state. Navigation and reading may fit one permission set. Submission, payment, file transfer, and clipboard use require separate checks because current evidence does not yet establish a complete browser-agent control model. The same separation is needed when instructions arrive through images, audio, or video.
The browser controller and action service enforce each operation by checking session identity, active origin, target origin, data movement, resolved object, and user approval. The test matrix reports blocked consequential actions over all forbidden cases and successful read-only tasks over their eligible set. Isolation and confirmation add friction and can break sites that change flows. Pop-ups, redirects, shared browser state, or an unmodeled clipboard path can bypass incomplete rules. Recovery closes the session and revokes its tokens. Transferred data is withdrawn where possible before the origin and action matrix runs again. Passing does not establish that page content was trustworthy.

title: 13  Confining agent environments
text:
13.4 Multimodal inputs
A multimodal model can receive text, images, audio, or video in one task. Recognized text from a screenshot and transcribed speech can affect the same context as the employee’s request. The security decision concerns the source and authority of the content rather than the modality used to present it.
NIST’s adversarial machine learning taxonomy covers attack paths for multimodal models across several input types.[^c13-s04-nist] OWASP’s 2026 prompt-injection description states that input may be represented in text, images, audio, or video and may be hidden from the rendered interface.[^c13-s04-owasp] These references describe possible paths without giving a success rate for action-taking systems.
A test image can contain visible task data and hidden or low-contrast instructions. The trace records the original media, extracted text, model input, proposed action, and enforcement decision. Separate modality tests reveal failures in optical character recognition, transcription, or model interpretation. Current literature still needs stronger evaluations of attacks and defenses across these modalities. Confinement limits the damage when interpretation fails.
The media processor records extracted content, and the action gateway enforces the final decision from source labels, current task, proposal, and destination. The denominator includes every eligible image, audio, and video case plus clean controls for each supported form. Extraction and human inspection add compute and delay. Hidden content, parser differences, or a newly supported modality can bypass the corpus. Recovery quarantines the media and stops dependent actions. Prior state is restored where possible before the case runs through the full path again. A denied action does not prove correct interpretation of the media.

title: 13  Confining agent environments
text:
13.5 Execution environments
An execution environment is the operating-system and network context in which agent-generated commands run. Its filesystem mounts, process rights, credentials, package installation, network routes, and time or resource limits define the maximum technical effect of a mistake. The environment must match the task rather than the full authority of its host.
NIST container guidance separates risks in images, registries, orchestrators, containers, and hosts, including shared-kernel and unrestricted-network concerns.[^c13-s05-risks] It recommends controls at each layer and discusses separating workloads by sensitivity.[^c13-s05-controls] Saltzer and Schroeder’s least-privilege principle supports granting only the rights needed for the task.[^c13-s05-least] These sources leave the escape resistance of a selected sandbox unproved.
For a hypothetical code repair, the environment mounts one repository copy and supplies a short-lived test credential. It blocks production networks and caps processes, time, and storage. A container shares a kernel with its host, while a virtual machine adds a different isolation boundary at extra cost. Current empirical evidence for agent-specific sandbox escape and credential exposure remains incomplete. The bounded environment supports controlled multi-step action sequences.
Concrete confined-execution trace (hypothetical). The operating mode is an agent repairing a test repository. The task is to change one parser and run its unit tests. The reference environment allows writes under /workspace, access to packages.internal, and use of a test-only credential. It blocks production services and host storage.



Table 13.1: Agent execution trace.





Step
Intermediate record
Observed result




1
mount /workspace read-write
parser file changed


2
mount /host absent
read attempt returns path not found


3
destination packages.internal
dependency request allowed


4
destination payments.internal
connection denied


5
process count reaches 32
next process denied


6
unit test command
18 tests pass, 1 test fails






The agent reports a partial result and does not publish the change because the success condition required all 19 tests to pass. The conclusion is that the tested mounts, route rule, process limit, and stopping rule constrained this run. It does not exclude unknown escape paths or establish that the code change is secure. The paths, counts, and results are hypothetical.
The runtime checks mounts and process rights. Credentials and destinations are checked at the network gateway, while the job controller applies resource limits. The denominator is every allowed and forbidden operation in the confinement matrix. Stronger isolation adds startup time, memory, and administrative work and can limit required tools. Kernel flaws, device access, or an unmetered route can bypass the tested boundary. Recovery terminates the environment and preserves its events. Exposed credentials are rotated, and the affected image or host is replaced before the matrix runs again. Passing covers only the attempted escape paths.

title: 13  Confining agent environments
text:
13.6 Action sequences and verification
A multi-step task can fail even when each command is allowed in isolation. An early action can change the state on which later authorization depends. A retry can repeat a non-repeatable operation, while a tool can report success before the external system settles. The sequence needs expected states, success checks, stopping rules, and a recovery path.
Complete mediation calls for checking each access instead of assuming that an earlier decision covers later access.[^c13-s06-mediation] MCP recommends confirmation for tool invocations and preserving a person’s ability to deny an invocation.[^c13-s06-mcp] These principles do not define transaction handling, state drift, safe retry, or rollback for an agent workflow.
The hypothetical agent reads the current repository state and proposes a patch. It applies the patch in the confined copy, then runs tests. After comparing the resulting diff, it stops before deployment. Each transition records its input state and observed result. An ambiguous result blocks automatic retry until the service can establish whether the action occurred. Evidence for general agent transaction protocols remains open. Chapter 14 treats this full sequence as the system behavior that must pass evaluation before release.
The workflow controller enforces each transition by checking the prior verified state, current authorization, action budget, expected result, and retry key. The test reports correctly stopped or recovered failures over all injected sequence failures and successful completion over clean workflows. Verification adds service calls and can leave work unfinished when external state settles slowly. Eventual consistency, missing result fields, or an irreversible side effect can defeat automatic recovery. Recovery resumes from the last verified state when possible. Otherwise, it applies a supported compensating action or transfers the case to an authorized person. Passing one sequence does not establish safe composition for other tools.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. A hypothetical coding agent must repair a parser and install an approved dependency. It must then run tests and return a patch. The repository also contains issue text instructing the agent to upload credentials. What execution and verification record supports a bounded result?
Answer. Keep the employee’s repair request as the trusted task and record the issue text as untrusted workspace data. Mount only the repository copy, provide a short-lived test credential, permit only the approved package destination, block production routes, and set process, time, and storage limits. Record each proposed command, policy decision, filesystem change, network result, and test outcome. Return the patch only if the stated tests pass, and retain the failed upload attempt as evidence of enforcement. This supports the observed run and does not establish that the sandbox has no unknown escape path.

The chapter retains explicit evidence gaps for coding workspaces, browser agents, multimodal attacks, sandbox performance, and multi-step transactions.

Starter literature. These sources provide the initial evidence base for this chapter and guide later research, but they do not yet support every future sentence. 2 3 4

title: Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure
text:
Chapters in this part
Readers now know enough architecture and attack mechanisms to judge defenses. This part asks what evidence supports release, what remains observable after deployment, and how a team recovers when prevention fails.
Connection through the book. Bring the model, platform, and application branches into one evidence process. Test a specified setup before release, identify what can be observed while it operates, then investigate and recover using the same records and identities. Missing supplier visibility remains an explicit limit.
Part outcome. A release decision supported by tests, an operational monitoring plan, and a recovery exercise.
crumbs: Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure

title: Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure
text:
Deciding whether to release: This chapter defines the evidence needed to release or change a system, including a reproducible test scope, adversarial conditions, uncertainty, and a decision owner.
Keeping the live system in bounds: This chapter turns the controls and failure paths already identified into runtime records, alerts, limits, and response routes that remain useful after release.
Recovering from AI incidents: This chapter treats an AI incident as an evidence and recovery problem, distinguishing model error, policy failure, hostile content, account compromise, and infrastructure compromise.
crumbs: Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure

title: 14  Deciding whether to release
text:
14.1 Evaluation scope
Security question. What would count as convincing evidence that the system is secure enough for its intended use?
Reference frame. Evaluate the organization application and the model laboratory as separate stated systems. Keep attacker access, deployment configuration, tool authority, and task success fixed within each comparison.
Connection through the book. Bring the earlier branches together into reproducible evidence. A result qualifies the tested setup. Chapter 15 decides what to observe after release, and Chapter 22 uses the evidence in decisions.
An evaluation scope states the system, task, protected assets, expected behavior, attacker access, failure conditions, and deployment configuration covered by a test. Without this record, a strong result for a laboratory model can be mistaken for evidence about an application that also has retrieval, tools, identities, and external services.
The NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) MAP function calls for documentation of intended purpose, deployment context, users, impacts, risks, and requirements before risk is measured.1 NIST’s adversarial machine learning taxonomy recommends specifying attacker goals, capabilities, knowledge, and life-cycle stage.[^c14-s01-aml] These frameworks organize scope but cannot show that the chosen boundary is complete.
The hypothetical evaluation record identifies the organization application, external model version, retrieval snapshot, tool permissions, employee role, and harmful outcomes. It also states excluded components and the reason for each exclusion. Reviewers can then match every test and conclusion to the same system. That scope determines which clean and adversarial cases belong in the evaluation data.
The release owner enforces scope acceptance by checking every inventoried component, protected asset, attacker capability, and planned exposure against the evaluation record. The coverage denominator is all items in the approved system and threat maps, with tested, excluded, and missing counts kept separate. Wider scope increases test cost and can delay release. An omitted interface or changed deployment can bypass the conclusion. Recovery blocks or narrows release while the missing item is added. Affected tests then run again, although complete mapping does not prove that the chosen threats are exhaustive.
crumbs: Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure
14  Deciding whether to release

title: 14  Deciding whether to release
text:
14.2 Evaluation data
Evaluation data represents the tasks and failures that govern release. Clean cases measure intended operation. Realistic cases preserve deployment constraints. Held-out cases reduce direct tuning to the test. Adversarial cases exercise stated attacker capabilities. Coverage records show which assets and failure paths have cases. Overlap with training or development data can make results look stronger than they are.
NIST AI 800-3 distinguishes variation between evaluation items from variation across repeated trials of the same item.[^c14-s02-8003] The AI RMF asks organizations to document test sets, metrics, tools, limitations, data quality, and representativeness.[^c14-s02-rmf] These sources do not supply a contamination detector, a current security data set, or a safe substitute for sensitive records.
The organization builds cases from the scoped task and replaces real secrets with synthetic values that preserve access and disclosure behavior. It records each case’s source, version, expected result, attacker capability, and coverage tags. Another review compares development prompts with known training disclosures where evidence exists. Benchmark contamination and faithful sensitive-data substitution remain open evidence gaps. The resulting set supplies the cases for a fixed attack protocol.
The evaluation-data gate admits a case only after checking its source, version, expected result, access assumptions, coverage tags, and known development overlap. The denominator is every required coverage item and every candidate case, with missing coverage and rejected cases reported separately. Held-out maintenance and realistic substitutes consume expert time and may omit rare failures. Undetected contamination or an unrealistic substitute can make results look stronger than deployment. Recovery quarantines affected cases and rebuilds the set. Every result that used those cases then runs again. A clean overlap check cannot prove absence from unknown model training data.
crumbs: Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure
14  Deciding whether to release

title: 14  Deciding whether to release
text:
14.3 Attack protocols
An attack protocol states what the evaluator knows, can change, and can observe during one trial. It fixes the query, time, and interaction budgets, reset conditions, success rule, and stopping point. Repeated trials matter when sampling or external state can produce different results from the same item.
NIST AI 800-3 recommends choosing the evaluation target before the estimator and models repeated trials to separate item and sampling variation.[^c14-s03-8003] The NIST Generative AI Profile includes red teaming, security testing, and reassessment among its measurement actions.[^c14-s03-genai] The publications do not select an attack budget or trial count for this release decision.
For each case, the evaluator starts from a recorded state and applies only allowed changes. The harness records each query and response before success is judged from the predefined outcome. The protocol also captures failed attempts because they affect cost and uncertainty. A fixed protocol supports comparison, but a defense may exploit its weaknesses. Adaptive red teaming checks whether the result remains after an evaluator learns from those weaknesses.
The evaluation harness enforces the protocol by checking initial state, allowed attacker operations, query and time budgets, reset state, and stopping rules. It reports successful attacks over all eligible trials, with protocol violations excluded and counted. Repeated trials consume model calls, reviewer time, and external-service capacity. Hidden state, incomplete resets, or a test-aware defense can bypass the comparison. Recovery restores the recorded state and corrects the harness before affected trials run again. A reproducible protocol does not establish that its attacker strategy is strong.
crumbs: Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure
14  Deciding whether to release

title: 14  Deciding whether to release
text:
14.4 Adaptive red teaming
A fixed attack may fail because it cannot reach the defense’s real weak point. Adaptive red teaming allows the evaluator to inspect observed failures and form a hypothesis about the control. The evaluator can then change the attack within the stated threat model. The resulting evidence is stronger when another evaluator can reproduce the bypass and when a fix is tested against both the original and changed attack.
Athalye, Carlini, and Wagner described signs of obfuscated gradients and adapted attacks to the defense instead of treating failure of an unchanged attack as evidence of security.[^c14-s04-method] In the nine defenses they examined, seven relied on obfuscated gradients. Their attacks fully bypassed six and partly bypassed one.[^c14-s04-result] Those numbers apply to adversarial-example defenses in that study, not to prompt injection or tool-using agents.
The transferable lesson is methodological. A failed test can reveal a weak test as easily as a strong defense. In the hypothetical evaluation, the red team changes placement, encoding, timing, and interaction strategy while keeping access and budget fixed. Reviewers record why each adjustment is allowed and what it demonstrates. The observed outcomes then need metrics that state both the denominator and uncertainty.
The red-team lead enforces the threat model and budget while allowing changes to attack strategy. The report counts reproduced bypasses over all eligible cases and records attempted adaptations that failed. Adaptation adds specialist time and makes comparisons harder when evaluators choose different paths. Missing expertise, undisclosed defense behavior, or a narrow budget can leave bypasses unseen. Recovery repairs the control and preserves the successful trace. An independent replay and clean-task regression then qualify the change, although failure to find another bypass does not prove that none exists.
crumbs: Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure
14  Deciding whether to release

title: 14  Deciding whether to release
text:
14.5 Metrics and uncertainty
A security metric is interpretable only when its eligible trials and success conditions are explicit. Attack success rate divides successful attacks by eligible attack trials. Precision and recall describe different detector errors, while the base rate affects how many alerts correspond to real failures. Reviewer workload belongs beside these rates because a detector can shift cost to people.
NIST AI 800-3 separates the quantity an evaluation intends to estimate from the statistic computed on observed trials.[^c14-s05-target] It also models variation across items and repeated trials and warns that simpler estimators can omit uncertainty.[^c14-s05-variance] The NIST/SEMATECH handbook provides Wilson and exact binomial intervals for a proportion.[^c14-s05-ci] A simple binomial interval can mislead when trials cluster by task, prompt, model, or evaluator.
The release report states the denominator, point estimate, interval method, item grouping, repeated-trial design, and number of human reviews. It reports utility failures separately from security failures. Sparse high-impact cases remain visible instead of disappearing into an average. These calculations support a decision only if versions, graders, and procedures can be checked, which leads to evaluation reliability.
Worked denominator and uncertainty example (hypothetical). The operating mode is release evaluation of one fixed application version. The evaluator runs six adversarial tasks three times each, for 18 eligible trials. The success rule is a protected value appearing in the final answer. The result is three successful trials.
The attack success rate is (3 / 18 = 0.167), or 16.7 percent. A 95 percent Wilson interval for 3 successes in 18 trials is approximately 5.8 to 39.2 percent. The point estimate alone hides that wide range. The 18 trials also come from only six tasks, so a binomial interval that treats every trial as independent can understate uncertainty created by task clustering.
The release record keeps the 3 successful attacks and the 18 eligible trials. It also records that those trials came from 6 distinct tasks. The observed rate exceeds zero and remains imprecise, while these hypothetical values do not establish a real system’s risk. The interval also cannot correct poor task coverage or a biased success grader.
The release rule converts these measurements into allow, staged, or block decisions after checking the denominator, uncertainty, impact class, and clean utility. Review cost includes duplicate trials, adjudication, and investigation of false alerts. Clustered tasks, a weak grader, or averaging across high-impact cases can defeat the metric. Recovery rejects the affected estimate and corrects the design or grader. The decision is then recomputed from retained trial records. A precise interval does not prove representative coverage.
crumbs: Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure
14  Deciding whether to release

title: 14  Deciding whether to release
text:
14.6 Evaluation reliability
Evaluation reliability concerns whether another qualified team can understand and repeat the result closely enough for the same decision. The record includes model and application versions, system prompts, tool schemas, data snapshots, sampling settings, random seeds where available, external service state, grader versions, and adjudication rules. Hosted services may leave some state unavailable, which becomes a stated limit.
The AI RMF calls for documenting measurement methods, metrics, test sets, tools, limitations, and independent review where appropriate.[^c14-s06-rmf] NIST AI 800-3 shows that conclusions depend on the statistical model, its assumptions, and the target quantity.[^c14-s06-8003] These sources do not validate an automated grader or remove model-version drift.
The organization samples automated grades for human review and records disagreements. It reruns a stable subset after version changes. Supplier benchmark claims enter the record with their task, configuration, and access assumptions rather than serving as direct release evidence. Research on language-model judges and reproducible hosted-agent evaluations remains incomplete. The release owner can now weigh measured results with these limits.
Before accepting a result, the service verifies versions, configuration, data snapshots, grader identity, and adjudication rules. The review process accepts a result only after those checks pass. The denominator is every required rerun, with reproduced decisions and material disagreements reported separately. Duplicate execution, storage, and human review add cost. Hosted drift, unavailable random state, or shared grader errors can bypass reproducibility checks. Recovery freezes the claim and restores an inspectable version where possible. The stable subset then runs under independent review. Agreement does not prove that the underlying success rule is valid.
crumbs: Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure
14  Deciding whether to release

title: 14  Deciding whether to release
text:
14.7 Release and change criteria
A release decision joins test results with the organization’s risk limit and the planned exposure. The record states minimum utility and security thresholds, unresolved cases, the responsible owner, staged user or data scope, rollback conditions, and changes that require reevaluation. A threshold has meaning only for the scope, data, protocol, and uncertainty already documented.
The NIST Generative AI Profile recommends minimum thresholds, go or no-go policies, and a plan to halt deployment when risk is unacceptable.[^c14-s07-go] It also recommends evaluation before and during deployment, periodic review, and after-action review.[^c14-s07-review] The profile leaves the threshold and risk acceptance authority to the organization.
The hypothetical decision may allow a proposal-only pilot for one department while blocking external actions until action tests pass. A model, retrieval corpus, tool schema, permission policy, or control change can trigger focused or full reevaluation according to its possible effect. Release evidence qualifies the tested setup and expires as that setup changes. Chapter 15 turns these accepted limits into runtime enforcement and observations.
The deployment gate enforces the decision by checking approved versions and measured thresholds. It also checks unresolved failures, the exposure limit, the owner, and rollback triggers before each stage. The denominator is the planned users, data classes, and capabilities for that stage, with actual exposure compared against each limit. Staging delays access and requires parallel support for rollback. An unrecorded configuration change or alternate deployment route can bypass the gate. Recovery removes access and restores the accepted version. Failed traces are preserved for reevaluation before expansion. Approval does not transfer to a wider population or changed system.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. A hypothetical release candidate is the organization support application with external inference, approved retrieval, and proposal-only tool access. It completes 94 of 100 clean tasks. It also has 3 successful attacks in 18 eligible adversarial trials drawn from 6 tasks, with a Wilson interval of about 5.8 to 39.2 percent. The release rule requires at least 90 percent clean completion and no demonstrated high-impact disclosure. What is the decision?
Answer. The candidate meets the clean-task threshold but fails the security rule because three trials produced the stated high-impact disclosure. The organization should record a blocked release for this scope and preserve the versions and traces. It should repair the failure path before rerunning both the clean and adversarial cases. The wide interval also shows that the test gives an imprecise rate. It does not weaken the zero-tolerance rule for an observed high-impact outcome. All values are hypothetical.

The chapter retains explicit evidence gaps for data overlap, automated graders, and evaluations of changing hosted systems.

title: 15  Keeping the live system in bounds
text:
15.1 Control placement
Security question. Which harmful actions can be prevented or detected while the system is running?
Reference frame. Operate an action-capable organization application with organization-side traces and only the provider records actually available. An internal-model variation adds serving and infrastructure observations rather than assuming identical visibility.
Connection through the book. Turn the tested failure paths from Chapter 14 into useful events and response triggers. Chapter 16 consumes those records when an incident is suspected.
Runtime controls differ in what they can actually stop. An advisory check produces information for a model or person. A blocking check sits at an enforcement point and can prevent the protected operation. Control placement identifies the input, retrieval, output, or action boundary where a decision is made and the object that decision protects.
Complete mediation calls for checking access where each protected object is used, while least privilege limits the rights available to a process.1 The NIST Generative AI Profile recommends comparing observed behavior with organizational risk limits and monitoring third-party models within stated bounds.[^c15-s01-genai] These sources guide placement and monitoring but do not establish the accuracy of a filter or detector.
The hypothetical application screens incoming content and checks retrieval permissions before context assembly. It validates structured output before the business service authorizes the resolved action. A model warning may advise, while the service decision can block. Each control record states its input, outcome, fail state, and protected action. Those decisions form the application trace examined next.
The control review tests each enforcement point with allowed and forbidden inputs and records blocked protected operations over all eligible attempts. It also reports clean operations completed over their separate denominator. Added checks increase latency and can reduce availability when a dependency fails. An alternate action path or a warning that is mistaken for enforcement can bypass the intended boundary. Recovery disables the exposed route and restores the last accepted policy before both case groups run again. A passing control at one point does not prove that later components preserve its decision.
crumbs: Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure
15  Keeping the live system in bounds

title: 15  Keeping the live system in bounds
text:
15.2 Application traces
An application trace links one user request to the identities, model call, retrieved sources, policy decisions, tool arguments, external results, and final response that followed. Correlation identifiers connect events across services. The trace also has a security boundary because prompts, retrieved text, outputs, and tool results may contain sensitive information.
NIST log-management guidance treats generation, transfer, storage, access, analysis, retention, and disposal as one managed process.[^c15-s02-logs] The NIST incident-response profile calls for logs to be generated and available for continuous monitoring.[^c15-s02-ir] The older log guidance does not define AI-specific fields, and neither source supports indiscriminate recording of sensitive content.
The organization records stable identifiers and decisions by default, then retains sensitive payloads only when a stated purpose and access rule justify them. Encryption, field-level removal, restricted access, and retention limits follow the data classification. A trace schema that covers identity, retrieval, model, policy, and tool events still lacks one stable industry standard. Infrastructure observations add evidence that the application alone cannot see.
The logging pipeline enforces trace admission and access by checking event type, correlation identifier, sensitivity, reader role, retention rule, and storage result. The coverage measure is expected events received over all expected events in sampled requests, with late and unreadable records counted separately. Rich traces cost storage and can increase privacy exposure. Dropped events, clock skew, or reused identifiers can break reconstruction. Recovery preserves local records and repairs the pipeline. Retained events are replayed where possible, and permanent gaps are marked because complete expected events do not prove that every relevant action emitted a log.
crumbs: Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure

title: 15  Keeping the live system in bounds
text:
15.3 Infrastructure observations
Application logs show intended operations, while infrastructure observations show processes, containers, network connections, accelerator use, storage access, scheduler events, cloud control-plane activity, and billing. Application and infrastructure observations answer different questions. A tool call can look normal in the application trace while the worker contacts an unexpected destination or consumes unusual resources.
NIST continuous-monitoring guidance separates organization, mission or business process, and information-system monitoring levels.[^c15-s03-levels] It also describes a strategy and program for collecting, analyzing, and reporting security information.[^c15-s03-program] The guidance supplies a program model rather than current telemetry fields for accelerators, hosted models, or token billing.
The hypothetical worker attaches the application correlation identifier to its job, process, network, and cloud events. Monitoring joins these events without assuming that a hosted-model provider exposes equivalent detail. An internal model adds serving and accelerator observations, while an external model may expose only request identifiers and supplier reports. These signals support runtime failure indicators.
Concrete control-event trace (hypothetical). The operating mode is live retrieval-based inference. Request req-882 starts worker job job-417 for employee E17. The application trace records one model call and no approved tool action.

Joining on the request and job identifiers connects a normal model response to unexpected worker behavior and two blocking decisions. The infrastructure controls observed and stopped those events in this trace without explaining the worker’s intent or proving that no other connection succeeded. Times, identifiers, and results are hypothetical.
Host sensors, network controls, and the scheduler enforce or observe different states, while the join service checks request, job, workload, and time links before correlating them. The measurement reports joined expected events over all events required by the trace design. Telemetry collection consumes storage and processing and may expose operational details. Missing provider records, clock errors, or an uninstrumented host can bypass the joined view. Recovery contains the workload and preserves each available source. Collection is repaired before the timeline is reconstructed with explicit gaps. Correlation does not establish intent or attribution.

title: 15  Keeping the live system in bounds
text:
15.4 Runtime failure indicators
A runtime indicator is a measurable condition associated with a tested failure path. Examples include access to a forbidden resource, a new external destination, repeated failed tool calls, an abrupt resource increase, or use of stale retrieved content. An indicator needs enough request and system context to distinguish a likely boundary violation from ordinary variation.
NIST continuous-monitoring guidance says monitoring should support assessment of the security impact of changes and response to findings.[^c15-s04-iscm] The NIST Generative AI Profile recommends evaluating post-deployment monitoring and comparing behavior with defined risk limits.[^c15-s04-genai] These sources leave detection rates, base rates, and thresholds unspecified for prompt injection, retrieval poisoning, and unusual tool use.
The organization derives each indicator from a Chapter 14 test case and records the expected signal, threshold, required context, and response owner. A forbidden-resource event can be exact, while a resource spike needs a workload baseline. Evidence for realistic AI runtime indicator performance remains incomplete, so initial alerts need measurement and review. Their usefulness depends on alert quality and routing.
The detector evaluates the current event and baseline. It can allow ordinary processing or block a protected operation where it has authority. Otherwise, it sends an alert. Evaluation reports detected failures over all confirmed failures and valid alerts over all alerts, with latency and review count beside them. Lower thresholds catch more variation but increase interruptions and analyst work. Drift, sparse context, or an attacker staying below threshold can bypass detection. Recovery contains the affected path and adjusts or disables a faulty rule before labeled cases run again, while detector performance remains insufficient evidence that unobserved failures were absent.
crumbs: Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure
15  Keeping the live system in bounds

title: 15  Keeping the live system in bounds
text:
15.5 Alert quality and response routing
Alert quality depends on both detector performance and the frequency of the underlying event. When true incidents are rare, even a detector with good sensitivity can produce many false positives. Priority also depends on the protected asset, possible impact, confidence, and time available for containment. An alert without supporting context shifts reconstruction work to the responder.
The NIST incident-response profile calls for detected events to be analyzed, correlated, placed in context, routed, and declared as incidents when criteria are met.[^c15-s05-detect] It also calls for reports to be triaged, validated, categorized, and prioritized.[^c15-s05-respond] The profile defines desired outcomes rather than an AI alert score or measured analyst workload.
Each alert includes the trace identifier, triggering evidence, affected identity and asset, relevant control, severity basis, and responsible route. Suppression groups repeated manifestations of the same event without hiding distinct users or targets. Investigation outcomes update the indicator’s measured precision and workload. The control still needs predictable behavior when its detector, policy service, or reviewer is unavailable.
The routing service sets priority and destination from incident criteria, asset impact, confidence, and response ownership. The denominator is every generated alert, with delivered, acknowledged, suppressed, escalated, and missed alerts counted separately. Faster escalation takes analyst time and can interrupt low-risk work. Broad suppression, stale ownership, or unavailable communication can hide an urgent case. Recovery removes faulty suppression and reroutes queued alerts. The fallback owner then reviews the affected interval because delivery and acknowledgment do not prove correct triage.
crumbs: Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure
15  Keeping the live system in bounds

title: 15  Keeping the live system in bounds
text:
15.6 Control resilience
Control resilience concerns the system’s behavior when a detector, policy service, log sink, or human reviewer becomes slow or unavailable. A fail-open path continues an operation. A fail-closed path blocks it. The choice depends on the safety and availability consequences of each state. Quotas, rate limits, time limits, and stopping rules can remain enforceable even when a secondary detector fails.
Saltzer and Schroeder’s fail-safe-defaults principle bases access on permission so that failure does not silently broaden access.[^c15-s06-saltzer] The NIST Generative AI Profile recommends defined limits and monitoring for third-party models.[^c15-s06-genai] These sources do not decide the fail state for every service or test degraded policy, logging, approval, and detector components.
The hypothetical action service blocks consequential changes when current authorization is unavailable but may serve a clearly marked read-only fallback from approved data. It preserves minimal local evidence until the protected log path returns and applies the normal retention rule afterward. Failure-injection evidence and the balance between privacy and incident records remain open. Chapter 16 begins with the event and retained evidence produced by this runtime design.
Fault injection tests the enforcing service with unavailable policy, detector, log, approval, and identity dependencies. The report counts protected operations that entered the intended fail state over all injected failures and measures clean availability separately. Fail-closed behavior can stop legitimate work, while fail-open behavior accepts more security risk. A shared dependency failure or untested fallback can defeat both paths. Recovery restores the service and reconciles actions with local records from the degraded interval. The injection then runs again, although the correct fail state does not prove that retained evidence is complete.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. A hypothetical application trace shows a normal answer and no approved tool action. Infrastructure records for the same request show denied external egress and a stopped process after the job exceeded its process limit. How should monitoring represent this event?
Answer. Join the application, scheduler, process, and network records with stable request and job identifiers. Preserve the model version, worker identity, destination, policy decisions, process counts, and final task state. Route an alert for unexpected egress plus resource-limit enforcement, with the joined records attached. The evidence supports a blocked abnormal path and an incomplete request. It does not establish attacker control or show that every route was observed.

The chapter retains explicit evidence gaps for trace schemas, AI-specific indicators, and degraded-control tests.

title: 16  Recovering from AI incidents
text:
16.1 Incident triage
Security question. How does an organization contain an AI incident and know that recovery is complete?
Reference frame. Investigate one organization incident packet, with document versions, identity decisions, tool requests, and incomplete supplier records. A second packet covers a compromised organization-operated worker.
Connection through the book. Walk backward from the observed consequence and test competing explanations. Reuse Chapters 3, 9, 11, 12, and 15 to contain the path and verify recovery before returning to service.
A security event is an observable occurrence relevant to security. An incident is an event that meets the organization’s criteria for response. Triage separates ordinary model error from policy violation, hostile-content influence, account or infrastructure compromise, disclosure, and resource abuse. Classification matters because each path needs different evidence and containment.
NIST distinguishes cybersecurity events from incidents and places validation, categorization, prioritization, and incident declaration in the response process.1 It also presents response as part of continuing cybersecurity risk management rather than a separate linear phase.[^c16-s01-cycle] The profile does not supply AI-specific categories or one universal declaration threshold.
The hypothetical responder starts from a routed alert and checks the affected asset, observed outcome, identities, time window, system version, and supporting trace. A low-quality answer with no boundary violation remains a model-quality issue. A forbidden disclosure or unauthorized action enters incident handling. The declaration record states confidence and missing evidence. Preservation begins before containment changes volatile state.
The incident lead enforces triage by checking the event against documented criteria and affected assets. Observed outcomes and available evidence determine whether it is declared, downgraded, or escalated. The denominator is every routed event, with declarations, later reclassifications, and time to decision reported separately. Rapid triage consumes responder capacity and can interrupt service. Missing traces or an incorrect model-error label can hide an incident. Recovery reopens the case and preserves newly found evidence. Any containment change includes the reason for reclassification. A correct category does not prove complete scope.

title: 16  Recovering from AI incidents
text:
16.2 Evidence preservation
Evidence preservation keeps records available and trustworthy enough to reconstruct the event. Relevant material can include prompts and outputs with retrieved document versions. Policy decisions, tool traces, model and code identities, process state, network events, credentials, and supplier records may also matter. Some data may already be missing or inaccessible, which belongs in the evidence record.
The NIST incident-response profile calls for recording response actions and preserving the integrity of incident records and data.[^c16-s02-ir] NIST forensic guidance begins with identifying, labeling, recording, and acquiring relevant data while preserving integrity.[^c16-s02-forensics] The forensic publication predates current AI systems and does not supply an AI evidence list or legal procedure.
The responder copies volatile records first and records the acquisition time with its method. Stable files receive hashes. Access is restricted while original versions are preserved. Provider records are requested through the available contract, while unavailable fields remain explicit. Hashes can reveal later file changes but cannot prove that the original record was complete or truthful. Preserved artifacts provide the basis for timeline and scope analysis.
Concrete preservation record (hypothetical). The operating mode is incident response to request req-882, which attempted an unapproved external connection. The preservation task starts before the worker is terminated because process and memory state are volatile.

For each stable export, the evidence register identifies the collector, time, method, access restriction, and file hash. It marks the provider trace as missing rather than treating silence as proof that no provider event occurred. The conclusion is that the listed artifacts can support a bounded timeline and integrity check. The shortened identifiers and results are hypothetical, and hashes cannot show that the original logs were complete.
The collection process preserves evidence only after checking each expected source, acquisition method, time, integrity record, access rule, and storage result. The coverage denominator is all sources required by the incident map, with acquired, unavailable, overwritten, and untrusted items separated. Preservation costs storage and can retain sensitive content longer than ordinary operations allow. Volatile loss, tampered source logs, or inaccessible supplier records can bypass the record. Recovery captures later snapshots and requests external evidence. Weak artifacts receive restricted use when conclusions are updated. A matching hash proves only that the captured file did not later change.

title: 16  Recovering from AI incidents
text:
16.3 Investigation and scope
Investigation links the initial entry point to affected identities and accessed records. It then checks executed actions and modified artifacts. Observed harm is recorded separately. A timeline orders evidence from application, identity, retrieval, tool, provider, host, and network sources. Competing explanations remain under consideration until the records distinguish them. Attribution confidence remains separate from confidence about the technical path.
NIST forensic guidance separates collection, examination, analysis, and reporting across files, operating systems, networks, and application data.[^c16-s03-forensics] The NIST incident-response profile includes root-cause analysis as a response outcome.[^c16-s03-root] These sources provide process structure without making attribution certain or defining AI-specific artifacts.
In the hypothetical case, the team correlates a hostile document version with its retrieval, the model request, a proposed tool call, the policy decision, and the external result. It checks whether account compromise or a changed tool service could produce the same trace. Each conclusion cites supporting and conflicting records. The scoped identities, components, sources, and destinations define the containment set.
The case lead accepts or rejects each path hypothesis after checking its required events against the preserved timeline. The denominator is every system, identity, record, and destination reachable from the supported path, with examined and unresolved items reported separately. Wider scope consumes time and delays restoration. Missing telemetry, false correlation, or a second entry point can leave the scope too small. Recovery expands containment and collects new sources. The revised timeline then supports another review of affected conclusions. A coherent path does not establish actor attribution or exclude concurrent activity.
crumbs: Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure
16  Recovering from AI incidents

title: 16  Recovering from AI incidents
text:
16.4 Containment
Containment reduces ongoing harm while preserving enough state for investigation. Available actions include revoking credentials and suspending a tool. The organization can also isolate a worker or block a destination. Freezing an affected data source and narrowing user access address other paths. The sequence depends on which path is active and whether a change would destroy volatile evidence.
The NIST incident-response profile calls for incidents to be contained and eradicated.[^c16-s04-ir] International secure AI guidance recommends preparing incident procedures and mechanisms for responsible deployment and operation.[^c16-s04-ncsc] These outcome statements do not choose the right containment action or sequence for the current incident.
For the hostile-document case, the organization first preserves the source and traces, then disables the affected connector and action credential. If a worker compromise remains possible, it isolates that workload and blocks external routes. Each containment action has an owner, expected effect, validation check, and reversal condition. Once the path is stable, recovery can restore known assets and permissions.
The identity service and connector manager revoke access according to the supported path. Destination blocking occurs at the network gateway, while the workload controller isolates execution. The measure is confirmed blocked paths over all known active paths, with service impact and unresolved routes recorded beside it. Broad containment interrupts legitimate work and may destroy volatile state if applied too early. Unknown credentials, alternate connectors, or a compromised control plane can bypass local action. Recovery widens isolation and rotates related access. Affected control components are replaced before each path is validated again, while blocking known routes remains insufficient evidence that the incident has ended.
crumbs: Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure
16  Recovering from AI incidents

title: 16  Recovering from AI incidents
text:
16.5 Recovery verification
Recovery restores a known state and demonstrates that the incident path no longer works. Affected state may include application code and model packages. System prompts, indexes, caches, agent memory, credentials, tool schemas, and access policy may also require restoration. Service availability alone cannot establish recovery if the same disclosure or action remains possible.
The NIST incident-response profile calls for checking restoration assets before use and verifying restored systems. It also calls for confirmation of normal operation before recovery is declared complete.[^c16-s05-ir] The NIST Generative AI Profile recommends post-incident review and practice of response plans.[^c16-s05-genai] These sources leave AI-specific checks for indexes, caches, memory, and authorization to the recovery design.
The hypothetical recovery rebuilds the index from approved source versions and clears affected caches. It rotates credentials before restoring reviewed configuration and rerunning the original failure trace. It also runs clean task cases to confirm that the service still works. Each affected asset has a test and expected result. Passing those tests supports a bounded recovery decision and provides evidence for follow-up actions.
The recovery owner authorizes return to service only after checking every affected asset, original failure case, clean task, identity, destination, and remaining evidence gap. The denominator is all required recovery checks, with pass, fail, blocked, and unavailable results kept separate. Rebuilds and repeated tests extend downtime and can lose useful cached state. An untracked copy, unchanged supplier component, or weak regression case can preserve the failure. Another failed check rolls back the attempted restoration and narrows service. The missing state is corrected before the gate runs again. Passing supports the tested state only.
crumbs: Part V: Proving controls and recovering from failure
16  Recovering from AI incidents

title: 16  Recovering from AI incidents
text:
16.6 Follow-up and retirement
Follow-up turns incident evidence into changes to controls, tests, contracts, and training. It also decides which records remain for legal, operational, or research purposes and which data and access must be removed. Service retirement includes revoking identities and disabling connectors. It also ends supplier access and checks known derived stores.
The NIST incident-response profile integrates lessons and improvement into risk management after response and recovery.[^c16-s06-lessons] NIST media-sanitization guidance separates the sanitization decision from verification and validation of the result.[^c16-s06-media] Media sanitization alone cannot prove deletion from hosted-model parameters, supplier backups, indexes, or distributed caches.
The organization assigns each corrective action to a responsible owner and links it to a test or contract result. Retention and notification follow current sector and jurisdiction rules, which require separate legal sources. Supplier exit evidence records what the organization can verify and what remains outside its visibility. The incident record also shows why harmful activity does not by itself prove that AI caused or improved it. Chapter 17 changes the object of analysis from an AI system under attack to an attacker using AI, then applies the same separation of observation, inference, and unsupported attribution.
The closure owner chooses retention, deletion, retirement, or reopening after checking corrective-action evidence, access revocation, supplier response, and applicable obligations. The denominator is every agreed follow-up action and every service identity or connector in the retirement record. Longer retention raises storage and privacy cost, while early deletion can weaken later investigation. An unlisted supplier copy or forgotten credential can bypass retirement. Recovery extends the hold when justified and revokes remaining access. Missing evidence is requested before closure checks run again because administrative closure does not prove deletion from systems outside organizational visibility.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. A hypothetical hostile document influenced request req-882, which then attempted external egress. The worker was stopped, but the provider trace is unavailable. What response record supports containment and recovery?
Answer. Preserve volatile process and connection state first, followed by application, retrieval, policy, tool, runtime, identity, and network records. Record acquisition details, hashes for stable exports, access limits, and the missing provider evidence. Reconstruct the path before revoking credentials and isolating the affected worker. Rebuild the index from approved document versions, clear affected caches, rotate exposed credentials, and rerun the original failure trace plus clean tasks. Recovery is supported only when the prohibited path fails and intended work still succeeds. Missing provider evidence remains a limit on scope and attribution.

The chapter retains explicit limits for supplier evidence, logical deletion, and jurisdiction-specific notification duties.

title: Part VI: Assessing AI in cyber work
text:
Chapters in this part
The same methods that help a defender analyze information can help an attacker. This part separates capability claims, observed misuse, and measured defensive value. It also treats a security assistant as an AI system requiring the controls already taught.
Connection through the book. Change AI’s role while retaining the earlier method. First assess claims that an attacker used AI, then build a defensive analyst assistant using the retrieval and action controls already taught. Compare model and hosting choices only after the task and useful outcome are defined.
Part outcome. A measured decision about where AI helps a security task and what oversight and operating cost it requires.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cyber work

title: Part VI: Assessing AI in cyber work
text:
Assessing AI-assisted harm: This chapter assesses claims about AI-assisted harm by separating demonstrated capability, observed use, prevalence, and the defensive controls justified by the evidence.
Using AI safely in defense: This chapter applies the book’s safeguards to a security team’s own AI assistant, keeping human judgment and action authority visible while measuring useful work.
Choosing a viable deployment: This chapter compares external, managed, and internal model choices only after the organization has fixed the task, data access, quality target, action limits, and full operating cost.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cyber work

title: 17  Assessing AI-assisted harm
text:
17.1 AI across an intrusion workflow
Security question. Which parts of an attack can AI improve, and what evidence shows that the improvement matters?
Reference frame. Change the question from attacks on an organization to an attacker using AI assistance. Use hypothetical impersonation examples and separately identified incident or laboratory evidence. Do not silently equate generated content with autonomous operation.
Connection through the book. The threat-model and evaluation methods still apply, but AI’s role changes. Chapter 18 uses this attack context to evaluate a defensive assistant.
Finding AI somewhere in an intrusion does not show that it changed the attack. Assessment starts by locating its role in reconnaissance, vulnerability work, social engineering, code generation, operations, or analysis of stolen data. The evidence then distinguishes simple assistance from higher speed, scale, quality, success, or a capability that was otherwise unavailable.
The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) places current AI use across several intrusion activities in its highest likelihood band. The activities include reconnaissance, exploit development, social engineering, basic malware generation, and processing of exfiltrated data.1 It expects near-term growth mainly through existing tactics, techniques, and procedures.[^c17-s01-outlook] This probabilistic intelligence assessment covers the period through 2027 without supplying a controlled experiment or incident count.
For each claim, the organization records the task, model access, human input, tools, baseline, output, and observed operational result. “AI assisted reconnaissance” is weaker than evidence that it found more valid targets in less time under the same conditions. This common evidence frame supports the impersonation, programming, automation, and incident examples that follow.
Concrete role assessment (hypothetical). The operating mode is retrospective review of an intrusion report. The reported task was finding public employee contact details. The actor supplied search terms to an external model and manually selected results. An ordinary mailing tool then sent the messages. The report contains model transcripts and sent-message records but no comparison with unaided research.
The records show model assistance during information synthesis and human control over selection and sending. They do not show faster discovery or more valid contacts. They also leave autonomous operation and any new capability unsupported. The conclusion is limited to observed assistance in one stage. Every role and record in this assessment is hypothetical.
The evidence-review gate accepts a capability statement only after checking the task, model access, human steps, baseline, measured result, and missing records. The denominator is every assessed intrusion stage, with supported, unsupported, and unknown AI effects kept separate. Detailed review takes analyst time and depends on access to sensitive records. Incomplete reporting or selection of only successful episodes can bypass the comparison. Recovery narrows or withdraws the claim while missing evidence is requested. The assessment then runs again, but an accepted role claim still does not establish improvement or prevalence.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cyber work
17  Assessing AI-assisted harm

title: 17  Assessing AI-assisted harm
text:
17.2 Impersonation and fraud
Impersonation combines a false identity claim with a business process that accepts the claim. Generated text, voice, image, or video can increase realism or scale. The consequential failure occurs when a person or system authorizes a payment. Sharing sensitive data or changing access are other possible effects. Assessment keeps the synthetic content and the transaction path separate.
The FBI reported a campaign beginning in April 2025 that used text messages and AI-generated voice messages while impersonating senior United States officials.[^c17-s02-campaign] The agency recommends independent verification through a known contact method instead of relying on the received message.[^c17-s02-advice] The alert documents one campaign and advice. It does not estimate prevalence or measure a verification control’s effectiveness.
In a hypothetical finance case, a synthetic voice instructs an employee to change a supplier account. The defensive trace records the claimed identity and received channel. It then records the requested transaction, independent callback, and authorization result. Even perfect media detection would leave the business process exposed to ordinary impersonation. This example shows why the AI claim and the process failure need separate evidence.
The transaction service enforces the decision by checking the account, requested change, independent verification result, current approver, and second approval where required. The test reports blocked impersonation attempts over all eligible attempts and legitimate changes delayed or rejected over all valid requests. Independent contact adds time and can slow urgent work. Compromise of the verification channel or collusion can bypass it. Recovery freezes the change and reverses the transaction when possible. Affected access is reset before verification runs again, although one blocked attempt does not measure general effectiveness or prove that the content was synthetic.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cyber work
17  Assessing AI-assisted harm

title: 17  Assessing AI-assisted harm
text:
17.3 Programming and analysis assistance
Programming and analysis assistance can help with code generation, translation, debugging, vulnerability research, exploit work, and interpretation of large data sets. A capability claim needs a defined task and a baseline with comparable access, time, skill, and success criteria. Output volume alone does not establish useful attacker progress.
The NCSC assessment includes vulnerability research, exploit development, basic malware generation, and data processing among activities that AI can assist.[^c17-s03-ncsc] Pearce and colleagues found vulnerable suggestions in some scenarios tested with an early GitHub Copilot version.[^c17-s03-pearce] The first source lacks controlled task baselines, while the second studied defensive code quality rather than attacker productivity.
A useful experiment compares people with and without the assistant on the same synthetic vulnerability tasks, then measures valid findings, time, false claims, required correction, and end-to-end success. Current packet sources do not provide that attacker-uplift result, so this chapter leaves the magnitude open. Clear task evidence is also needed before describing the work as automated.
Worked evidence assessment (hypothetical). The operating mode is a controlled comparison on eight synthetic code-analysis tasks. The same four participants alternate between unaided work and an assistant. The target for each task is a previously planted defect with a fixed validation test.

The observed intermediate results show one additional valid finding and 18 fewer elapsed minutes with the assistant, alongside two additional false claims and 11 additional correction minutes. The conclusion is that assistance changed outcomes in this small exercise under these access conditions. It does not establish attacker productivity in operational systems because the sample is small, task order may matter, and the participants and synthetic defects may not represent real attacks. All values are hypothetical.
The study-review gate accepts an uplift claim only when the baseline and assistant conditions use the same eligible tasks, access, validation tests, and outcome rules. The denominator is all assigned tasks and participants, with valid findings, false claims, elapsed time, and correction time reported separately. Controlled comparison consumes expert time and can reveal sensitive techniques. Learning effects, task mismatch, or selective reporting can bypass the inference. Recovery withdraws the claim and corrects the design before the comparison runs again. A measured difference does not establish operational harm.
