title: 17  Assessing AI-assisted harm
text:
17.4 Degrees of automation
Automation has observable steps. A person may request and select each output. A fixed script may repeat preset operations, while a model may choose a sequence. A tool loop may change that sequence after observing results. Claims of autonomy become specific only when they identify who sets the goal and chooses actions. They also identify who supplies credentials and reviews results. The stopping authority is recorded separately.
MITRE ATLAS labels technique evidence as Feasible, Demonstrated, or Realized.[^c17-s04-atlas] The NCSC assessment distinguishes AI assistance across intrusion stages but does not define a general automation scale.[^c17-s04-ncsc] ATLAS maturity concerns evidence for a technique rather than the level of agent control. These sources do not support a precise universal autonomy taxonomy.
The chapter uses a descriptive trace with separate records for human selection and fixed automation. Model planning, tool execution, and adaptation also receive separate records. A system can plan without permission to act, or execute a fixed script without model planning. The absence of an established operational scale remains an evidence gap. This trace lets benchmark and incident reports state exactly what occurred.
The claim reviewer allows an automation label only after checking who set the goal and selected actions. The review also checks who supplied credentials and approved effects. It records who observed results and stopped the sequence. The denominator is every consequential step in the reported workflow, with human, fixed-software, model-selected, and unknown control recorded separately. Detailed tracing costs storage and investigative time. Missing tool logs or hidden human intervention can bypass the classification. Recovery lowers the claim to the strongest supported level and seeks the absent records. A complete step trace does not establish greater capability or success.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cyber work
17  Assessing AI-assisted harm

title: 17  Assessing AI-assisted harm
text:
17.5 Incident and benchmark evidence
Security sources answer different questions. Feasibility means a mechanism can work under stated conditions. A controlled demonstration shows it in an experiment. An observed incident records operational use. Prevalence estimates how often it occurs in a defined population. Attribution links activity to an actor or system with stated confidence. Moving up this ladder requires new evidence.
MITRE ATLAS separates Feasible, Demonstrated, and Realized technique maturity.[^c17-s05-atlas] The NCSC report states assessed likelihoods and a forecast horizon, while the FBI alert records a specific campaign.[^c17-s05-ncsc] The FBI case supports observed AI-assisted impersonation without establishing frequency.[^c17-s05-fbi] Combining an intelligence assessment and one alert cannot create a prevalence estimate.
An evidence record captures source type, access and task conditions, model or tool version, baseline, observed result, reporting incentives, and uncertainty. A vendor demonstration may establish feasibility. A first-party incident report may establish observed use but still omit attribution detail. This ladder prevents a laboratory result from becoming a claim about common operational harm and sets the standard for information-manipulation claims.
The evidence gate assigns the strongest supported class only after checking all required fields and the source’s direct observations. The denominator is every report assessed for the claim, with accepted, rejected, duplicate, and incomplete sources separated. Collection and verification consume analyst time, while strict admission can leave timely questions unresolved. Publication bias, missing incidents, or copied reporting can distort the evidence set. Recovery changes the label and retracts unsupported synthesis. After the corpus is refreshed, several accepted incidents still do not create a prevalence estimate without a defined population.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cyber work
17  Assessing AI-assisted harm

title: 17  Assessing AI-assisted harm
text:
17.6 Information manipulation
Information manipulation involves more than producing synthetic content. A complete claim connects content generation, coordinated distribution, audience exposure, measured effect, and attribution. Evidence for one link cannot silently stand for the others. Source verification also differs from judging whether the content changed beliefs or behavior.
The NCSC cyber-threat assessment explicitly excludes influence operations from its scope.[^c17-s06-ncsc] MITRE ATLAS can organize technique and case evidence but cannot establish audience effect or campaign attribution by itself.[^c17-s06-atlas] These limits mean that neither source supports a prevalence or behavioral-effect claim about information manipulation.
The organization records each link as supported, disputed, or unknown and keeps platform observations separate from claims about human effect. Synthetic content may be confirmed while coordination and attribution remain uncertain. Reputable research that measures generation, distribution, exposure, effect, and attribution is still required. Defensive priorities can proceed from verified failure paths without waiting for every broader campaign claim.
The assessment gate accepts a campaign-effect claim only when evidence covers content, distribution, audience exposure, measured response, and attribution under stated criteria. The denominator must be the defined exposed population rather than the number of collected posts. Such measurement is costly, raises privacy concerns, and often arrives after the response decision. Activity outside the platform, weak sampling, or correlated reporting can bypass the study. Recovery narrows or withdraws the claim and updates controls from the links that remain supported. This correction still treats verified synthetic content as insufficient proof of coordination or behavioral effect.

17  Assessing AI-assisted harm

title: 17  Assessing AI-assisted harm
text:
17.7 Defensive response to AI-assisted abuse
A defensive response targets the verified path by which harm occurs. Identity and transaction verification can reduce impersonation risk without identifying whether media was generated. Rate limits, reporting channels, account controls, and detection rules address other observed steps. The response record links each control to the evidence and outcome it is expected to change.
The FBI recommends verifying identity through a known contact method and treating urgent requests for money or sensitive information as warning signs.[^c17-s07-fbi] The NCSC expects much near-term AI impact to use existing intrusion methods.[^c17-s07-ncsc] Applying controls to those existing paths follows from that assessment. It does not compare the measured performance of defensive products.
In the hypothetical supplier-change process, an independent callback and second transaction approval protect the change even when content detection is uncertain. The organization records attempted bypasses, false positives, response time, and confirmed outcomes. New evidence can change control priority without changing the basic asset and authorization analysis. Chapter 18 applies the same discipline to an AI assistant used by the defensive team itself.
The identity and transaction services enforce the callback and approval rules from the trusted contact record, requested change, current account state, and approver identities. The evaluation reports harmful changes prevented over all confirmed attempts and legitimate changes delayed or denied over all valid requests. Added verification increases workload and transaction time. A compromised contact record, insider collusion, or recovery process with weaker checks can bypass it. Recovery freezes affected accounts and reverses supported changes. Verification channels are reset before the route is reviewed. Passing does not measure media detection or stop abuse through a different business process.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. A report states that an attacker “used AI autonomously” in a fraud attempt. The available records show that a person prompted a model and selected one generated message. The person sent it through an ordinary account, and the attempt failed when the employee used an independent callback. What can the organization conclude?
Answer. Human-directed generation assistance and the observed impersonation attempt are the strongest supported claims. Model-selected goals and tool execution remain unsupported. Prevalence and improvement against an unaided baseline remain unmeasured. The failed transaction shows that the independent callback protected this case, while one case cannot measure the control’s general effectiveness. The assessment should preserve those supported and unsupported claims separately.

The chapter retains explicit evidence gaps for attacker productivity, automation levels, influence effects, and defensive effectiveness.

title: 18  Using AI safely in defense
text:
18.1 Alert triage
Security question. When does AI improve security work without creating unacceptable new errors or access?
Reference frame. Use a defensive analyst assistant that reads synthetic alerts and intelligence documents through an external model and retrieval application. Add response proposals first and execution only with specified permissions and oversight.
Connection through the book. Chapter 17 separated a demonstrated capability from observed use and measured effect for attacker assistance. This chapter applies the same evidence discipline to a defensive assistant. It also applies the retrieval, authorization, evaluation, and recovery controls already taught. Chapter 19 compares implementations of this fixed task.
An AI assistant can help an analyst connect related events and draft an alert summary, but the summary must preserve the evidence needed to check it. Inputs include normalized events, identity and asset context, prior activity, and the rule that produced the alert. Evaluation counts missed incidents, unsupported statements, correction work, and analyst time as well as apparent speed.
The NIST incident-response profile calls for analysis and correlation of detected events before responders place them in context and route them.1 It also calls for validation and categorization of reports before prioritization and response.[^c18-s01-respond] The profile does not evaluate AI summaries or define how they should express uncertainty.
In the hypothetical workflow, the assistant links each summary sentence to event identifiers and marks missing context. The analyst can inspect the source events before accepting a priority or incident declaration. A baseline compares the same alert set without the assistant. Strong field evidence for AI-assisted triage quality, time, correction, and missed incidents remains unavailable. The evidence-display rule carries into investigation and threat intelligence.
Control review. The triage application checks whether each summary statement includes an event identifier and whether the analyst accepted the priority. It withholds an incident declaration when either check fails. The test reports unsupported statements and missed incidents over all alerts in the fixed set, together with analyst minutes per accepted alert. Source linking and review add latency. They can still fail when the event store is incomplete or the analyst accepts a weak summary. Recovery returns the alert to the ordinary queue and preserves the draft, correction, and source events. This evidence supports the tested alert population only.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cyber work
18  Using AI safely in defense

title: 18  Using AI safely in defense
text:
18.2 Threat intelligence and investigation
Investigation moves from observations to explanations. An observation records something seen. An indicator describes a pattern that may support detection or assessment. The assistant can retrieve reports and connect objects, but it must preserve external references, versions, confidence, and competing explanations so that the analyst can inspect the basis of a conclusion.
Structured Threat Information Expression (STIX) 2.1 separates observations, indicators, relationships, external references, confidence, and object versions in a structured threat-intelligence model.[^c18-s02-stix] STIX also defines confidence as a common property and provides example scales.[^c18-s02-confidence] The schema can carry evidence and confidence. It cannot make the assistant’s inference correct.
The hypothetical assistant produces a claim, supporting observation identifiers, external references, confidence method, and at least one plausible alternative when the evidence permits. A confidence number without a method remains a label. Version links show when a report changed. This source-linked record supports later vulnerability and development decisions without hiding uncertainty.
Control review. The investigation workspace checks for a source identifier, source version, confidence method, and review status before a claim enters a case record. It accepts, returns, or marks the claim unresolved. A test counts complete claim records over all assistant claims and separately counts accepted claims later corrected. The check costs analyst time and storage. Copied text that enters another system without its record can bypass the check, while even an attached record does not establish a claim as true. Recovery withdraws the claim and restores the earlier case state. Affected analysts receive an alert.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cyber work
18  Using AI safely in defense

title: 18  Using AI safely in defense
text:
18.3 Vulnerability and development work
For vulnerability and development work, the assistant may explain a finding or inspect dependency data. It may also draft a patch or propose a test. The security decision still depends on the real code, build, deployment conditions, and authorization for testing. A generated fix needs review and execution evidence rather than acceptance based on a plausible explanation.
The NIST Secure Software Development Framework calls for verification of third-party components, code review, executable-code testing, and triage of results.[^c18-s03-ssdf] Pearce and colleagues found vulnerable suggestions in some scenarios tested with an early GitHub Copilot version.[^c18-s03-pearce] That finding does not transfer automatically to later models or workflows with independent review.
The organization links the assistant’s recommendation to the finding, dependency identity, generated diff, authorized test environment, test output, reviewer, and deployment result. Production testing requires separate permission. A rejected suggestion remains part of evaluation evidence because it contributes to correction cost. These records separate recommendation quality from the authority to act.
Control review. The change pipeline checks the finding identifier, repository revision, test-environment authorization, reviewer decision, and required test result before allowing a merge or deployment. It blocks incomplete or failed candidates. Evaluation reports accepted fixes, rejected fixes, and later regressions over all submitted suggestions, plus review minutes per accepted fix. The gate delays delivery and can miss a defect outside the test set. Because the gate covers only the tested deployment conditions, recovery reverts to the recorded accepted revision and revokes temporary test access.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cyber work
18  Using AI safely in defense

title: 18  Using AI safely in defense
text:
18.4 Analyst and automation roles
The assistant’s role can range from summary to constrained execution. A suggested action tells the analyst what could be done. A drafted action prepares exact arguments for review. Constrained execution runs only an authorized operation within fixed limits. Escalation transfers the decision and evidence to a person or service with the required authority.
Least privilege and complete mediation support granting only task-specific rights and checking access when the protected object is used.[^c18-s04-saltzer] MCP recommends making exposed tools visible to users and preserving their ability to deny an invocation.[^c18-s04-mcp] These principles do not identify the best division of labor or measure the quality of human approval.
The hypothetical assistant may query read-only telemetry and draft a host-isolation request. A separate service resolves the host and checks policy. Before execution, it displays the effect and records approval. Recovery tests cover an incorrect recommendation and a partial action. Controlled comparisons of analyst-only, assistant-only, and combined workflows remain an evidence gap. This authority map defines what an attacker could misuse.
Control review. The action service enforces the boundary by checking the analyst identity, target host, requested operation, approval, and current incident state. It allows only the approved action or returns a denial. Tests count unauthorized and incorrectly completed actions over all attempted actions, including partial failures. Approval adds delay, while constrained execution adds engineering and support cost. A stale approval or alternate management interface can bypass the intended path. The test does not measure whether the recommendation itself was correct. Recovery cancels pending work and restores the host where possible, while irreversible effects receive escalation.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cyber work
18  Using AI safely in defense

title: 18  Using AI safely in defense
text:
18.5 Attacks on the defensive assistant
A defensive assistant consumes attacker-influenced material by design. Logs, tickets, repositories, malware reports, and intelligence documents can contain instructions or data crafted to influence its output. The resulting risk depends on sensitive telemetry, retrieval access, tool permissions, and retained memory available to the assistant.
Greshake and colleagues demonstrated indirect prompt injection through external content and effects on connected actions in selected systems.[^c18-s05-greshake] OWASP’s 2026 description includes tool output, retrieved content, and persistent memory as prompt-injection paths and links impact to available functions and permissions.[^c18-s05-owasp] These demonstrations establish selected attack paths, but they do not prove that a current security assistant is vulnerable or that a proposed control works.
A hypothetical test places a hostile instruction in a synthetic ticket that the assistant must summarize. The trace follows retrieval, context, response, proposed tools, and policy decisions. The expected result is an evidence-linked summary with no unauthorized query or action. This test counts failures alongside useful work when the organization measures operational value.
Control review. The retrieval application limits eligible records, and the action service checks every proposed operation independently of model text. The test denominator is all hostile tickets replayed under the specified identities and permissions. It reports summaries changed by hostile text, restricted records returned, and actions allowed. Filtering and independent authorization consume compute and review time. Encoded instructions, a compromised connector, or an unmediated tool path can defeat parts of the design. Recovery removes the ticket from active context and revokes affected credentials. It then restores the accepted configuration and retests the same cases. A clean run does not cover unseen instruction forms.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cyber work
18  Using AI safely in defense

title: 18  Using AI safely in defense
text:
18.6 Operational value
Operational value is the measured benefit of the assistant after errors, correction work, review, security controls, privacy effects, and total operating cost are included. A fair comparison uses the same alert or investigation workload and a human or deterministic baseline. Quality measures depend on the decision, such as correct triage, supported findings, or safe completion.
The AI RMF MEASURE function calls for documented methods, metrics, test sets, limitations, human review, and monitoring.[^c18-s06-rmf] NIST AI 800-3 says the evaluation target should match the decision and separates item variation from repeated-trial variation.[^c18-s06-8003] The publications do not supply an operational-value result for a security assistant.
The organization reports how often the task succeeds, how much analyst time and correction it requires, which incidents are missed, which consequential errors remain, and what the system and its review cost. Sampling and uncertainty belong in the same report because faster summaries do not justify deployment when they hide missed incidents or create unsafe actions. A strong field study that combines these measures is still needed. Chapter 19 uses this measured task and boundary to compare deployment options.
Operating fallback. The service owner operates a deterministic severity queue and documents an analyst-only path for the same alert population. During a continuity test, the record shows alerts processed through each fallback over all alerts received during the outage, time to first usable result, and unresolved backlog at restoration. Maintaining parallel rules and analyst capacity raises ongoing cost. A fallback can fail when source systems are unavailable or staff capacity is exhausted. Because one exercise does not establish capacity for a longer or broader disruption, recovery returns work in priority order and reconciles duplicate decisions.
Controlled comparison. This hypothetical evaluation runs in evaluation mode. It does not update model parameters or permit an external action. The task is to prioritize 120 synthetic alerts drawn from 12 incident stories. Senior analysts establish the reference priority and supporting event identifiers before the comparison. Each method receives the same alerts, identity context, time limit, and read-only access.

In this example, the combined method saves 120 analyst minutes compared with the analyst-only method and has one fewer consequential error. The fourteen corrected drafts show why accepted output alone is an incomplete measure. The result supports a limited pilot under the tested read-only conditions. It does not support autonomous response or transfer to a different alert population.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. Does the lower analyst time for the combined method justify giving the assistant permission to isolate hosts?
Answer. No. The evaluation measured read-only triage under analyst control. Host isolation changes external state and can interrupt service. That operating mode needs a separate authorization path, action tests, recovery tests, and evidence about harmful interventions. The comparison supports only the task and permissions that were tested.

The chapter retains explicit evidence gaps for triage outcomes, analyst and assistant roles, and full operating cost.

title: 19  Choosing a viable deployment
text:
19.1 Deployment and rights
Security question. Which combination of model, hosting, and controls fits a specified security task?
Reference frame. Run the same defensive task and organization workload under explicitly described external-model and internal-model configurations. Hold data access, allowed actions, quality targets, and oversight requirements constant where possible.
Connection through the book. Compare value and cost using the measurements from Chapter 18 and the operating duties from Chapters 7-9. Chapters 20-22 use the resulting constraints in adoption and investment decisions.
A deployment label leaves inspection rights and operating duties unclear. A hosted model service provides model access through a supplier-operated interface. A self-hosted model deployment runs model software that loads specified weights on infrastructure operated or controlled by the adopting organization. Access to the weights, license rights, runtime control, dependencies, and update duties remain separate facts.
Modification rights are permissions granted by a license or contract to alter and reuse supplied material. The Open Source Initiative definition goes further than access to model weights: it requires freedom to use, study, modify, and share an AI system, together with access to the preferred form for modification.1 This definition does not classify every downloadable model or settle how a license applies in a license dispute.
Security also depends on the operator who patches the runtime and controls the network. Incident handling and failure inspection add separate duties. International secure-design guidance treats model choice as a comparison across security, privacy, performance, and transparency, without ranking one hosting arrangement as generally best.2 These rights and duties define the feasible choices for the intervention comparison that follows.
Rights trace. The hypothetical organization compares a hosted service with a self-hosted deployment for the Chapter 18 triage task. The input is redacted alert text. The target is a cited priority recommendation. Neither option may execute a response. The hosted service contract permits use through its interface but does not provide model weights. The self-hosted option permits local runtime inspection and modification under its selected license, while the organization assumes patching and recovery duties. The observed result is a deployment record with two field pairs: operating control and access to weights, followed by modification rights and update responsibility. The conclusion is that the words hosted and self-hosted do not answer those four questions.
Decision control. The architecture review checks those four fields, the allowed data, and the recovery duty before approving either option. It holds the choice when a required right or operator is missing. The review reports complete deployment records over all candidates and the annual labor required to maintain each accepted option. Contract ambiguity and undocumented subcontracting can defeat the check. Recovery uses the tested alternate service or manual path while the organization resolves the missing right. A complete record does not prove that the supplier or internal operator will meet the stated duty.

title: 19  Choosing a viable deployment
text:
19.2 Choosing the intervention
The deployment decision becomes confused when the organization treats every missing capability as a reason to train a model. The useful question is what is missing. Prompting supplies task instructions with a request. Retrieval adds selected external material to the current context. Tool access allows the application to call another function or service. Fine-tuning changes model parameters through further training on task data.
NIST’s generative AI profile says that intended-purpose analysis includes internal or external use, narrow or broad scope, fine-tuning, and retrieval-based data sources.3 The list identifies factors to examine but does not establish the right intervention for a task. The packet lacks a controlled study comparing all four choices under the same task, model, data, and evaluation conditions.
The mechanism determines the security work. Retrieval adds source eligibility and instruction-data confusion. Tool access adds identity and action authorization. Fine-tuning adds training data, versioned parameters, and regression testing. A conservative design uses the smallest change that addresses the observed gap, then treats that choice as a hypothesis to test. The selected intervention determines the evidence and recovery material in the adaptation workflow.
Decision control. The change review records the observed gap and checks whether prompting, retrieval, a tool, or fine-tuning changes data access, parameters, or action authority. It allows a pilot only when the selected change has a matching test and rollback point. Results report accepted task cases and security failures over all pilot cases. More capable interventions increase integration, review, and recovery work. The rule can fail when the original gap is measured poorly or several changes are bundled. Recovery disables the added capability or restores the previous model and application state. The pilot supports only the tested intervention.

title: 19  Choosing a viable deployment
text:
19.3 Adaptation workflow
An adapted model or prompt can improve the target task while weakening a security property. The organization needs a controlled path from baseline to candidate version. A held-out test set is the general form of the evaluation holdout used in Chapters 3 and 4: it contains examples excluded from training and reserved for later evaluation. A security regression occurs when a security property becomes worse after a change. A known-good state is the recorded version that generalizes Chapter 4’s model baseline into a complete system state accepted for restoration.
NIST recommends renewed evaluation after a third-party model is fine-tuned and after adaptation to a new domain where earlier assumptions may fail.4 Secure-operation guidance also states that changes to data, models, or prompts can alter system behavior. It recommends versioning major updates and retaining a route to a known-good state.5 These recommendations do not specify one validation set or prove that re-evaluation prevents failure.
The process compares the candidate with the accepted baseline and records every security regression. The release decision also references a rollback condition. A hypothetical support assistant might pass ordinary answer tests after fine-tuning but reveal restricted case details under adversarial prompts. The fine-tuned version would remain a candidate until that regression is understood. This workflow produces versioned alternatives for a comparable evaluation.
Control review. The release pipeline checks the candidate version against the held-out task set and the fixed security regression set. It accepts the version only when every mandatory threshold passes. The report gives failures over all cases for each set and records review time and training cost. Data leakage into the held-out set or an untested attack can create a false pass, so the recorded sets apply only within their data and attacker assumptions. Recovery restores the known-good model, prompt, index, and runtime versions.

title: 19  Choosing a viable deployment
text:
19.4 Comparable evaluation
A valid comparison gives each deployment the same task difficulty, permissions, and context allowance. A comparable evaluation tests alternatives with the same task set and decision criteria. A failure cost is the operational consequence assigned to an incorrect, unavailable, or unauthorized result. An adversarial case is a test in which an actor intentionally tries to cause a security failure.
The AI Risk Management Framework calls for validity and reliability under expected deployment conditions and for security and resilience to be evaluated and documented.6 It does not provide a complete head-to-head protocol. A worked comparison under constant workload, permissions, context size, and scoring rules remains an open need.
For a hypothetical incident-triage task, both candidates would receive the same redacted alerts and the same action prohibition. Reviewers would measure accepted classifications and unsafe disclosures. They would also record unauthorized action attempts, latency, and unavailable results. The resulting rates remain specific to that test set and operating setup. They supply the quality and failure evidence needed for the cost model.
Measurement rule. The evaluation harness checks that both deployments receive the same case identifiers, context allowance, permissions, and time window. It rejects a comparison when any of those inputs differ. Each rate uses all assigned cases as its denominator, while latency and reviewer effort use accepted results. Comparable inputs may still omit a feature that matters in production or fail to represent future work. A failed comparison returns the pilot to the accepted baseline.

title: 19  Choosing a viable deployment
text:
19.5 Total ongoing cost
Purchase price alone can reverse a deployment decision once the system is operated. Unit cost divides the total cost recorded for a period by a defined unit of useful work. Fully loaded cost adds assigned infrastructure, labor, and operating cost to direct service cost. Utilization is the share of available compute capacity doing useful work.
FinOps describes unit economics as a relationship between technology cost and business outcomes. Example units include cost per token, request, customer, transaction, or case resolved. Its more mature view includes fully loaded costs.7 The same guidance notes costs from data centers and enterprise agreements. Software services, model suppliers, and several cloud providers can add further costs.8 These categories organize the calculation. Actual prices and economic value require deployment evidence.
The calculation adds service charges or hardware depreciation, storage, energy, utilization loss, engineering labor, patching, monitoring, human review, and incident handling. The denominator counts only results that meet the acceptance criteria. Actual prices, staffing effort, utilization, and incident cost remain organization-specific inputs that require current evidence. This full cost view exposes the availability, fallback, and exit assumptions examined next.
Cost control. Finance and service records supply the period cost, while the evaluation record supplies accepted work for the same period. The decision rejects a unit-cost comparison when either period or acceptance rule differs. Collection and allocation add accounting effort. Shared infrastructure, deferred maintenance, and rare incident costs can remain hidden. The recovery route is to recalculate with a stated range and reopen the deployment decision when actual cost crosses its condition. A lower unit cost does not establish lower risk or better continuity.
Comparable cost calculation. The following exercise values describe one year of the same read-only triage workload. Both options process 600,000 alerts and must meet the same quality threshold. Accepted work is the number of alert results that pass review. The values are hypothetical and use currency units rather than current supplier prices.



Table 19.1: Annual cost comparison.

The hosted unit cost is 414,000 divided by 570,000, or about 0.73 currency units per accepted result. The self-hosted unit cost is 547,000 divided by 576,000, or about 0.95. The self-hosted option accepts 6,000 more results in this example, but costs 133,000 more. Cost alone favors the hosted option. Data-transfer limits, supplier exit, inspection needs, or a failed continuity test can still change the decision. The calculation is a comparison method, not evidence that either option has these costs in practice.

title: 19  Choosing a viable deployment
text:
19.6 Operational constraints
An option with good test results and acceptable cost can still fail an operating requirement. An outbound dependency is an external service required during operation. A fallback is an alternate service or manual path used when the primary path fails. Exit cost is the work and cost required to leave a supplier or deployment design.
NIST recommends documenting dependence on third-party AI data and systems. It also recommends identifying fallbacks and testing rollover or manual procedures.9 Secure-development guidance also recommends recording where models, data, prompts, software, logs, and assessments are stored and retaining versions that permit restoration.10 The selected organization still needs legal analysis for location rules and system tests for continuity.
The final deployment record joins task quality, rights, action limits, full cost, required service level, fallback test results, and exit cost. A hypothetical internal model may remove an online supplier dependency while adding scarce operations staff and hardware recovery duties. A hosted service may reduce local maintenance while adding transfer and supplier-exit constraints. This bounded record becomes the input to organization-wide adoption in Chapter 20.
Continuity control. The service manager tests supplier loss and internal runtime loss against the same workload. The application routes work to the manual or deterministic fallback when the health check fails. The test reports completed fallback cases over all cases arriving during the disruption, time to switch, backlog, and total staff hours. Standby capacity and rehearsals raise ongoing cost. A shared identity, network, or data dependency can disable both paths. Because one exercise does not prove continuity for every outage duration, recovery restores the approved service and reconciles duplicate work. Normal routing resumes after credential verification.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. Choose between the two hypothetical deployments in the cost table. The pilot permits redacted alerts and prohibits response actions. It also requires a tested manual fallback. State the decision and one condition that would reopen it.
Conclusion. The hosted option is the current choice because it meets the stated task while producing the lower cost per accepted result. The approval remains limited to redacted, read-only triage. A failed supplier-exit test, a change in transfer rules, or evidence that local inspection is required would reopen the decision. This conclusion does not claim that hosted service is generally safer or cheaper.

title: Part VII: Governing organizational AI use
text:
Chapters in this part
This part translates technical evidence into repeatable organizational decisions. It gives managers concrete deliverables while showing engineers how their tests and logs support those decisions.
Connection through the book. The organization now has several concrete deployments and their evidence. Decide who may use them, which party owes which duties, what records are available, and which improvements justify their cost. Organizational choices connect directly to the same system boundaries rather than forming a separate policy catalog.
Part outcome. An adoption and investment decision with explicit responsibilities, review triggers, and accepted residual risk.

title: Part VII: Governing organizational AI use
text:
Adopting AI safely: This chapter turns an organization’s scattered AI use into an inventory, acceptable-use rules, account and connector controls, and practical employee support.
Assigning responsibility: This chapter assigns responsibilities across developers, providers, deployers, data owners, purchasers, and affected people, using system evidence rather than generic assurances.
Steering security investment: This chapter gives executives and the CSO a way to prioritize security investment with measures, evidence, responsible owners, review dates, and explicit residual-risk decisions.
crumbs: Part VII: Governing organizational AI use

title: 20  Adopting AI safely
text:
20.1 The enterprise AI inventory
Security question. How can an organization allow useful AI work without losing sight of systems, data, permissions, and changes?
Organization setting. Employees use approved assistants, purchased software with AI features, and some unapproved services in examples that do not describe a real organization or product.
Connection through the book. Treat the Chapter 18 security assistant and Chapter 19 deployment decision as one row in an organization-wide inventory. This introduces organization-wide management scope. The limited read-only approval still covers only the one security-assistant row. Every additional use repeats the system map, threat, data, action, evaluation, and deployment decisions. Chapter 21 assigns responsibility for the resulting systems and supplier relationships.
Policy cannot govern an AI use that the organization cannot see. An enterprise AI inventory is a controlled record of AI systems and AI-enabled services used by the organization. An embedded AI feature is an AI capability included inside another purchased product. A data flow records movement of data among users, systems, suppliers, and stores.
The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 separates inventories of software, services, supplier services, data, metadata, and authorized internal and external data flows.1 The AI Risk Management Framework also includes maintaining an inventory of AI systems according to organizational risk priorities.2 Completeness and currentness require separate discovery evidence.
For each entry, the record links the business task, responsible owner, users, model or service, data types, connectors, data flows, action permissions, supplier, and review date. Discovery may combine procurement and identity records. Expense data, network observations, and employee reports add other views. These are common inventory practices, and their coverage depends on the available evidence. The resulting population defines which uses the acceptable-use rules govern.
Inventory trace. The hypothetical organization compares four discovery inputs for one month: procurement lists an approved assistant and identity logs show two AI services. Expense records show a third service, while an employee report identifies an AI feature inside a support product. The intermediate state is a reconciliation table with service identity, business task, data class, connector, responsible role, and review date. One expense entry has no responsible role and one embedded feature has no data-flow record. The observed result is four candidate uses, two complete records, and two unresolved records. The conclusion treats the inventory as evidence-linked records with visible gaps. It does not claim completeness.
Inventory control. The service that maintains the inventory reconciles procurement, identity, expense, network, and employee reports and marks incomplete entries for review. It allows onboarding only for a record with the required task, data, connector, responsible role, and review date. Coverage is confirmed records divided by all candidate uses found through the stated inputs. Discovery and reconciliation require staff time and can miss personal accounts or hidden product features. Because high coverage across these inputs does not prove that every AI use has been found, recovery suspends unresolved connectors or routes the task to an approved service.
crumbs: Part VII: Governing organizational AI use

title: 20  Adopting AI safely
text:
20.2 Acceptable-use rules
A general instruction to “use AI responsibly” does not tell an employee if a real task is allowed. An acceptable-use rule sets conditions on permitted AI tasks, data, outputs, or actions. A consequential output can materially affect a person, asset, obligation, or decision. A safe alternative is an approved method offered when the requested AI use is restricted.
NIST recommends updating generative AI acceptable-use policies to cover proprietary and open-source technology and data, as well as contractors and other third parties.3 This is governance guidance, not a complete policy or evidence that publication alone changes behavior.
In a hypothetical organization, an employee may summarize public material in an approved assistant but may not paste customer secrets into an unapproved service. A generated contract clause requires legal review, and a generated payment request cannot execute a transaction. When a rule blocks a useful task, the safe alternative might be a restricted internal assistant or a human review channel. The rules become enforceable only when account and connector permissions match them.
Use control. The application and connector check the employee identity, task, data class, target service, and requested action. They either allow the request or block it. A field filter can change the request before the application shows the safe alternative. Tests report blocked prohibited cases and blocked allowed cases over all policy cases. Classification, support, and exception handling add cost and delay. Copying data through an unmanaged device or misclassifying a field can bypass the rule. Recovery revokes exposed access and removes retained data where the service permits. Work then moves to the approved path. A passed policy test does not prove employee behavior outside managed channels.
crumbs: Part VII: Governing organizational AI use

title: 20  Adopting AI safely
text:
20.3 Accounts and connectors
An approved service can still exceed policy if a broad connector or shared account bypasses individual access limits. A connector is an integration that lets an AI application read from or act on another system. The security decision identifies the human or service identity used for each call. Its permission scope states the resources and operations allowed to that identity.
CSF 2.0 calls for identities and credentials for users, services, and hardware to be managed. It also calls for permissions and authorizations to be defined, enforced, reviewed, and limited through least privilege and separation of duties.4 These outcomes do not specify an identity product or prove that a connector applies the intended rule.
The mechanism follows the employee from onboarding to offboarding. The application authenticates the employee, the connector uses a distinct service identity or delegated token, the target service performs a current authorization check, and logs connect the request to both identities. Shared credentials break this chain. Review dates and revocation tests show whether access changes take effect. These details provide concrete evidence for procurement and onboarding.
Revocation test. In this hypothetical test, employee E17 loses access to customer case C44 at 10:00. At 10:05 the employee submits a request for a C44 summary. The application stores an earlier conversation, but the connector sends E17’s current identity to the case system. The case system denies access, so the application records the denial without receiving the customer record. The observed result meets the expected result. If the connector had used a shared service account and returned the record, the test would show that approval of the AI service did not enforce the employee’s current permissions.
Control review. The target case system enforces access from the current employee identity and record identifier. The connector passes through the denial and clears any queued result for that record. A revocation test reports denied former permissions over all revoked user-resource pairs, plus time from source revocation to effective denial. Delegated identity and frequent checks add integration and latency cost. Cached content, shared credentials, or a second connector can bypass the path. Because one successful pair does not establish complete offboarding, recovery purges affected caches and revokes connector tokens before the full revoked set is retested.
crumbs: Part VII: Governing organizational AI use

title: 20  Adopting AI safely
text:
20.4 Procurement and onboarding
A supplier review has little value when it examines a brand while leaving the intended use, data, and actions unspecified. A pilot limit is a temporary restriction on users, data, actions, duration, or scale during evaluation. Supplier due diligence examines the supplier before a relationship begins. A time-limited exception is an approved deviation that expires or requires renewed review.
NIST recommends procurement checks for intellectual property, privacy, security, embedded AI, ongoing monitoring, model and tool changes, and incident or vulnerability records.5 CSF 2.0 also calls for due diligence before a supplier relationship and continued recording, treatment, and monitoring of supplier risk.6 These lists do not certify a supplier or settle sector-specific contract duties.
The onboarding record ties the use case to permitted data, action limits, identity design, supplier evidence, acceptance tests, pilot expiry, and an accountable decision. A time-limited exception records why an ordinary requirement cannot yet be met and when renewed review occurs. The people operating the approved use then need task-specific competence and a practical route for help.
Approval control. The procurement workflow checks the use record, supplier scope, required contract terms, pilot limits, test results, exception expiry, and decision authority. It approves, restricts, or holds onboarding. The review reports complete approvals over all proposed uses and overdue exceptions over all active exceptions. Supplier review and negotiation consume legal and engineering time. A product update or unreported subprocessor can invalidate the evidence after approval. Recovery disables the feature or connector and returns users to the stated alternative while review is renewed. Approval does not certify the supplier beyond the inspected service and period.

title: 20  Adopting AI safely
text:
20.5 Employee competence and support
Employees encounter the system at the point where an unreliable answer, suspicious instruction, or unexpected request becomes a business decision. Human oversight assigns review or intervention to a person with sufficient authority and support. A help channel is a specified route for advice, reporting, or escalation. Training needs to match the assigned task and the decisions the employee can make.
CSF 2.0 distinguishes general awareness from training for specialized roles, with both tied to the knowledge and skills needed to perform work while considering cybersecurity risk.7 Within its scope, the European Union AI Act requires deployers of covered high-risk systems to assign human oversight to people with suitable competence, training, authority, and support.8 That legal rule is limited to the systems and dates covered by the Act.
A hypothetical customer-support employee may need to verify a refund instruction through the case system, while an administrator needs to inspect connector permissions and logs. Questions and incident reports pass through the help channel, so employees do not have to guess. Reports, repeated confusion, and support demand become evidence for adoption and change review.
Competence check. The employee receives a synthetic message that asks for a refund and includes an assistant-generated bank-account change. The task is to decide what can proceed. The expected path ignores the generated payment instruction and verifies the case in the authoritative support system. The account change then goes to the established review channel. The observed exercise result records the employee’s choice, the evidence consulted, and whether escalation occurred. A correct answer supports competence for this scenario only. It does not show readiness for administration, incident response, or legal review.
Oversight control. The business workflow requires the authoritative record and the specified approval role before a consequential change can proceed. The competence test reports correct decisions over all assigned scenarios and records unsafe approvals and unnecessary escalations separately. Training, review, and support time are operating costs. Time pressure, ambiguous cases, or an unavailable help channel can defeat the human step. Recovery stops the transaction and uses the ordinary manual process. Staff review any action already taken. A high exercise score does not prove reliable performance during real incidents.
crumbs: Part VII: Governing organizational AI use

title: 20  Adopting AI safely
text:
20.6 Adoption and change review
High use does not by itself show that adoption is safe or valuable. An adoption measure is a count or rate describing approved use of an AI capability. Policy friction is delay or work created by a policy during ordinary tasks. A retirement trigger is an observed condition that starts removal or replacement review.
CSF 2.0 calls for policy review when requirements, threats, technology, or mission change. It also calls for changes and exceptions to be assessed, recorded, and tracked.9 The framework does not define AI adoption measures or universal retirement thresholds. The evidence packet also lacks validated examples of measures that avoid rewarding unsafe volume or discouraging incident reporting.
The review keeps that limit visible. A rise in reports can reflect growing abuse or better awareness. Both causes may be present. Low use can reflect poor value or excessive friction, while incomplete discovery offers another explanation. New model capabilities, contract terms, connectors, or data access can invalidate the original approval even when usage is stable. The resulting practice, exceptions, and open questions become inputs to the responsibility analysis in Chapter 21.
Adoption review record. The example below uses hypothetical values for one quarterly review.



Table 20.1: Adoption change record.











Record field
Pilot approval
Observed quarter
Review conclusion




Task
Summarize internal policy
8,400 summaries requested
Task unchanged


Data
Public and internal policy
23 requests included customer text
Retrain users and block customer fields


Accounts
80 specified employees
77 active users and 3 departed users revoked
Revocation worked


Connectors
Read-only policy store
Supplier proposes email connector

Support

The intermediate comparison checks observed use against the approved task, data, accounts, connectors, and support route. The conclusion is to continue the policy summary pilot with a block on customer fields and focused employee support. The proposed email connector remains outside approval because it changes available data and actions.
Change control. The application configuration checks the approved connector list and data rules before enabling a supplier feature. The review board checks new capabilities, terms, regions, permissions, and incident results before expanding the approval. Measures use changed systems over all inventoried approved systems and policy violations over all inspected requests. Review and field filtering create cost and user friction. Supplier-side activation or incomplete inventory data can bypass the gate. Because stable usage and answer quality do not prove that the boundary remained unchanged, recovery disables the added capability and restores the accepted configuration. Work moves to the documented fallback.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. A supplier update adds an email connector to an approved assistant that summarizes policy. Usage and answer quality remain unchanged. Can the existing approval continue without review?
Answer. No. The connector changes the data flow, possible content, and account permissions even though usage and answer quality did not change. The adoption record should mark the connector as outside the approved boundary and keep it disabled. The record must also identify the responsible role and tests required for a new decision.

20  Adopting AI safely

title: 21  Assigning responsibility
text:
21.1 Roles and responsibility
Security question. Who is responsible for each AI system decision, and which legal, contractual, and governance duties apply?
Organization setting. A hypothetical organization buys model access and builds an application around it. The application connects internal data and serves employees or customers. Several parties can affect the same outcome, but their authority and duties differ.
Connection through the book. Chapter 20 identified the approved systems, accounts, connectors, exceptions, and changes that need owners. Chapters 2, 7, and 19 established the threat, supplier, and deployment boundaries. This chapter attaches duties and evidence to those records. Chapter 22 uses the resulting responsibility map to direct security investment.
Responsibility becomes unclear when a project calls every outside party a vendor and every internal party an owner. The analysis begins with the act each party performs. A provider legally or contractually supplies an AI system or model. A deployer uses an AI system under its authority. An affected person is a person whose rights, safety, access, or interests may be affected.
The European Union AI Act defines a provider as the party that develops or has an AI system developed and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own identity. It defines a deployer as a party using an AI system under its authority.1 For covered high-risk systems, branding, substantial modification, or a change in intended purpose can cause another party to assume provider obligations.2 These definitions apply only within the Act’s scope and dates. A project still needs a system-specific responsibility map.
The map links each lifecycle decision to authority, evidence, and escalation. A supplier may operate inference. The organization selects the data and grants connector access. It also decides if an output affects a customer. An affected person may have no operating role but still requires consideration in risk decisions. The role map identifies which obligations need examination next.
Responsibility trace. In the hypothetical employee assistant, the supplier operates model inference, the application team selects retrieved fields, the identity service checks the employee’s access. The support director has authority over whether a proposed account change can enter the business process, while the Chief Security Officer accepts specified residual security risk. The intermediate record links each act to one decision role and one evidence source. A supplier report cannot approve the organization’s connector permissions. A technical test cannot replace the authorized business-risk decision. The conclusion is that responsibility follows the act and authority, not a general label applied to the whole system.
Responsibility control. The decision workflow checks that each consequential act has one responsible role, stated authority, evidence source, escalation route, and review date. It holds approval when any field is missing or conflicting. The measure is complete assignments divided by all consequential acts in the system map. Maintaining the map and resolving conflicts take staff time. Informal decisions outside the workflow can bypass it. Recovery withdraws the unsupported decision and escalates it to a role with authority. A complete assignment shows who must decide, not that the decision is correct.
crumbs: Part VII: Governing organizational AI use
21  Assigning responsibility

title: 21  Assigning responsibility
text:
21.2 Applicable obligations
The same technical system can face different duties when its use, location, operator, or date changes. A jurisdiction is a legal territory whose rules may apply. Legal scope is the set of facts that brings a person, organization, system, or act under a rule. An effective date is the date from which a provision applies.
The consolidated EU AI Act text applies generally from August 2, 2026, while amended Article 113 sets later dates for specified Annex III and Annex I systems.3 The dates differ across provisions, so one headline date cannot replace provision-level checking. In the United States health setting, the Department of Health and Human Services stated in its August 7, 2026 review that the current Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act Security Rule remained in effect while proposed cybersecurity changes had not become a final rule.4
These examples show the process rather than a global legal survey. A final decision needs current primary law and qualified interpretation for the organization’s actual locations and sector. Once binding duties and contract terms are identified, voluntary frameworks can organize the remaining work without being mistaken for law.
Scope trace. The organization records five inputs before applying a rule. The inputs cover the operating and user locations. They also cover the affected person and intended use, together with the decision date. A hypothetical credit-scoring use and an internal alert-triage use share a model supplier but have different intended purposes. The legal reviewer checks the current provision and effective date for each use. The intermediate record marks the credit use for provision-level analysis and leaves the alert-triage use outside that specific classification pending other duties. The observed result is a scoped question. It does not classify the model in general.
Dated scope gate. The legal review checks the five inputs against current primary text and records the provision, date, reviewer, and unresolved facts. It either allows or holds the proposed use, and an allowed use can carry limits. Coverage is reviewed obligations divided by all candidate obligations identified for the use. Qualified review, updates, and supplier fact gathering create ongoing cost. A stale summary, changed use, or missing location can invalidate the result. Because the record does not prove compliance beyond its facts, law, and date, recovery pauses the affected function and preserves the prior permitted path. The legal review then repeats with current facts.
crumbs: Part VII: Governing organizational AI use
21  Assigning responsibility

title: 21  Assigning responsibility
text:
21.3 Frameworks and standards
A framework organizes outcomes or practices used to structure risk work without specifying one implementation. CSF 2.0 presents a technology-neutral hierarchy of cybersecurity outcomes and states that it does not prescribe how organizations achieve them.5 It can connect risk work across teams, but it is not an AI control catalogue and does not demonstrate implementation quality.
A management system is a connected set of policies, roles, processes, and reviews used to meet organizational objectives. The public ISO page describes ISO/IEC 42001 as requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining, and continually improving an AI management system.6 Clause-level claims require the licensed normative text, so the public page supports only this scope description.
An organization may use a crosswalk, a scoped mapping between related items in different sources. It records the relationship and the gap instead of treating differently scoped documents as interchangeable. Those categories now guide the data, documentation, supplier, and contract questions in the remaining sections.
Crosswalk comparison. The organization starts with the concrete decision “Who can expand the assistant to customer data?” CSF 2.0 supplies outcomes for responsibility, supplier risk, and access control. The AI Risk Management Framework supplies AI context, measurement, and risk-management questions. ISO/IEC 42001 supplies management-system requirements only to the extent available in the licensed text. The intermediate crosswalk records the relevant item, the system evidence, and any uncovered question. The observed gap is the actual legal basis for customer-data use. No framework row fills that gap. The conclusion is that a crosswalk organizes evidence but does not turn guidance into law or prove compliance.
Crosswalk control. The review register checks every selected framework or standard item against a concrete system record and marks missing evidence or scope. It prevents a framework row from closing a legal or technical question that the source does not answer. Coverage is supported mappings divided by all mappings used in the decision. Building and maintaining the register costs review time. Broad labels and copied mappings can hide a gap. Recovery reopens the affected decision and obtains the missing source or test. A complete crosswalk shows organized coverage, not control effectiveness or legal compliance.
crumbs: Part VII: Governing organizational AI use
21  Assigning responsibility

title: 21  Assigning responsibility
text:
21.4 Data and intellectual property questions
Data can be technically accessible while still being unavailable for collection, training, retrieval, or reuse. Collection permission is the legal, contractual, or organizational basis for obtaining data. A reuse right permits use of material for a later purpose. Confidential information is information protected from unauthorized disclosure by duty or agreement.
NIST recommends categorizing generative AI content by third-party rights and setting policies for how third-party intellectual property and training data are used, stored, and protected.7 This guidance identifies governance work. It does not decide ownership, infringement, fair use, database rights, trade secrets, privacy duties, or license enforcement.
A hypothetical organization may have permission to store a customer document for service delivery but no permission to use it for model training. Retrieval for an authorized employee may also differ from disclosure to an external model supplier. Current jurisdiction-specific primary law and qualified interpretation remain necessary for substantive legal conclusions. The permissions and restrictions determine which decision and change records need to remain available.
Permission control. The data gateway checks the data class, person or service identity, intended purpose, destination, retention rule, and recorded permission before collection, retrieval, training, or external transfer. It allows, removes fields, or blocks the operation and logs the basis. Tests report allowed and denied flows over all purpose-destination cases. Classification and legal review add cost. Copied data, wrong labels, or supplier reuse outside the observed interface can defeat the control. Recovery revokes access and removes affected copies where possible. Rights questions receive qualified review. A technical denial does not settle the underlying legal interpretation.
crumbs: Part VII: Governing organizational AI use
21  Assigning responsibility

title: 21  Assigning responsibility
text:
21.5 Documentation and oversight
A responsible role cannot review a system if the reason for a decision disappeared with a meeting. A decision record captures the options, evidence, responsible role, date, conditions, and unresolved issues behind a decision. Related records describe the system, tests, oversight authority, access, incidents, and changes.
The AI Risk Management Framework connects system context, intended purpose, task, legal risk, human oversight, testing, and lifecycle decisions across its MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions.8 For covered high-risk systems, the EU AI Act connects technical documentation, automated logging, information for deployers, human oversight, and deployer monitoring duties.9 These sources do not establish one record format or universal retention period.
The documentation set follows the system boundary. It links versions and decisions without claiming that the record itself proves the system is safe. A human oversight assignment identifies the person or role with review and intervention authority. A change record preserves evidence of a system change and its assessment. These records supply the questions and evidence requests used in supplier assurance.
Decision-record test. A model version changes on 4 October in this hypothetical case. The prior record approved version V7 for policy summaries with read-only retrieval. The change record identifies version V8, the supplier notice, affected tests, responsible reviewer, and the decision to hold expansion. The team can trace each test result back to V7 or V8. If the record contained only “model updated,” a later reviewer could not tell which evidence remained relevant. The observed result tests whether the documentation supports a decision rather than whether a form was completed.
Change control. The release workflow checks the system version, affected assumptions, required tests, oversight assignment, and approval before routing users to the change. It either allows release or keeps the accepted version. A release can carry restrictions. The measure is fully linked material changes divided by all detected material changes. Version tracking and review delay delivery. An emergency change or silent supplier update can bypass the workflow, and complete documentation still cannot show that every failure was detected. Recovery restores the accepted configuration and reconstructs missing records from logs and supplier notices.
crumbs: Part VII: Governing organizational AI use
21  Assigning responsibility

title: 21  Assigning responsibility
text:
21.6 Supplier assurance
A certificate or audit title can appear relevant while covering the wrong service, location, control period, or customer configuration. Assurance scope identifies the systems, services, locations, controls, and period covered by evidence. A subprocessor is another party used by a supplier to process data or deliver service. The review also records exclusions, shared responsibilities, and customer actions required for the assurance to apply.
CSF 2.0 calls for coordination of supplier roles and inclusion of security requirements in contracts. It also calls for due diligence before a relationship and risk monitoring during it.10 NIST also recommends contract clauses that permit evaluation of third-party generative AI processes and standards.11 A service-specific review still needs to establish the audit quality and the relevance of supplier controls to the organization’s system.
The evidence packet lacks a strong public source on detailed scope and customer-control sections in common assurance reports. This section keeps that gap visible. The practical method compares the assurance scope with the actual data flow and service configuration, then lists every uncovered dependency. Those gaps become contract and exit requirements.
Supplier-scope comparison. The hypothetical supplier report covers inference service S1 in region R1 for January through June. The organization uses S1 in region R2 from August and supplies its own connector. The intermediate comparison marks service, region, period, supplier control, and customer control. The observed gaps are region R2, the later operating period, and the customer connector. The report may still provide useful evidence for covered controls, but it cannot support a conclusion about the uncovered configuration. The responsible role requests current evidence and records the connector as an organization duty.
Assurance control. The procurement gate compares service, region, period, configuration, subprocessors, supplier controls, and customer duties with the actual deployment. It either accepts the evidence or leaves the related use unapproved. Acceptance can carry a condition. Coverage is matched scope items divided by all scope items required for the decision. Obtaining and reviewing evidence adds supplier and internal cost. A stale report or omitted customer control can produce a false assurance. Recovery restricts the service and disables the uncovered path. Work can move to the approved fallback. A matched report supports only its stated scope and does not prove the whole application secure.
crumbs: Part VII: Governing organizational AI use
21  Assigning responsibility

title: 21  Assigning responsibility
text:
21.7 Contract and exit provisions
Dependence becomes difficult to change after data, connectors, workflows, and staff practices accumulate around one service. Portability is the ability to move data, configurations, and necessary artifacts to another service. Termination assistance is supplier support for an orderly end or transfer. A continuity term is a contract condition intended to preserve essential operations during disruption or exit.
NIST recommends reviewing AI supplier contracts for termination, responsibility, incident notice, response times, support availability, and service levels.12 CSF 2.0 includes supplier participation in incident activity and risk management after a service agreement ends.13 These are governance outcomes. Contract language and enforceability require separate legal work.
A hypothetical exit test exports allowed records and removes connector access. It then revokes service credentials and checks deletion evidence. The fallback workflow runs after those checks. Jurisdiction-specific clauses and evidence about practical exit testing remain open research needs. The resulting responsibility, supplier, and continuity record provides the input for security investment decisions in Chapter 22.
Exit control. The exit workflow checks required data, configurations, logs, open cases, credentials, supplier deletion evidence, and fallback readiness. It completes termination only after each item is transferred, retained under an approved basis, or recorded as unresolved. Measures include recovered required items over all required items and revoked credentials over all active credentials. Portability tests, standby service, and supplier support add ongoing cost. Proprietary formats, supplier delay, or a shared dependency can block exit. Recovery keeps the manual path active and limits new data while unresolved items are escalated. A supplier deletion statement does not by itself prove removal from every copy.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. A supplier operates inference, the organization selects customer data, and an internal support director approves account changes. Assign responsibility for model service operation, retrieval eligibility, and the final account decision. State one evidence item and one limit for each assignment.
Answer. The supplier is responsible for the contracted operation of the model service, supported by service records and limited to the contract and assurance scope. The organization role that controls retrieval is responsible for eligible customer fields, supported by permission and retrieval tests and limited by current law and data rights. The support director is responsible for the account decision under the organization’s authority, supported by approval and action logs and limited by the director’s approval range. Each assignment remains limited to its stated act and authority.
