title: 22  Steering security investment
text:
22.1 Program ownership
Security question. How can leaders decide which AI security work receives staff, money, and time?
Organization setting. A hypothetical organization operates several AI uses with different data, permissions, suppliers, consequences, and evidence quality. Leaders cannot fund every proposed control at once.
Connection through the book. Chapters 14 through 21 produced assurance, monitoring, deployment, adoption, and responsibility evidence. This chapter turns that evidence into investment decisions. Chapter 23 tests the method across different operating settings.
A register full of risks and controls does not create a decision. Each asset, use case, exception, escalation, and review needs a person with authority to act. An accountable owner can accept or escalate a result. The same person can require more work before deciding. Risk acceptance records a decision to retain specified residual risk. Review frequency sets an interval or event rule for reassessment.
CSF 2.0 places accountability with organizational leadership. It calls for cybersecurity roles, responsibilities, and authorities to be established, understood, and enforced, with resources allocated in line with risk strategy.1 These outcomes do not select one organization chart.
The program record connects each owner to a decision and a review rule. A technical lead may own a test result, while the Chief Security Officer may own escalation and an executive may have authority to accept residual risk. The record states the boundary instead of treating “ownership” as a vague label. These assignments give each coverage measure a reader and a purpose.
Program control. The governance workflow checks each active system, exception, escalation, and risk decision for an authorized role and a current review rule. It blocks expansion or risk acceptance when either is missing. Coverage is complete assignments divided by all active decision records. Maintaining the register and resolving authority conflicts consume management time. Informal approval or an incomplete inventory can bypass the workflow. Recovery pauses the affected decision and escalates it to the correct authority. A complete register does not show that the selected control is effective.
crumbs: Part VII: Governing organizational AI use
22  Steering security investment

title: 22  Steering security investment
text:
22.2 Coverage and exposure measures
A count such as “twenty systems reviewed” has no clear meaning without the total population. A coverage measure combines a numerator with the full population that the count is meant to represent. Examples include reviewed high-impact systems divided by all known high-impact systems, or tested sensitive connectors divided by all sensitive connectors in the inventory.
NIST distinguishes implementation measures, which show progress in putting controls in place, from effectiveness, efficiency, and impact measures.2 It also states that the source, collection method, and validation process for measurement data need definition so results can be repeated and compared over time.3 Repeatable data does not make an irrelevant measure useful, and high implementation coverage does not establish control effectiveness.
The mechanism starts with an inventory and a clear denominator. An overdue exception is an approved deviation whose review or expiry date has passed. The measure records missing items, exclusions, stale records, and overdue exceptions instead of silently dropping them. A hypothetical result of 90 tested connectors out of 100 known connectors shows 90 percent coverage. It says nothing yet about the ten untested connectors or the quality of the tests. Outcome measures address that different question.
Coverage decision. The reporting service checks connector inventory status, test date, result, exception, and expiry. The responsible role can continue, restrict, or pause use based on a stated threshold. The denominator includes every known connector in scope, including failed, untested, and excepted items. Collection and follow-up add operating cost. Unknown connectors and stale inventories can inflate the rate, while 90 percent coverage still says nothing about the amount of risk reduction. Recovery adds missing items and tests the unresolved population before the decision is reissued.
crumbs: Part VII: Governing organizational AI use
22  Steering security investment

title: 22  Steering security investment
text:
22.3 Outcome measures
Completion counts describe work performed. An outcome measure observes the result a control is meant to change. A rate divides an event count by a relevant exposure or opportunity count. Recovery time is elapsed time from a specified disruption point to a specified restored state.
NIST describes effectiveness measures as evidence of how well controls meet desired outcomes, efficiency measures as the speed of useful feedback and correction, and impact measures as effects on mission, cost, value, penalties, or trust.4 It also states that one measure may be insufficient for a risk decision and that resource limits prevent measuring everything.5 These categories do not supply AI-specific measures or establish that a control caused an observed change.
Every result reports its denominator. A harmful-action count has a different meaning across one hundred authorized calls than across one million. Prevented attempts, duplicate events, incomplete reports, and changed exposure can also alter the rate. The packet lacks a validated worked denominator for these cases, so the examples require testing before operational use. The measured outcomes then inform renewed assessment and change decisions.
Outcome control. The measurement pipeline joins action, denial, incident, recovery, and exposure records for the same period and configuration. It reports harmful completed actions over all eligible action attempts, plus missing or duplicate records. A threshold can trigger restriction or renewed testing. Instrumentation and investigation add cost, and logging gaps can hide failures. Recovery repairs the data path and recomputes the measure. Earlier decisions remain uncertain until review. A changed rate does not by itself prove that one control caused the change.
crumbs: Part VII: Governing organizational AI use
22  Steering security investment

title: 22  Steering security investment
text:
22.4 Assurance and change decisions
An approval is tied to the system and evidence that existed at the time. A material change is large enough to invalidate an assumption, test, approval, or duty. A renewed assessment repeats review after a trigger. A release condition is an evidence threshold required before deployment or expansion.
CSF 2.0 calls for improvements to be identified from evaluations, security tests and exercises, operational work, and incident planning.6 NIST’s generative AI profile recommends renewed model risk review after fine-tuning or adaptation to a new domain.7 These sources identify triggers but do not set a universal release threshold or prove that a proposed improvement works.
The decision record links each trigger to stale evidence and the required renewed assessment. It also identifies the authority that can pause or expand use. A minor interface change may need a focused regression test. A new action permission may reopen the threat model and authorization tests. It may also require a new incident plan and legal review. These decisions create evidence-based options for investment prioritization.
Change gate. The release service checks the component version, permission change, supplier notice, affected assumptions, required tests, and decision authority. It either permits the change or keeps the prior version. Permission can carry limits. The measure is reviewed material changes divided by all detected material changes, with failed tests retained in the count. Review and rollback capacity increase ongoing cost. Silent supplier changes and untracked configuration can bypass the gate. Recovery restores the accepted version and repeats affected tests. Passing those tests supports only the changed paths and cases they cover.

22  Steering security investment

title: 22  Steering security investment
text:
22.5 Investment choices
Exposure alone gives an incomplete priority. A priority decision uses business value, possible harm, and uncertainty. Control cost, legal duty, and displaced work also affect it. Expected loss is a probability-weighted estimate of adverse impact, but rare AI events may leave both probability and impact highly uncertain. Opportunity cost is the value of work displaced by the selected investment.
NIST says measurement priorities can consider risk strategy, mission, data availability, asset value, control cost, partial controls, risk assessments, policy, and legal requirements.8 It also says likelihood and impact need to be considered together because either alone is insufficient for deciding the importance of a potential measure.9 The guidance does not provide a universal scoring formula or validate probability estimates for rare events.
The decision can use ranges and scenarios when point estimates would imply false precision. A control required by law may remain mandatory even when its expected-loss estimate is small. A cheap control with broad benefit may receive priority over a costly control aimed at a narrow, uncertain scenario. The selected priorities and their uncertainty need a durable executive record.
Investment comparison. The hypothetical organization has 180,000 currency units and two optional projects after funding its required controls. Project A limits connector permissions for six assistants. It costs 110,000 and addresses a tested path that reached restricted records in 4 of 200 adversarial cases. Project B adds a model-behavior filter to one public assistant. It costs 150,000 and addresses a plausible misuse scenario for which no local rate is yet available. These exercise values support only the comparison and do not measure control effectiveness.
The intermediate decision record compares affected systems, observed evidence, possible harm, implementation cost, displaced work, and uncertainty. Project A has direct local evidence and broader system coverage. Project B may address serious harm, but the organization first needs a focused test that measures the path and the filter under its actual application conditions. The current conclusion funds Project A and reserves 70,000 for that test and other unresolved work. A legal duty or stronger evidence could change the order.
Investment control. The portfolio review checks each option for affected systems, required duty, evidence quality, cost range, displaced work, bypass risk, and recovery benefit. It funds, defers, or rejects the option and records the condition that reopens it. Coverage is funded required controls over all required controls, while optional work retains its uncertainty range. Analysis and delayed projects have real cost. Optimistic estimates or missing systems can distort the order, and the ranking does not establish that the funded control will achieve its expected effect. Recovery reserves capacity for newly observed failures and repeats the comparison when a condition changes.

22  Steering security investment

title: 22  Steering security investment
text:
22.6 Executive decision records
A funding, expansion, pause, or acceptance decision needs enough context to be reviewed after staff, suppliers, or evidence change. Residual risk is the risk remaining after the selected measures. A decision condition is an event or threshold that changes an approval. A due date sets the date by which an action or review is expected.
NIST measurement guidance says a report can state the indicated risk and its fit with risk appetite. The report can also identify the needed decision and compliance concerns. It can record audit effects separately.10 CSF 2.0 calls for oversight results to adjust strategy and for risk responses to be selected, prioritized, tracked, and communicated.11 Legal and organizational authority determine who may accept a specific risk.
A decision condition makes approval contingent on an event or threshold. Expansion may depend on completing permission tests and resolving two critical supplier gaps. A due date keeps a temporary exception from becoming permanent through neglect. Teams can reuse the record and its reasoning in the sector cases in Chapter 23 and the whole-system review in Chapter 25.
Executive record trace. The decision record for Project A identifies the Chief Security Officer as the decision role, the six affected assistants, the 4 of 200 test result, the 110,000 exercise cost, and the remaining risk from untested connectors. It approves implementation for the six systems and requires a repeated authorization test before expansion. The application team is responsible for delivery by 30 November. A new action connector or a failed regression test pauses expansion and returns the decision for review. The observed output is a conditional funding decision that another reviewer can reconstruct from its inputs and limits.
Decision control. Before approval, the executive decision workflow checks the responsible authority, evidence date, scope, cost, due date, residual risk, and stop condition before recording approval. It rejects a record that lacks any required field. Quality is reconstructable decisions divided by all consequential decisions reviewed in the period. Preparation and challenge sessions consume leadership and technical time. Decisions made outside the record or based on stale evidence can bypass the check. Recovery suspends the affected approval and returns it to the stated role. Reconstructability does not prove that the judgment was optimal.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. The organization can fund Project B only by cancelling the test reserved in the Project A decision. Should it do so when Project B has higher possible harm but no local exposure or control-effectiveness result?
Conclusion. The present record does not support cancelling the test. Possible harm matters, but the missing exposure and effectiveness evidence prevents a comparable investment decision. The organization should keep required controls funded and complete the focused test. It should also record the condition that would move Project B ahead. This answer applies to the hypothetical evidence and budget, not to every high-impact risk.

title: Part VIII: Applying the method when systems change
text:
Chapters in this part
The final part tests whether readers can transfer the method to a new setting. Domain chapters should reuse the established concepts and add only the assumptions that change the analysis.
Connection through the book. Change a stated assumption in the established cases and explain which earlier conclusions survive. Sector and advanced cases exercise transfer of the method. The final capstone joins the branches around one system and one defensible release or recovery decision.
Part outcome. A defended system design and recovery decision, with clear explanations of which assumptions change in a new setting.
crumbs: Part VIII: Applying the method when systems change

title: Part VIII: Applying the method when systems change
text:
Adapting controls to the setting: This chapter transfers the reference frame to sector settings by stating which assets, duties, permissions, and consequences change before selecting controls.
Extending security when assumptions change: This chapter extends the method when physical access, participant trust, persistence, delegated authority, or systemic uncertainty invalidate earlier assumptions.
Defending a whole-system decision: This capstone requires a defensible whole-system decision that connects architecture, data, model and platform controls, authority, assurance, recovery, cost, and accountability.
crumbs: Part VIII: Applying the method when systems change

title: 23  Adapting controls to the setting
text:
23.1 Enterprise knowledge and customer support
Security question. Which assumptions, controls, and evidence change when the users, data, authority, and consequences change?
Organization setting. Each case is hypothetical. The examples isolate design differences and do not establish legal compliance, clinical safety, financial fitness, or product security.
Connection through the book. Chapter 22 supplied a common decision record. This chapter applies it to five settings, then compares what changed. Chapter 24 reopens the assumptions again for edge, federated, physical, persistent-agent, and frontier systems.
Compare every setting with the same fields before reading its details: user population, data, application authority, applicable duty, possible consequence, scale, fallback, and recovery path. When a field changes, review the related control and evidence claim again. Unchanged fields retain their earlier records.
An enterprise assistant may answer a low-impact policy question or expose another customer’s records through the same text interface. The analysis starts with the tenant boundary, retrieval boundary, user identity, eligible records, and any account action that the application can request. A disputed answer is an answer whose correctness or authority is challenged and resolved outside the model.
The NIST Privacy Framework calls for inventories of systems, roles, people, data actions, purposes, data elements, processing environments, and mapped interactions.1 The 2026 OWASP list separates prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, excessive agency, misinformation, and vector or embedding weaknesses for analysis.2 These frameworks organize the review. They do not show that a weakness exists in the hypothetical assistant or that a proposed control works.
The request path authenticates the employee and filters eligible records before retrieval. The application labels the source and generates an answer. It sends any proposed account action to a separate authorization service. A disputed answer returns to an authoritative record or responsible specialist. This relatively low physical-harm case supplies a comparison point for health information, where an answer can influence care.
Control review. The system of record checks the employee identity and tenant eligibility before returning a document, while the action service checks any account operation separately. Tests report denied cross-tenant requests over all unauthorized pairs and corrected disputed answers over all reviewed answers. Per-request checks, source links, and specialist review add latency and staff cost. Cached records or an alternate connector can bypass the intended route, and these tests cannot establish answer correctness for unreviewed topics. Recovery removes exposed context and revokes affected access. It restores the accepted connector and routes disputed work to the ordinary support process.
crumbs: Part VIII: Applying the method when systems change
23  Adapting controls to the setting

title: 23  Adapting controls to the setting
text:
23.2 Health information assistants
A health assistant changes the stakes when it reads regulated records or appears to direct care. Electronic protected health information means electronic health information within the legal scope of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). Clinical authority is permission and responsibility to make or direct a clinical decision. Role-appropriate access limits access to what a person’s assigned work requires.
Within its scope, the HIPAA Security Rule requires administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic protected health information, including access suited to assigned roles.3 The Department of Health and Human Services also requires periodic evaluation after environmental changes such as new technology or newly recognized risks.4 These duties address information security compliance. They do not establish clinical safety or model accuracy.
The hypothetical assistant may summarize an authorized patient’s record for a clinician but cannot diagnose, prescribe, or change an order. Identity, record scope, output labeling, clinical review, correction, and emergency fallback are separate control points. Clinical safety, medical-device scope, and evidence for human review still require use-specific regulation and clinical evaluation. Financial authority provides the next comparison because the system may initiate a reversible or irreversible monetary action.
Control review. The health-record system checks clinician identity, patient relationship, and requested fields. The clinical workflow treats the output as a draft and permits only an authorized clinician to enter an order. Tests report wrong-patient disclosures over all unauthorized patient pairs and unsupported statements over all reviewed summaries. Access checks and clinical review consume time and can delay care. Copied text, stale role data, or use outside the workflow can bypass the controls. Recovery removes the draft and corrects the record. The established clinical or emergency path remains active while staff investigate any affected decision. A passing information-security test does not establish clinical safety or legal compliance.
crumbs: Part VIII: Applying the method when systems change
23  Adapting controls to the setting

title: 23  Adapting controls to the setting
text:
23.3 Financial workflows
A financial assistant may classify an alert. Other configurations may prepare or approve a transfer. Those acts need different authority. Transaction authority is permission to initiate, approve, modify, or reverse a financial action. An approval limit sets the maximum value or action class an identity may approve. A reversal is a controlled action that restores an earlier financial state where the rules permit it.
Under the EU AI Act, specified systems used to evaluate a person’s creditworthiness or establish a credit score appear in Annex III, while systems used to detect financial fraud are excluded from that item.5 Classification still depends on intended use, conditions, exceptions, and applicable dates. CSF 2.0 calls for identities to be authenticated and for permissions and authorizations to be defined, enforced, reviewed, and separated by duty.6 Those general outcomes do not define payment rules or reversal rights.
In the hypothetical workflow, the model can explain an alert and prepare a proposed action. The payment system verifies the employee identity, amount, approval limit, separation of duties, and current account state before execution. Logs connect proposal, approval, execution, and reversal. A final case requires current banking, payment, securities, credit, and recordkeeping law for one jurisdiction. The public-service case adds legal effects, explanation, and challenge rights.
Financial action trace. The operating mode is inference with a proposed action, not autonomous execution. Employee E8 asks the assistant to prepare a 14,000 currency-unit transfer after reviewing a fraud alert. The assistant returns the proposed recipient, amount, and reason. The payment system then checks E8’s current identity and 10,000 approval limit. The intermediate decision is a denial followed by escalation to a second authorized employee. The observed result is no transfer and a linked proposal, denial, and escalation record. All values are hypothetical. The trace shows that fluent financial text does not replace transaction authority.
Control review. The payment system checks current identity, amount, approval limit, separated approval, recipient state, and transaction status. It allows, denies, or holds the transfer and records each decision. Tests report unauthorized transfers over all attempted restricted transfers and mistaken denials over all allowed cases. Independent approval and reversal capacity add cost and delay. Shared credentials, a second payment route, or a stale limit can bypass the path. Recovery cancels pending work and reverses eligible transactions. It freezes affected credentials and escalates irreversible loss. A zero-failure test does not establish performance against untested fraud or operational error.

23  Adapting controls to the setting

title: 23  Adapting controls to the setting
text:
23.4 Public-sector services
A public service may affect access to benefits or a person’s legal status. It can also influence emergency response or access to justice. Contestability is the ability to challenge a decision and seek correction or review. A legal effect changes a person’s legal rights, duties, or status. Accessibility is the ability of people with differing needs to use the service.
EU AI Act Annex III includes specified uses involving essential public benefits, emergency response, law enforcement, migration, justice, and democratic processes.7 Article 86 provides a limited explanation right when a covered Annex III high-risk system contributes to a decision with legal effects or comparably serious adverse effects.8 Both claims have express conditions, exceptions, and dates. They do not create a general explanation right for every public-sector output.
The hypothetical service keeps the AI output as reviewable input to an authorized decision process. The record identifies the legal basis, evidence, human authority, explanation route, correction path, accessibility needs, and appeal mechanism. This setting emphasizes bounded public authority. The consumer-platform case changes the scale and permits open user access, which shifts attention toward abuse volume and resource limits.
Control review. The case-management system checks the legal basis, required evidence, authorized official, notice, and challenge status before a consequential decision takes effect. It approves, returns, or blocks the decision and preserves the record used. Tests report complete notices and successful challenge routing over all consequential cases in scope, plus decisions corrected after review. Accessibility and human review add time and service cost. Informal channels, incomplete records, or inaccessible notices can defeat the process. Because process evidence does not prove the underlying decision was lawful or correct, recovery pauses the effect where permitted and corrects the record. The person then enters the established review or appeal path.
crumbs: Part VIII: Applying the method when systems change
23  Adapting controls to the setting

title: 23  Adapting controls to the setting
text:
23.5 Consumer platforms
An open consumer platform receives high request volume from users whose identity, intent, and content are uncertain. Account abuse is unauthorized or deceptive use of a user account. Impersonation and automated sign-up can occur alongside harmful content. Tool misuse or resource exhaustion may follow even when each request appears minor.
OWASP describes its August 2026 Large Language Model (LLM) Top 10 as a community guide to critical risks in LLM-powered applications.9 Its 2026 list treats excessive agency and unbounded consumption as distinct application risks.10 The list supplies a taxonomy. Prevalence and mitigation effectiveness require separate evidence.
The application can bind rate limits to accounts, devices, payment state, and action classes. It can require stronger verification before consequential actions and give users a reporting path. A hypothetical limit of one hundred requests per hour remains only a design value until load and abuse tests show its effects on legitimate work, attack cost, and service availability. The cross-setting comparison includes this unresolved evidence.
Rate-limit comparison. A hypothetical test replays the same 1,000 ordinary requests and 500 automated abuse requests under limits of 50, 100, and 200 requests per account per hour. The intermediate record separates blocked abuse, blocked ordinary work, queue time, and account switching. At 50, the system blocks more abuse but also blocks a simulated support surge. At 200, it permits more abuse. The test does not choose a universal value because device identity, distributed accounts, and real demand remain uncertain. Its conclusion is that the selected limit needs both abuse and legitimate-work evidence under the platform’s operating conditions.
Control review. The gateway checks account, device, payment state, request rate, and action class before admitting work. It allows, slows, challenges, or blocks the request. The test reports blocked abuse over all simulated abuse and blocked ordinary work over all ordinary requests, together with queue time and infrastructure cost. Stronger checks increase user friction and support demand. Distributed accounts or shared infrastructure can bypass or overwhelm the limit, while the replay cannot estimate real abuse prevalence or prove resilience at a larger scale. Recovery reduces expensive features and protects essential paths. Legitimate users receive a support route.

title: 23  Adapting controls to the setting
text:
23.6 Comparison across cases
Each case uses the same system-mapping method, but its assets, authority, duties, error costs, and recovery evidence differ. A transfer analysis compares what changes when a design enters another setting. Oversight depth combines the frequency, authority, and technical detail of human review.
The AI Risk Management Framework states that risk management is tailored to context and that priorities account for organizational goals, affected people, legal requirements, and available resources.11 CSF 2.0 also states that implementation varies with risk, tolerance, mission, technology, and requirements.12 These sources support tailoring. They do not rank the hypothetical cases or make their controls equivalent.
The method remains constant while each case changes the facts. Enterprise support emphasizes tenant and retrieval separation. Health adds regulated records and clinical boundaries. Finance adds transaction authority and reversal. Public services add legal effects and contestability. Consumer platforms add open access and scale. This analysis shows which assumptions need renewed examination when Chapter 24 introduces exposed devices, distributed training, physical action, persistent agents, and frontier capabilities.
Sector comparison. Each row below changes one condition in the recurring hypothetical organization. It does not establish legal compliance or rank sectors.

The comparison uses the same mapping method while changing the user population, data, authority, consequence, and expected evidence. A control transfers only when those conditions and its mechanism remain the same.
Transfer control. The architecture review compares the source and target setting for data, identity, authority, duty, consequence, operating scale, fallback, and recovery. It accepts a control unchanged only when its enforcing component and checked state remain valid. The measure is retested transferred controls over all controls reused in the target setting. Reassessment adds delivery and specialist cost. Superficial similarity can hide a changed legal or physical condition. Because successful transfer of one control does not validate the rest of the design, recovery withdraws the transferred approval and returns the task to the prior setting or manual route.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. Move the enterprise support assistant into the health-information setting. Which parts of the earlier design can remain, and which decision must be reopened first?
Answer. Identity checks, source links, retrieval filtering, and a disputed-answer route can remain as candidate controls. Their tests must use health-record roles and data. Authority must be reviewed first. An employee-support answer cannot become clinical direction merely because the same model and retrieval pattern are used. The organization needs current legal scope, clinical evaluation, authorized oversight, correction, and emergency fallback before approving the changed use.

title: 24  Extending security when assumptions change
text:
24.1 Edge deployment
Security question. Which controls and evidence stop applying when access, time, location, coordination, or possible impact changes?
Organization setting. The examples are hypothetical extensions of the organization used throughout the book. Each section changes one major condition and keeps the resulting evidence limit explicit.
Connection through the book. Chapter 23 showed that context changes control choices. This chapter examines settings where the technical assumptions also change. Chapter 25 requires the reader to state those assumptions in a complete system decision.
For each branch, record the earlier assumption and the changed condition. Then identify the affected control and the new possible failure. Record which evidence must be collected again. The final comparison uses these fields for every branch.
A centrally operated application can rely on a stable network and controlled facilities. It can also send records to consolidated logs. An edge deployment runs a model or AI application on or near the device that supplies data or receives action. Offline operation continues without a remote dependency. A device security state reports if security functions operate as expected.
NIST’s Internet of Things baseline covers protection of stored and transmitted data, limits on local and network interfaces, authenticated software updates, rollback, and reporting of device security state.1 The same baseline permits local or remote updates and requires verification and authentication. It also includes authorized rollback.2 It does not establish protection of AI weights or select a cryptographic design for a specific device.
The threat model now includes physical access, extracted secrets, intermittent links, delayed revocation, limited storage, and lost telemetry. A hypothetical inspection camera may continue inference while disconnected, but it can accept only a signed model version and records enough state to reconcile after reconnection. A rollback also has to match the compatible software and data state. Edge operation changes location and connectivity. Federated learning changes who computes training updates and what the coordinator can inspect. Both changes reopen parts of the Chapter 1 system record, but neither requires the other.
Control review. The device boot and update service checks software and model identity, signature, compatible state, local authorization, and offline budget. It runs, holds, or restores the accepted package and records the decision for later reconciliation. Tests report rejected unauthorized packages over all attempted packages, bounded offline actions over all offline actions, and time to reconcile after reconnection. Secure storage, update capacity, and retained logs add hardware and operating cost. Extracted signing keys, damaged sensors, or full device compromise can defeat a control whose checks cover only specified physical attacks. Recovery enters the specified safe mode and restores a verified package. It rotates keys and reconciles records.
crumbs: Part VIII: Applying the method when systems change
24  Extending security when assumptions change

title: 24  Extending security when assumptions change
text:
24.2 Federated learning
Federated learning is training in which participants compute local updates and a coordinating process combines them. Raw training records can remain on participant devices. Client updates and participant selection still create disclosure and manipulation paths, as do aggregation and the resulting model.
McMahan and colleagues described Federated Averaging as a process that samples clients and runs local updates. A server then forms a weighted average.3 Secure aggregation is a protocol that reveals an allowed aggregate while hiding individual participant values under a stated threat model. Bonawitz and colleagues evaluated such a protocol under specified honest-but-curious, active-adversary, and dropout assumptions.4 The protocol does not detect a malicious update merely because that update is hidden.
A model replacement attack scales a malicious local update to steer the next combined model. Bagdasaryan and colleagues evaluated model-replacement backdoors in tasks where an attacker controlled one or a few participants and their submitted updates.5 Those results apply to the tested models, data, aggregation, and attacker access. Distributed computation changes which parties can see or change training, and the next section adds physical consequences to that trust problem.
Changed-assumption trace. The base training design assumes one controlled data store and one training operator. The hypothetical federated design changes the input path: ten branches compute updates from local records, and the coordinator receives only submitted updates. In one round, nine branches submit updates near the previous direction while branch B7 submits an update with much larger magnitude. The record for the intermediate state includes participant identity, update norm, aggregation rule, and resulting model version. Secure aggregation could hide individual values from the coordinator under its threat model, but it would not show that B7’s update is benign. The observed result is a model candidate that requires robustness and backdoor evaluation before release. The values and branch behavior are exercise assumptions.
Control review. The coordinator checks participant eligibility, round identity, submitted format, allowed contribution, aggregate result, and candidate-model tests before release. It either accepts the round or rejects the candidate. A rejection restores the prior model. Measures report accepted participants over all scheduled participants, rejected rounds over all rounds, and security-test failures over all candidate cases. Secure aggregation and repeated evaluation add communication and compute cost. Colluding participants, hidden malicious updates, or a test blind spot can defeat the design. Recovery discards the candidate and revokes affected participants. Training resumes from the accepted model. A passed aggregate and test set do not prove that individual updates were benign or private outside the protocol assumptions.
crumbs: Part VIII: Applying the method when systems change
24  Extending security when assumptions change

title: 24  Extending security when assumptions change
text:
24.3 Embodied and cyber-physical systems
A model output becomes a safety concern when software can move equipment or alter a process. A cyber-physical system joins computing, communication, people, and physical components. An actuator changes the physical process. A safe state is a specified physical condition selected to limit harm after a fault or loss of control.
NIST describes operational technology as systems that detect or cause direct changes in physical devices, processes, and events. Such systems have distinct safety, reliability, availability, and performance requirements.6 Its guidance says safety-critical systems need detection of unsafe conditions, movement toward safe conditions, and often human oversight. It also discusses fail-to-a-known-state design and independent non-digital safeguards.7 These are general design considerations. Evidence for one architecture still requires system-specific tests.
In a hypothetical warehouse, an AI model may propose a route while a separate controller enforces speed, zone, load, and emergency-stop limits without depending on the model’s explanation. Tests include sensor failure, stale state, lost communication, and unsafe commands. Physical supervision makes time and authority limits visible, which prepares the analysis of agents that retain state across extended work.
Control review. The independent controller checks current sensor state, route command, speed, zone, load, and communication status. It allows a bounded motion or changes the command. An unsafe state moves the equipment to the specified safe state. Tests report blocked unsafe commands over all injected unsafe commands, mistaken stops over all allowed scenarios, and time to safe state. Independent hardware, validation, and downtime add cost. Shared sensors, common power loss, or a failed actuator can bypass the intended separation. Recovery isolates the equipment and uses the physical emergency path. Motion resumes only after a verified reset. These tests are part of a safety case, not proof of complete physical safety.

title: 24  Extending security when assumptions change
text:
24.4 Long-running agents
A short request ends when the response returns. A long-running agent retains state or authority across multiple tasks or an extended period. A stale permission no longer matches the current task, role, or risk. Reauthorization is a new decision that confirms or changes continued access or action authority.
OWASP’s agentic risk taxonomy separates identity and privilege abuse, memory and context poisoning, tool misuse, and cascading failures.8 Zero trust architecture bases access decisions on the subject, resource, and current context rather than network location alone.9 The taxonomy does not measure prevalence, and zero trust guidance does not set goal refresh or memory retention periods for AI agents.
The control loop binds credentials, memory, remaining budget, and allowed actions to a current task state. Time expiry, role change, unexpected resource growth, or a new action class can trigger reauthorization. The packet contains no peer-reviewed or standards-based evaluation that establishes the right intervals, memory expiration, or resource caps. Those values remain hypotheses for system-specific testing. Delegation across multiple agents adds message and conflict problems to the same state-management challenge.
Changed-assumption trace. The earlier assistant handled one request with credentials that expired after the response. The hypothetical long-running version works for eight hours, retains a task queue, and can create support tickets. At hour four, the employee changes role and loses access to customer C44. The agent’s next step attempts to reuse the earlier customer context. Reauthorization checks the current employee role and rejects the customer access. It removes the queued action and records the stale context reference. The observed result is a denied action rather than a carried-over permission. The four-hour point and eight-hour duration are test values. They do not establish suitable intervals for another system.
Control review. The authorization service checks the current employee role, task state, retained context, credential age, action class, and remaining resource budget before each consequential step. It permits, changes, or stops the step and records discarded state. Tests report denied stale actions over all stale-action attempts, orphaned tasks over all interrupted tasks, and cleanup time. Reauthorization and state review add latency and storage work. An alternate tool path, shared token, or hidden memory store can bypass the loop, and the test cannot establish the right reauthorization interval for another workload. Recovery revokes credentials and clears or quarantines retained state. Work restarts from an approved checkpoint.
crumbs: Part VIII: Applying the method when systems change
24  Extending security when assumptions change

title: 24  Extending security when assumptions change
text:
24.5 Multi-agent systems
A multi-agent design divides work among several software actors. A delegation chain records how one actor grants another limited authority. An inter-agent message encodes information, a request, or an instruction sent between agents. Conflicting authority exists when two instructions or permissions cannot both be followed safely.
OWASP’s agentic taxonomy includes insecure inter-agent communication and cascading failures alongside identity, privilege, and memory risks.10 CSF 2.0 calls for service identities and credentials to be managed and for permissions and authorizations to be defined, enforced, reviewed, and separated by duty.11 These sources do not establish a standard multi-agent architecture or resolve conflicting goals and message meaning.
The system needs authenticated senders and typed messages. Bounded delegation and conflict rules constrain behavior. Separate action authorization limits the resulting operations. Records connect a final action to its delegation chain. A hypothetical research agent can ask a retrieval agent for documents but cannot transfer its own write permission. The packet still lacks a primary specification or evaluated system covering authentication, delegation, conflict, and audit assumptions together. This distributed uncertainty provides a contrast for frontier release decisions.
Control review. The message gateway checks sender identity, message type, task identifier, delegated rights, expiry, and conflict state. The action service then checks the final operation against the complete delegation chain. It permits, rejects, or escalates the request. Tests report rejected forged messages over all forged cases and blocked excess rights over all delegation attempts. Signing, policy checks, and trace storage add latency and compute cost. Shared credentials, colluding agents, or ambiguous message meaning can defeat parts of the scheme. Because these checks do not prove that the agents share a correct goal, recovery stops the chain and revokes delegated credentials. It restores the last accepted task state and replays the trace.

title: 24  Extending security when assumptions change
text:
24.6 Frontier capabilities and release choices
Past test results become weaker evidence when a model’s capabilities, access, or deployment scale move beyond the evaluated range. In the Seoul commitments, frontier AI refers to highly capable general-purpose models or systems near the most advanced capability level. Systemic risk is a legal or governance category whose meaning depends on the controlling source.
The 2024 Seoul commitments ask participating organizations to assess severe risks across the lifecycle, define assessable thresholds, specify mitigations, and avoid development or deployment when residual risk cannot be kept below those thresholds.12 These voluntary commitments have no legal force, and publication does not establish implementation by each organization. The European Commission states that the Safety and Security chapter of the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice applies only to providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk under Article 55.13 The code is voluntary, while binding duties come from the AI Act.
A release record connects capability evidence, attacker access, misuse tests, safeguard results, deployment scale, and uncertainty to a release threshold. No universal capability threshold or reliable rule for extending laboratory results to every deployment was found in the packet. The decision remains specific to the organization, model, use, law, and available evidence. Chapter 25 makes those assumptions and unresolved needs part of the final whole-system decision.
Release control. The release authority checks each specified capability threshold, attacker-access condition, safeguard result, deployment scale, legal duty, and unresolved uncertainty. It either allows a restricted stage or holds release. An active deployment can also be stopped. Coverage is supported release claims divided by all claims required for the decision, with failed and missing evidence retained. Evaluation, restricted staging, and rollback capacity consume substantial staff and compute. Unknown capabilities, weak tests, or access outside the staged boundary can defeat the decision. Because meeting the selected thresholds does not prove that every severe risk is absent, recovery withdraws access and restores the last accepted model and system configuration. The assessment then reopens.

title: 25  Defending a whole-system decision
text:
25.1 The shared case
Security question. Can a technical team defend an AI system decision with evidence that management, legal, operations, and affected-person reviewers can examine?
Organization setting. The capstone organization and incident are hypothetical. Case facts are fixed so different designs can be compared, while uncertain facts remain explicit research or testing needs.
Connection through the book. Chapters 1 through 24 supplied the concepts and evidence methods used here. The final review tests if those parts form one coherent decision rather than separate checklists.
A capstone becomes unreviewable when each participant assumes a different system. A shared case is one fixed hypothetical system used across several assignments. A case fact is an assumption supplied by the exercise rather than inferred by the reader. An operating budget fixes the resources available for deployment and control work.
The AI Risk Management Framework calls for intended purpose, context, users, requirements, task, and system assumptions to be understood and documented before risk is measured and managed.1 The framework does not supply this scenario. The following statements are exercise assumptions rather than claims about a real organization.
The organization operates an employee support assistant. It retrieves internal policy and customer records, uses an external model service, and can prepare but cannot approve account changes. Five hundred employees use it. Customer data stays within approved regions. The annual operating and control budget is fixed at 600,000 currency units. The system needs a manual support fallback and a tested two-hour recovery objective. These facts freeze the boundary for the design assignment.
crumbs: Part VIII: Applying the method when systems change
25  Defending a whole-system decision

title: 25  Defending a whole-system decision
text:
25.2 Design assignment
A defensible design connects each control to a stated asset, attacker capability, and consequence. A system map identifies components, actors, stores, trust boundaries, and data or action flows. A threat model states attacker goals, access, knowledge, limits, and target assets. A control tradeoff records both the benefit and cost created by a security choice.
International guidance for secure AI puts threat modeling, model choice, and secure design across the lifecycle. It also covers asset tracking, supply chain controls, deployment protection, incident procedures, and secure operation.2 The AI Risk Management Framework also connects task, requirements, human oversight, legal and third-party risk, security evaluation, deactivation authority, and supplier monitoring.3 These sources identify work to cover. They do not determine the correct capstone architecture.
The assignment produces a diagram or structured record of the request, retrieval, model, output, proposed action, authorization, logging, and support paths. It states why each identity and permission exists, which component enforces each limit, and what evidence would show failure. The result is a testable design rather than an assertion of safety. Its claims and permissions become the input to assurance.
Learner packet and deliverables. The learner receives the case facts in the preceding section, the staged evidence in the next three sections, and an annual budget of 600,000 currency units. Every number is hypothetical. The completed packet contains five linked deliverables:

System and data map: users, application, identity service, policy index, customer-record connector, external model service, action proposal, approval service, logs, supplier boundary, and manual support path.
Threat record: one request-only attacker and one attacker-edited retrieved document. It also contains one compromised connector. Each entry states access, target asset, unwanted outcome, entry point, and evidence that would confirm or reject the path.
Control table: the enforcing component, input, decision, allowed result, denied result, log record, bypass test, and recovery action for retrieval and account-change controls.
Deployment and cost record: hosted and self-hosted options evaluated under the same task, permissions, acceptance thresholds, service requirements, and cost units.
Responsibility record: the roles for retrieval eligibility and account-change approval. It also states the supplier duty, the residual-risk authority, open legal questions, and the review trigger.

The learner assigns a stable identifier to every component, claim, test, and decision. A control row must point back to a threat path and forward to an assurance case. A cost entry without a period and unit remains incomplete. This structure makes each later conclusion traceable to the fixed case rather than to an unstated system.
Whole-book coverage record. The capstone does not force every earlier mechanism into this case. For each branch, the learner records applied, not applicable with a reason, or requires new evidence.

title: 25  Defending a whole-system decision
text:
25.3 Assurance assignment
A design claim becomes credible only when the test matches its conditions. An assurance claim is a specific statement about behavior or risk supported by reviewable evidence. An acceptance threshold is the measured result required by an acceptance criterion before a test passes. A rollback trigger is an observed condition that returns the system to an earlier accepted state.
The AI Risk Management Framework calls for validity and reliability under expected conditions and for security and resilience to be evaluated and documented.4 NIST measurement guidance states that a measure includes its data source, calculation, collection timing, responsible parties, and reporting context. It separates implementation, effectiveness, efficiency, and impact.5 The capstone still needs its own cases, sample size, and release threshold.
The assignment combines ordinary tasks, adversarial retrieval content, cross-customer access attempts, tool-permission tests, supplier failure, and recovery exercises. Each test records inputs, model and application versions, intermediate decisions, expected result, observed result, and uncertainty. A pass supports only the stated claim under those conditions. These expectations allow the incident assignment to expose contradictions and missing evidence.

The learner can calculate the cross-customer failure rate as 1 divided by 12 for this small exercise set. That result is about 8.3 percent, but the small, constructed sample does not estimate a production rate. Stage B blocks release because the acceptance threshold is zero unauthorized records in the stated test. Stage D also fails its stated two-hour objective. These results define the evidence that the incident and recovery work must explain.
Assurance control. The test runner checks the fixed configuration, case identifiers, expected result, observed result, and acceptance threshold before it issues a pass. It reports each failure over every assigned case, never only over successful responses. Running adversarial cases, review, and fallback exercises consumes model, infrastructure, and staff time. Incomplete logs, changed versions, or cases that omit a real attack path can produce weak evidence. Failure at any stage blocks release and returns the system to the prior accepted state or manual path. Success supports only the stated claim, configuration, and case population.

title: 25  Defending a whole-system decision
text:
25.4 Incident assignment
The hypothetical incident begins with a customer record shown to the wrong employee after a retrieved document contains hostile instructions. Logs also show a recent connector change, so prompt injection and authorization failure are competing explanations. The incident analysis identifies affected users, systems, data, actions, and time, then preserves evidence before changing the system.
NIST incident-response guidance calls for event sequencing, root-cause analysis, recorded response actions, protected evidence, and an estimate of incident scope.6 It also calls for containment and eradication and includes suppliers in planning, response, and recovery where relevant.7 These outcomes do not identify the cause or select one containment action for this case.
The assignment builds a timeline from application, identity, retrieval, model, connector, and supplier records. It distinguishes direct observations from inferences and lists evidence that would reject each explanation. Containment may disable the affected connector and restrict retrieval. It may also revoke credentials or suspend the assistant while preserving the manual path. The resulting scope, changes, and unresolved uncertainty define the recovery work.

The incident lead immediately disables connector K7 and preserves its logs and configuration. The service credential is revoked, and users move to manual support. The main explanations are hostile document influence, connector authorization failure, or both. The hostile text explains why the output may have followed an instruction. It does not by itself explain how C44 entered the eligible set. The connector records and cache test are necessary before assigning the root cause.
Incident control. The incident lead checks affected identities, customers, records, connector versions, actions, and time range before narrowing scope. The response allows only evidence-preserving containment actions approved for the case. Coverage is examined customer-record accesses divided by all accesses through K7 during the suspected period, with missing logs recorded. Manual support and evidence preservation add service delay and staff cost. Incomplete supplier logs or another connector can hide part of the incident. Because containment limits further exposure but does not prove the root cause or the full affected population, recovery isolates K7 and rotates its credential. The competing explanations are tested before restoration.
crumbs: Part VIII: Applying the method when systems change
25  Defending a whole-system decision

title: 25  Defending a whole-system decision
text:
25.5 Recovery assignment
Restoring service is not the same as starting an old copy. A restoration point is the specific known-good state selected for rebuilding or recovery. Credential rotation replaces authentication material and revokes the old material. Return-to-service evidence consists of checks showing that the specified recovery and acceptance conditions are met.
NIST’s incident-response profile calls for recovery actions and backup-integrity verification before restoration. It also calls for checks on restored assets and documentation of completion against incident criteria.8 Secure-AI guidance recommends versioning models, data, prompts, software, and related records so they can be restored to a known-good state.9 A recorded version still needs integrity and suitability checks before reuse.
The assignment identifies the configurations, index, software, secrets, and logs that need restoration or replacement. It retests authorization and customer separation, then verifies the manual fallback. Any unresolved risk enters the final record. Recovery evidence and remaining risk then enter the joint decision review.
Executable recovery trace. The recovery target is the last accepted connector version K6 with policy index P12, application version A4, and a new service credential. The learner records each step and result:

Preserve K7, its cache, identity decisions, retrieval records, and hashes as incident evidence.
Restore K6 and P12 in an isolated environment. Verify the recorded versions before use.
Rotate the connector credential and verify that the old credential is rejected.
Replay the 12 customer-separation cases, including E17 requesting C44. The required result is 12 denials and no returned customer record.
Replay the 10 hostile-document cases. The action service must continue to reject every unapproved account action. Output failures remain separate findings.
Run the manual support path and then restore the automated service within the two-hour objective.

In the hypothetical rerun, all 12 separation cases are denied, the old credential fails, no account action executes, and automated service returns after 92 minutes. The intermediate records link each result to K6, P12, A4, and the new credential. The recovery test now meets its stated thresholds. It does not resolve why two hostile documents changed summaries, and it does not prove that untested customers or attacks are safe. That remaining output risk enters the joint decision.
Return-to-service control. The recovery lead checks artifact identity, credential rejection, all 12 separation cases, all 10 action cases, fallback readiness, and the two-hour objective. It restores the restricted service only when every mandatory condition passes. The report keeps failures over the full assigned sets and records manual-support hours during recovery. Preserving standby staff and an accepted restoration point raises ongoing cost. Hidden retained data, an untested connector path, or a shared dependency can defeat the restored boundary. A later failure pauses service and returns work to manual support. Meeting these conditions does not close the unresolved hostile-summary finding.
crumbs: Part VIII: Applying the method when systems change
25  Defending a whole-system decision

title: 25  Defending a whole-system decision
text:
25.6 Joint decision review
Technical evidence, business value, legal duty, cost, and affected-person impact can point in different directions. A joint decision review brings technical and organizational roles to the same proposal and evidence. Accepted risk is specified remaining risk approved by an authorized role. Explanatory feedback states the evidence and reasoning behind an assessment.
The AI Risk Management Framework assigns executive leadership responsibility for AI risk decisions and connects priorities, resources, response, monitoring, and continual improvement across GOVERN and MANAGE.10 CSF 2.0 is intended to help executives, managers, technical staff, risk staff, lawyers, and auditors communicate through common cybersecurity outcomes.11 A common structure does not guarantee agreement or make the decision correct.
The review records approval, restriction, pause, or rejection, together with conditions, due dates, accepted risk, and unresolved evidence needs. The grading and role-weighting method was created for this exercise and still needs piloting. It is not presented as an empirically validated decision process. The book ends with a reviewable whole-system decision and an explicit list of what remains uncertain.
Scoring rubric. The rubric checks the completeness and reasoning of the capstone packet. It is an instructional scoring method without empirical validation as a safety score.



Table 25.4: Capstone scoring rubric.










Area
Full-credit evidence
Points

15


Threat reasoning

15

Enforcing component, decision input, bypass test, failure result, and recovery link
15


Assurance

20


Incident and recovery

15

Missing reasoning loses credit even in a polished submission. This includes a diagram without an explanatory record, a control without an enforcing component, a test without an expected result, or a conclusion that reaches beyond its evidence.
Annotated decision. The hypothetical review issues a restricted approval for the restored K6 configuration. The decision is annotated as follows:

Approved task: employee support answers using policy and eligible customer records. This matches the tested inference mode.
Action limit: the assistant may prepare an account-change request but cannot approve or execute it. Stage C supports this boundary only for the ten tested hostile documents.
Required configuration: connector K6, policy index P12, application A4, and the rotated credential. The recovery rerun is tied to these versions.
Accepted risk: summaries can still follow hostile document text. The organization accepts this only for nonconsequential drafts under employee review while a stronger output test and control are developed.
Rejected expansion: autonomous account action and connector K7 remain outside approval. The evidence does not support either change.
Review conditions: any connector, permission, model, data-region, or action change reopens the decision. A customer-separation failure or recovery time above two hours pauses the service.
Open evidence: the organization still needs broader customer-separation cases and a supported hostile-document evaluation. It also needs current legal review for its locations and practical supplier-exit evidence.

The decision follows from the staged evidence, not from a claim that the system is safe in general. It permits a useful task within the recovered boundary and leaves failed or untested claims outside approval.
Ongoing decision control. The service owner checks the required configuration, customer-separation result, recovery time, action log, supplier notice, and open hostile-summary finding at each review trigger. The owner continues, restricts, or pauses the service and records the decision authority. Measures use failures over all cases or actions in the stated period and include manual-support cost. A missing notice, incomplete log, or decision outside the review path can preserve a stale approval. Because continued approval does not extend to a new connector, model, region, permission, or action, recovery invokes the manual route and restores the accepted configuration. The affected evidence stages then repeat.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. A learner scores 92 points but recommends full autonomous account changes because the action service blocked all ten hostile-document attempts. Is the recommendation defensible?
Answer. No. The tested action boundary is supported only for the current configuration and case set. The evaluation omits autonomous approval and broader attacks. It also omits mistaken ordinary requests and recovery from a harmful action. The recommendation also conflicts with the fixed case, which allows preparation but not approval. The score cannot override a failed scope argument. A defensible decision keeps autonomous action outside approval and states the evidence required to reconsider it.

The opening question has a conditional answer. A team can defend a decision when it states the system and assumptions. Each risk must link to an enforcing component and a test. Every conclusion must stay within the available evidence, with decision authority and a recovery route recorded. When the model, data, operator, access, task, or consequence changes, the affected branch of the record requires review again.
